docs.title: PSScriptBuilder
docs.text:
PSScriptBuilder A PowerShell module that builds a single deployable script from multi-file projects — with automatic dependency resolution, topological sorting, and integrated release management.

  • Getting Started

    The fastest path from zero to a working, dependency-ordered script — install the module, scaffold a project, and run your first build.

    Getting Started

  • Tutorials

    End-to-end walkthroughs for three independent scenarios: a first project, migrating existing code, and release management.

    Tutorials

  • Guides

    In-depth explanations grouped by area: building a script, analyzing its structure, and publishing a release.

    Guides

  • Reference

    Complete reference for every public cmdlet and the PowerShell types they return — parameters, outputs, and properties.

    Reference

  • Examples

    Seventeen runnable examples from a simple function build to a full release workflow.

    Examples

  • Troubleshooting

    Common problems and their solutions, covering builds, configuration, templates, and environment diagnostics.

    Troubleshooting

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Seventeen standalone, runnable examples cover the complete PSScriptBuilder feature set — designed to be read and run in order. Each example introduces one or two new concepts and builds on the previous ones, from a minimal function-only build up to a full workflow with release management and module output. Examples 01-08 use an HR domain, examples 09-12 use an AppConfig domain. Example 13 uses PSScriptBuilder's own source code as the analysis subject. Example 14 demonstrates the cold-start scaffolding workflow with New-PSScriptBuilderProject. Example 15 demonstrates real-time file watching with Watch-PSScriptBuilderProject. Example 16 demonstrates the source map feature: generating a .sourcemap.json sidecar and resolving runtime errors in the compiled output back to their originating source files. Example 17 demonstrates code coverage translation: mapping a Pester CodeCoverage result, measured against the built output, back to per-source-file coverage. The examples are part of the PSScriptBuilder repository on GitHub and must be cloned locally before running them — see Prerequisites.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Clone the repository before running any example:

git clone https://github.com/PSScriptBuilder/PSScriptBuilder
cd PSScriptBuilder

Each example is then run from its own folder:

cd examples/01-functions-only
.\Run-Example.ps1

Run in a fresh PowerShell session

The using module statement loads types into the current session. Reloading or switching between examples in the same session can cause type conflicts. Always open a new PowerShell window or terminal tab before running each example.

Example 17 requires Pester

Example 17 runs a Pester test suite to demonstrate code coverage translation and requires Pester 5.0 or later (Install-Module Pester -MinimumVersion 5.0 -Scope CurrentUser). No other example needs Pester.

docs.title: 01 - Functions Only
docs.text:
The simplest possible build: a FunctionCollector scans a source folder, extracts all function definitions, and replaces the {{FUNCTION_DEFINITIONS}} placeholder in the template. No enums, no classes, no configuration file — just the essential build pipeline.

examples/01-functions-only

docs.title: 02 - Classes and Enums
docs.text:
Introduces EnumCollector and ClassCollector. PSScriptBuilder analyzes the class hierarchy, builds a dependency graph, and topologically sorts all components before writing them to the output file. Base classes always appear before derived classes — no manual ordering required.

examples/02-classes-and-enums

docs.title: 03 - With Configuration
docs.text:
Introduces psscriptbuilder.config.json. Template and output paths are read from the configuration file via Get-PSScriptBuilderConfiguration instead of being hardcoded. The source content is identical to Example 02 — only the build setup changes.

examples/03-with-configuration

docs.title: 04 - Flexible File Structure
docs.text:
Shows that PSScriptBuilder does not care how source files are organized. Enums, classes, and functions are deliberately mixed in the same files. Each collector uses AST parsing to extract exactly the component type it is responsible for, regardless of file structure.

examples/04-flexible-file-structure

docs.title: 05 - All Collectors
docs.text:
Demonstrates all five collector types in a single build:

  • UsingCollector — extracts and deduplicates using namespace statements
  • FileCollector — injects raw file content (headers, configuration blocks) via custom collection keys
  • EnumCollector, ClassCollector, FunctionCollector — as before

examples/05-all-collectors

docs.title: 06 - Hybrid Mode
docs.text:
The template uses only the {{ORDERED_COMPONENTS}} placeholder instead of separate {{ENUM_DEFINITIONS}}, {{CLASS_DEFINITIONS}}, and {{FUNCTION_DEFINITIONS}} placeholders. Because no cross-dependencies exist in this project, PSScriptBuilder activates Hybrid Mode: all components are emitted as a single topologically-sorted block.

Get-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis is called before the build to make the selected mode visible.

examples/06-hybrid-mode

docs.title: 07 - Ordered Mode
docs.text:
Some projects have a class method that calls a standalone function — here, Employee's own ToString() calls Format-EmployeeDisplayName. That function needs a class (Person) but is itself needed by another class (Employee), so the topological sort must interleave classes and functions — separate {{CLASS_DEFINITIONS}} and {{FUNCTION_DEFINITIONS}} placeholders are no longer sufficient. PSScriptBuilder detects this automatically and requires {{ORDERED_COMPONENTS}}, activating Ordered Mode.

Get-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis is called before the build to show HasCrossDependencies: True and the interleaved OrderedComponents sequence.

examples/07-ordered-mode

docs.title: 08 - Cycle Detection
docs.text:
Deliberately introduces a circular Inheritance dependency (ServiceA → ServiceB → ServiceC → ServiceA). PSScriptBuilder detects the cycle during dependency analysis and fails fast with a descriptive error message that includes the full cycle path. No partial output file is written.

Note: only fatal cycles — Inheritance and StaticInitializer — cause a build failure. Type reference cycles (classes referencing each other in method bodies) are valid in PowerShell 5.1 and are resolved automatically.

Get-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis is used before the build to inspect the HasCycles and CyclePath properties of the result.

examples/08-cycle-detection

docs.title: 09 - Module Build
docs.text:
Introduces module output: instead of building a standalone .ps1 script, PSScriptBuilder generates a .psm1 module file that can be loaded with using module. A separate Demo-Module.ps1 script loads the built module and demonstrates its types and functions.

The type check at the end of the demo ($entry.GetType().Name) shows that PowerShell class types defined in the module are fully available — which is only possible when the module is loaded via using module, not Import-Module.

examples/09-module-build

docs.title: 10 - Multiple Collectors
docs.text:
Shows how to use multiple collectors of the same type to model a layered project structure. A logging framework is split into a Core layer (LogLevel, LogEntry, LogFormatter, LoggerBase) and an Extensions layer (ConsoleLogger, FileLogger). Each layer gets its own Class collector and Function collector with a distinct CollectionKey. Five template placeholders ({{CoreEnums}}, {{CoreClasses}}, {{CoreFunctions}}, {{ExtensionClasses}}, {{ExtensionFunctions}}) control the output order explicitly.

Write-Log deliberately constructs [LogEntry]::new(...) directly instead of calling a New-LogEntry factory function, specifically to avoid an unrelated function-to-function ordering dependency within the same collector — see Cross-Dependencies in the Dependency Analysis Guide, and Example 07 for a project where a class-to-function dependency genuinely requires Ordered Mode.

examples/10-multiple-collectors

docs.title: 11 - Mixed Bump Mode
docs.text:
Demonstrates Mixed Bump Mode: a single bump target that handles both the initial state (token placeholders like {{VERSION}}) and all subsequent runs (regex patterns that match already-substituted values).

The template and manifest start with {{VERSION}} placeholders. After the first bump, those are replaced with concrete values. On every subsequent bump, the Regex items in the same entry update those values in place — no manual intervention required.

Includes Reset-Example.ps1 to restore all files to their initial token state so the example can be run multiple times.

See the Release Management Guide for a detailed explanation of bump modes and tokens.

examples/11-mixed-bump-mode

docs.title: 12 - Full Workflow
docs.text:
Combines the complete PSScriptBuilder lifecycle in a single script: version bump → file update → module build → post-processing → demo. Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData increments the patch version and refreshes build metadata. Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles propagates the new version into the module manifest, template header, and CHANGELOG.md using Mixed Bump Mode — the CHANGELOG.md entry demonstrates two tokens (VERSION and BUILD_DATE) in a single bump target. Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild produces the .psm1 from the updated template. Compress-PSScriptBuilderScript accepts the build result via pipeline and writes a comment-free, blank-line-free version to AppConfig.compressed.psm1. Finally, Demo-Module.ps1 loads the built module and confirms the version was correctly carried through all five phases.

Includes Reset-Example.ps1 to restore all files to their initial token state so the example can be run multiple times.

See the Release Management Guide for a detailed explanation of bump modes and tokens.

examples/12-full-workflow

docs.title: 13 - Dependency and Code Analysis
docs.text:
Unlike all previous examples, no build is performed. PSScriptBuilder's own source code is registered as the analysis subject — providing a real-world codebase with 60+ components, multiple inheritance hierarchies, and cross-subsystem dependencies.

The example covers ten scenarios:

  • Codebase metrics: component counts, total nodes and edges, cycle and cross-dependency flags
  • Cycle check: confirms the project is cycle-free (HasCycles: False)
  • Topological order: full ordered component list from OrderedComponents
  • Mermaid diagram: scoped to the Dependencies subsystem (8 classes) — directly renderable in VS Code, GitHub, and MkDocs
  • Graphviz DOT diagram: scoped to Collectors + Core + Dependencies (~17 classes) with edge-type annotations — visualize at viz-js.com
  • Drill-down traversal: dependency tree of PSScriptBuilderBuildOrchestrator, inheritance subtree of PSScriptBuilderCollectorBase (-EdgeType Inheritance), all dependents of PSScriptBuilderDependencyGraph
  • Top 5 components: ranked by transitive dependency count
  • Inheritance hierarchy: flat table of all Class → BaseClass relationships plus per-root tree rendering

Includes Reset-Example.ps1 to remove the generated output files so the example can be run multiple times.

See the Dependency Analysis Guide for a detailed explanation of the analysis cmdlets.

examples/13-dependency-analysis

docs.title: 14 - Scaffolding
docs.text:
Starts with an empty folder and runs the full workflow in five phases: scaffold, set root, bump version, apply version to files, build.

New-PSScriptBuilderProject creates the complete project structure including source directories, configuration file, build and release scripts, template, sample source files, and release management files. Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot then points all subsequent cmdlets to the correctly scaffolded directory before the remaining phases execute.

Phases:

  1. Scaffold — New-PSScriptBuilderProject -IncludeReleaseManagement creates the full project tree including sample files
  2. Set root — Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot explicitly registers the new project path
  3. Release data — Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData -Patch -UpdateBuildDetails bumps the patch version
  4. Bump files — Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles writes version and timestamp into the template header
  5. Build — Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild collects sample components and produces the output file
  6. Run — executes the generated script to verify the result end-to-end

Includes Reset-Example.ps1 to remove the generated MyProject/ directory. The run script also removes and recreates it automatically — no manual cleanup required to run the example again.

examples/14-scaffolding

docs.title: 15 - Watcher
docs.text:
Demonstrates Watch-PSScriptBuilderProject in both operating modes.

Build mode (Watch-Build.ps1) monitors the source directories and rebuilds automatically on every .ps1 change. The optional -OnSuccess parameter accepts a custom script block that receives a PSScriptBuilderBuildResult after each successful build — useful for running tests or printing a summary. The optional -OnError parameter accepts a custom script block that receives a PSScriptBuilderWatchBuildErrorResult when a build fails.

Script mode (Watch-Script.ps1) skips the build entirely and passes the changed file paths as a string[] to a custom script block. This is useful for invoking an external build tool, sending notifications, or simply observing which files are changing.

Both scripts use the AppConfig/ConfigEntry domain from Example 09. The watcher runs until stopped with Ctrl+C. Build failures and script block errors do not stop the watcher.

examples/15-watcher

docs.title: 16 - Source Maps
docs.text:
Demonstrates the source map feature: PSScriptBuilder merges components from multiple source files into a single output script — making it hard to trace runtime errors back to their origin. This example builds a small HR project with -WriteSourceMap, which generates a .sourcemap.json sidecar alongside the output file.

Three scenarios show the full resolution workflow:

  • Full map inspection: $result | Resolve-PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation | Format-Table — lists every component with its output line and source file
  • Line number resolution: resolve a specific output line number obtained from an error message back to Get-EmployeeById.ps1
  • ErrorRecord resolution: Get-EmployeeById throws a KeyNotFoundException for an unknown Id; the caught $_ is passed directly to Resolve-PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation -ErrorRecord $_, mapping the error to its exact source line

examples/16-source-maps

docs.title: 17 - Code Coverage
docs.text:
Builds directly on the source map from Example 16 to demonstrate code coverage translation. Pester's CodeCoverage.Path must point at the built, merged output script rather than the original source files — the built output is the only file Pester has any execution record for, since the classes are only fully resolved once merged. Get-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage reads the .sourcemap.json sidecar to map the raw, output-line-based Pester result back to the original per-source-file coverage.

The bundled test suite (tests\HRTools.Tests.ps1) is deliberately incomplete, producing three distinct outcomes side by side in one run:

  • Full coverage: Person.ps1, Employee.ps1, and New-Employee.ps1 are all exercised by every test that constructs an Employee
  • Partial coverage: Get-EmployeeById.ps1's "found" path is tested, but its "not found" branch (the throw) is never reached
  • Zero coverage: Get-EmployeesByDepartment.ps1 is built into the output but never called by any test

Format-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage -Detailed lists the exact source lines not covered beneath each file, collapsing consecutive lines into a range — useful for deciding where to add a test next. A file at 0% coverage, like Get-EmployeesByDepartment.ps1 here, shows uncovered: entire file instead, since enumerating every line would add nothing the Coverage column doesn't already say.

examples/17-code-coverage

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text: PSScriptBuilder analyses source code by parsing PowerShell as an abstract syntax tree (AST). It requires no module imports, no code execution, and no runtime environment during the build. The following constraints follow from this design and from the tool's scope.

docs.title: Static Analysis Only
docs.text:
The AST parser reads source code as text — it does not execute code at build time. Dependencies that are only knowable at runtime are not detected.

Not detected:

# String-based type name passed to New-Object — not detected
$typeName = 'MyClass'
$instance = New-Object $typeName

# Dynamically constructed type name — not detected
$instance = New-Object "My$($suffix)Class"

# Type reference inside Invoke-Expression — not detected
$instance = Invoke-Expression '[MyClass]::new()'

Detected:

# Direct type reference — detected
$instance = [MyClass]::new()

# Typed parameter — detected
param([MyClass] $obj)

# Inheritance — detected
class DerivedClass : MyClass { }

Implication: If a project uses dynamic type loading, the dependency graph may be incomplete. In most cases the output script is still collected correctly — the risk is incorrect load order: if a dynamically referenced class appears after its dependent in the output, the script fails at load time with a type-not-found error.

Workaround: Replace dynamic type references with direct references where possible. If that is not feasible, assign the dynamically-loaded class its own collector with a dedicated key, then position that placeholder before any placeholder whose components depend on it:

# DynamicallyLoaded is referenced via New-Object — assign it a dedicated key so its
# placeholder can be positioned before all classes that depend on it.
$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -CollectionKey "DYNAMICALLY_LOADED" -IncludePath "src\Shared"  |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -CollectionKey "APP_CLASSES"        -IncludePath "src\Classes" |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function                                     -IncludePath "src\Public"
Template — DYNAMICALLY_LOADED must appear before APP_CLASSES
{{DYNAMICALLY_LOADED}}
{{APP_CLASSES}}
{{FUNCTION_DEFINITIONS}}

This workaround requires Free Mode. In Ordered Mode, individual Class, Enum, and Function placeholders are forbidden — dedicated collector keys have no effect there.

If a dynamic dependency causes a runtime error in the compiled output, see Runtime error due to undetected dynamic type dependency in the Troubleshooting guide for a diagnosis workflow and the Ordered Mode constraints.

docs.title: No Constant Dependency Tracking
docs.text:
PSScriptBuilder's five collectors extract dependency information for Using statements, Enums, Classes, and Functions. Top-level module-scope variable assignments ($Script:X = ...), commonly used as shared constants or lookup tables, have no dedicated collector. They can only be captured via the generic File collector, which includes content verbatim without AST-based dependency extraction.

Not detected:

# Content of Constants.ps1, included via the File collector
$Script:StatusLookup = @{ [MyEnum]::Active = 'A' }   # dependency on MyEnum not tracked

Detected (for comparison — Class/Function type references are tracked):

class MyService {
    [MyEnum] $Status   # detected: MyService depends on MyEnum
}

Implication: If a module-scope constant's initializer references an Enum, Class, or another constant, PSScriptBuilder does not know about this dependency and cannot guarantee correct load order automatically. If the constant ends up before the type it references in the merged output script, the build succeeds but the output script fails at load time with a type-not-found error — no warning is raised at build time, since File-collected content is never analyzed for structural dependencies. Simple, literal constants ($Script:DefaultTimeout = 30) are unaffected, since they have no dependency on other components.

Workaround: Same approach as for undetected dynamic type dependencies above: assign the file containing the constants a dedicated File collector with its own CollectionKey, and manually position that placeholder before any placeholder whose components the constant references:

$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Enum -IncludePath "src\Enums"     |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type File -CollectionKey "CONSTANTS" -IncludePath "src\Constants" |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class -IncludePath "src\Classes"
Template — CONSTANTS must appear after ENUM_DEFINITIONS, before CLASS_DEFINITIONS
{{ENUM_DEFINITIONS}}
{{CONSTANTS}}
{{CLASS_DEFINITIONS}}
{{FUNCTION_DEFINITIONS}}

This workaround requires Free Mode, the same constraint as the dynamic type dependency workaround above.

docs.title: No Conditional Compilation
docs.text:
PSScriptBuilder includes all components that match the configured collectors. There is no mechanism to conditionally include or exclude individual components based on a build target, environment variable, or flag.

Implication: Projects that need different builds for different targets — for example, a debug build with diagnostic helpers and a production build without them — cannot express this in a single build configuration.

Workaround: Maintain separate build scripts with separate collector configurations per target. Both can share the same template and the same core source directory:

build-debug.ps1
$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath "src\Public"      |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath "src\Diagnostics"

Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild -ContentCollector $contentCollector `
    -TemplatePath 'build\Templates\MyProject.ps1.template' `
    -OutputPath   'build\Output\MyProject.debug.ps1'
build-release.ps1
$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath "src\Public"

Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild -ContentCollector $contentCollector `
    -TemplatePath 'build\Templates\MyProject.ps1.template' `
    -OutputPath   'build\Output\MyProject.ps1'

The debug build includes src\Diagnostics; the release build does not.

docs.title: No Incremental Builds
docs.text:
Every build re-parses all collected source files from scratch. There is no change detection and no caching layer.

Implication: For the intended target — module-level projects with tens to low hundreds of source files — full builds complete in well under a second. This is not a practical constraint at that scale.

For projects that grow significantly beyond this range, consider splitting into independent sub-modules, each with its own psscriptbuilder.config.json and build script. Each sub-module then builds only its own components, and the overall build time stays proportional to the size of each individual module rather than the total project size.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Common problems and their solutions. Entries under Build and Runtime Errors, Configuration and Session Errors, and Template Errors follow the same structure: Symptom: what you observe, Cause: why it happens, Fix: how to resolve it. Entries under Diagnosing Your Environment are direct how-to answers instead, since they are not tied to a specific error.

Problems are grouped by area — build and runtime errors, configuration and session errors, template errors, and environment diagnostics. Use the table of contents on the right to jump directly to the relevant section.

If your problem is not listed here, run the failing command with -Verbose for detailed execution output. Most collection and build failures include the source file and the exact component that caused the issue. For environment information to include in a bug report, see How do I check which version of PSScriptBuilder is loaded?.

If you cannot resolve the issue, open a GitHub issue with the error message, the -Verbose output, and the version information.

docs.title: Parse errors at build time: invalid UTF-8 encoding
docs.text:
Symptom: Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild fails with an InvalidOperationException whose message contains "due to invalid UTF-8 encoding", naming the offending source file.

Cause: The source file is not valid UTF-8 — for example, it was saved in a legacy codepage (e.g. Windows-1252) instead of UTF-8. PSScriptBuilder reads every source file explicitly as UTF-8, regardless of byte order mark (BOM) presence, so a file that genuinely isn't valid UTF-8 fails clearly instead of silently producing corrupted output.

Fix: Re-save the file as UTF-8 (with or without a BOM — both are read correctly) in your editor, then re-run the build.

docs.title: Duplicate class or function name: InvalidOperationException at collection time
docs.text:
Symptom: Collection or dependency analysis fails with InvalidOperationException, for example Duplicate class 'X' found in file: ..., Component name conflict: 'X' is defined as a Class more than once - in '...' and '...', or Component name conflict: 'X' is defined as both a Class (in '...') and a Function (in '...').

Cause: Two source files define a class, enum, or function with the same name (case-insensitive) - either within the same collector's scanned files, across two different collectors of the same type (e.g. two Class collectors scanning separate directories), or as both a Class and a Function. PSScriptBuilder uses fail-fast duplicate detection at every level: the build stops immediately rather than silently dropping one component's source code or producing ambiguous output.

Fix: Rename one of the conflicting definitions. Use -Verbose to see which files are being scanned by which collector.

docs.title: Generated script fails at load time: type-not-found error for a type that exists in the project
docs.text:
Symptom: The build succeeds but running or importing the generated script fails immediately with an error such as: Unable to find type [BaseClass] or Cannot convert null to type [BaseClass]

Cause: The generated script contains a class or function that references a type defined later in the file. This happens when multiple collectors of the same type are used with custom keys, and the template placeholders are in the wrong order. PSScriptBuilder sorts components correctly within each placeholder block, but it cannot reorder placeholders in your template. If {{DOMAIN_CLASSES}} appears before {{CORE_CLASSES}} in the template, and a class in DOMAIN_CLASSES inherits from a class in CORE_CLASSES, the generated script is invalid — even though each individual collector has the correct internal order.

Fix: Reorder the template placeholders so that dependencies appear before the components that depend on them. Use Get-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis to identify which components depend on which:

$result = Get-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis -ContentCollector $contentCollector
$result.OrderedComponents  # shows the globally correct dependency order

Compare the order of component names against the template placeholder order and adjust accordingly. See the Dependency Analysis Guide for a full explanation.

docs.title: Runtime error in compiled output: line number points to generated file
docs.text:
Symptom: An error thrown when running or importing the compiled output script shows a line number (e.g. At line:1042 char:5) that refers to the generated file. Finding the actual source requires manually searching through the combined output.

Cause: PSScriptBuilder merges components from multiple source files into a single output script. All error line numbers refer to that generated file, not to the original source files.

Fix: Build with -WriteSourceMap to generate a sidecar .sourcemap.json alongside the output script. Then use Resolve-PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation to map the error back to its original source file and line.

Resolve a specific line number obtained from the error message:

Resolve-PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation `
    -OutputPath 'build\Output\MyProject.ps1' `
    -LineNumber  1042

Resolve an ErrorRecord directly — the most common case when the error is caught in a try/catch block. The cmdlet extracts the line number from InvocationInfo.ScriptLineNumber automatically:

$result = ... | Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild -OutputPath 'build\Output\MyProject.ps1' -WriteSourceMap

try { . $result.OutputPath }
catch { $result | Resolve-PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation -ErrorRecord $_ }

The output shows the component name, its source file, and the corresponding source line:

ComponentName       : Employee
ComponentType       : Class
SourceFile          : C:\MyProject\src\Classes\Employee.ps1
SourceLineNumber    : 18
ComponentLineNumber : 18
OutputLineNumber    : 1042
Offset              : 0

A warning is emitted if the output script has been modified since the source map was written. Resolution still proceeds but line numbers may be inaccurate — rebuild with -WriteSourceMap to refresh the sidecar.

For the complete workflow including the configuration file option and full source map inspection, see Source Maps in the Source Maps Guide.

docs.title: Code coverage reports 0% or "referenced a file other than the build output"
docs.text:
Symptom: Pester's CodeCoverage result shows 0% coverage for every file, or Get-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage emits a warning such as: 214 coverage entr(y/ies) referenced a file other than the build output.

Cause: CodeCoverage.Path was pointed at the original source files (e.g. src\Classes) instead of the built output script. Pester only has execution records for files it actually loaded — for class-based projects loaded via using module, or any project tested by dot-sourcing the built output, that is the merged file, not the individual source files.

Fix: Set CodeCoverage.Path to the same output path used when building:

$config.CodeCoverage.Path = $buildResult.OutputPath

Then translate the results back to per-source-file coverage with Get-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage. See Translating Pester Code Coverage in the Source Maps Guide for the complete workflow.

docs.title: Runtime error due to undetected dynamic type dependency
docs.text:
Symptom: The output script loads successfully but fails at runtime with an error such as: Cannot find type [PluginClass] or New-Object : Cannot find type [PluginClass]. The class exists in the project and is present in the build output.

Cause: The class is referenced through a dynamic type name — for example, New-Object $typeName or New-Object "PluginClass". PSScriptBuilder's static AST analysis cannot detect this dependency and may place the referenced class after the class that uses it. The missing dependency is only exposed at runtime when the dynamic reference is resolved.

Fix: Step 1 — Identify the source file using the source map. Build with -WriteSourceMap, then resolve the failing line number back to the originating source file:

Resolve-PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation `
    -OutputPath 'build\Output\MyProject.ps1' `
    -LineNumber  <line from error message>

Step 2 — Fix the load order. Assign the dynamically-referenced class its own collector with a dedicated key, then place that placeholder before the placeholder whose components depend on it:

$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class -CollectionKey "PLUGINS"     -IncludePath "src\Plugins"  |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class -CollectionKey "APP_CLASSES" -IncludePath "src\Classes"  |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function                           -IncludePath "src\Public"
Template — PLUGINS must appear before APP_CLASSES
{{PLUGINS}}
{{APP_CLASSES}}
{{FUNCTION_DEFINITIONS}}

Ordered Mode

This fix requires explicit placeholder control and only works in Free Mode. In Ordered Mode all Class, Enum, and Function collector placeholders — including custom keys like {{PLUGINS}} — are forbidden. All components are merged into {{ORDERED_COMPONENTS}} and sorted by the dependency graph. Because the dynamic dependency is not in the graph, the relative order of the two classes remains unpredictable and cannot be controlled through template placement. The only resolution in this case is to replace the dynamic type reference with a direct reference so PSScriptBuilder can include it in the dependency graph.

See Static Analysis Only for the full explanation of this limitation.

docs.title: Wrong configuration loaded: tokens unreplaced or build path incorrect
docs.text:
Symptom: After running one example (or project), a second run in the same PowerShell session produces errors such as unreplaced {{VERSION_FULL}} placeholders, or files are read from or written to the wrong directory.

Cause: PSScriptBuilder stores the project root as a process-level global ($Global:PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot). If Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot was called earlier in the same session for a different directory, the cached value still points to the previous project.

Fix: Always run each project or example in a fresh PowerShell session, or call Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot explicitly at the start of your script:

Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot -Path $PSScriptRoot

docs.title: Release data validation fails: git.branch or git.tag too short
docs.text:
Symptom: Test-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData reports: Value at path 'git.branch' is shorter than the minimum allowed length of 1

Cause: The psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json file contains empty strings ("") for optional git fields. The validator accepts null for optional fields, but rejects empty strings because a branch or tag name of length zero is not a valid value.

Fix: Set unused git fields to null, not "":

"git": {
    "commit":      null,
    "commitShort": null,
    "branch":      null,
    "tag":         null
}

Git fields are populated automatically when Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData -UpdateGitDetails is run in a Git repository.

docs.title: Template placeholder not replaced: remains as {{PlaceholderName}} in output
docs.text:
Symptom: The generated output file still contains a literal {{PlaceholderName}} instead of the expected content.

Cause: The placeholder name in the template does not match the CollectionKey of any registered collector. Matching is case-sensitive.

Fix: Verify that the collector's CollectionKey matches the placeholder exactly. Use Get-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis or Test-PSScriptBuilderTemplate to list all placeholders found in the template and compare them against the registered collectors:

Test-PSScriptBuilderTemplate -TemplatePath $templatePath -ContentCollector $contentCollector

docs.title: Bump files not updated: {{VERSION_FULL}} remains in template after bumping
docs.text:
Symptom: After running Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles, the template still contains {{VERSION_FULL}} or {{BUILD_DATE}} and the subsequent build fails.

Cause: The bump step ran in a different session from the one that set the project root, or the bumpconfig file path is relative and was resolved against the wrong working directory.

Fix: Ensure Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot is called before any release management or bump cmdlets in the same script.

docs.title: How do I check which version of PSScriptBuilder is loaded?
docs.text:
When reporting a bug or diagnosing unexpected behaviour, it helps to include the module version and runtime details. PSScriptBuilder exposes two read-only global variables after import:

# Module version, build number, Git commit details
$Global:PSScriptBuilderModuleInfo

# PowerShell version, host application, computer name
$Global:PSScriptBuilderRuntimeInfo

Both variables are populated automatically when using module PSScriptBuilder is executed. Do not modify them directly.

docs.title: How do I make a CurrentUser install visible to both PowerShell editions on Windows?
docs.text:
This applies to Windows only. Windows is the only platform where PowerShell exists as two separate editions side by side — Windows PowerShell (powershell.exe) and PowerShell 7+ (pwsh.exe) — each with its own default module folder. Linux and macOS only ever run PowerShell 7+, so there is nothing to unify there.

On Windows, Install-Module run from one edition is not automatically visible to Get-Module in the other, even though both point at the same user account. Both editions start from the same persisted PSModulePath value at startup and layer their own default module folders on top of it, so you can permanently add one edition's module folder to the other's search path instead of installing PSScriptBuilder twice:

# 1. Read the current persistent PSModulePath for this user account — often empty by
#    default, since most machines never set it explicitly
$currentPath = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('PSModulePath', 'User')

# 2. Append the PowerShell 7+ module folder, keeping whatever was already there
if ($currentPath) {
    $newPath = "$currentPath;$HOME\Documents\PowerShell\Modules"
}
else {
    $newPath = "$HOME\Documents\PowerShell\Modules"
}

# 3. Save it back, permanently, for this user account
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('PSModulePath', $newPath, 'User')

Run this once, from either edition, then open a new PowerShell window for it to take effect. From then on, a -Scope CurrentUser install done from either edition is visible to both.

Two things worth knowing before using it:

  • It is a permanent, global change, not something scoped to one script or session. It sets a User-level environment variable that every future PowerShell session on this account — of either edition — will read from then on.
  • It only unifies -Scope CurrentUser. -Scope AllUsers installs to a separate, edition-specific folder under Program Files for each edition; unifying that as well requires the same change at Machine scope, which needs administrator rights and affects every account on the machine, not just yours.

docs.title: Cmdlet Reference
docs.text:
PSScriptBuilder provides 38 public cmdlets, grouped below into five categories that follow the natural project lifecycle: scaffolding a new project, building and assembling scripts, analyzing and validating a project's structure, managing shared configuration, and handling releases. Each entry links to a full reference page generated directly from that cmdlet's own comment-based help — the same syntax, parameter list, and usage examples Get-Help -Full already shows you in the console, organized here for browsing instead.

Many of these cmdlets return PowerShell objects rather than plain values. For what those objects actually contain — their properties, types, and how several of them relate to one another — see the Type Reference.

docs.title: Scaffolding
docs.text:
Start a brand-new project from nothing: folder structure, configuration file, and a first template, ready for the first build.

Cmdlet Description New-PSScriptBuilderProject Scaffolds a new PSScriptBuilder project structure New-PSScriptBuilderTemplate Generates a PSScriptBuilder template file from a content collector configuration

docs.title: Script Building
docs.text:
The core pipeline: define collectors, assemble a build, watch for source changes, post-process the output, and trace results back to their original source files.

Cmdlet Description New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector Creates a new content collector for managing multiple component collectors New-PSScriptBuilderCollector Creates a new collector for PowerShell script components Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector Adds a collector to a ContentCollector for fluent pipeline configuration Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector Retrieves collectors from a ContentCollector Get-PSScriptBuilderCollectorContent Retrieves collected data from a collector Remove-PSScriptBuilderCollector Removes a collector from a ContentCollector Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild Executes the complete PowerShell script build process Watch-PSScriptBuilderProject Watches project source files and triggers a build or custom script block on every change Compress-PSScriptBuilderScript Post-processes a built PowerShell script by removing comments, blank lines, or output statements Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult Formats and displays the result of a build operation Export-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult Exports a build result to a JSON file Resolve-PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation Resolves an output script line number or ErrorRecord back to its source file location Get-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage Translates Pester code coverage data back to the original source files Format-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage Formats and displays per-source-file code coverage results

docs.title: Analysis & Validation
docs.text:
Inspect a project's dependency graph, template structure, and collector configuration without necessarily running a build — useful for debugging and for CI checks that should fail fast.

Cmdlet Description Get-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis Analyzes dependencies between components without performing a build Format-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis Formats and displays the result of a dependency analysis operation Get-PSScriptBuilderComponentDependency Retrieves all dependencies or dependents of a named component from the dependency graph Find-PSScriptBuilderUnusedComponent Finds unused components in a PSScriptBuilder content collector configuration Export-PSScriptBuilderDependencyGraph Exports the dependency graph to a visual diagram format ConvertTo-PSScriptBuilderComponentDependencyTree Converts component dependency entries to a hierarchical tree string Get-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis Analyzes a template file for placeholders and structure Format-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis Formats and displays the result of a template analysis operation Test-PSScriptBuilderTemplate Validates a template file without performing a build

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Read, create, and pin the project-wide settings — paths, defaults, and the project root — that every other cmdlet relies on.

Cmdlet Description Get-PSScriptBuilderConfiguration Retrieves the global PSScriptBuilder configuration New-PSScriptBuilderConfiguration Creates a new PSScriptBuilder configuration file with default values Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot Sets the PSScriptBuilder project root directory

docs.title: Release Management
docs.text:
Track version numbers and other release metadata, then propagate them into the files that need to reflect the current version — templates, manifests, and changelogs.

Cmdlet Description New-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData Creates a new release data file with default values Get-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData Retrieves the current release data configuration Get-PSScriptBuilderReleaseDataTokens Retrieves available release data tokens for substitution in bump files Test-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData Tests the release data file for validity Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData Updates release data including version and metadata Format-PSScriptBuilderReleaseDataResult Formats and displays the result of a release data update operation Get-PSScriptBuilderBumpConfiguration Retrieves the bump configuration Test-PSScriptBuilderBumpConfiguration Tests the bump configuration file for validity Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles Updates configured project files with current version information Format-PSScriptBuilderBumpResult Formats and displays the result of a bump operation

docs.title: Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector
docs.text: Adds a collector to a ContentCollector for fluent pipeline configuration.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Creates a collector and registers it on a PSScriptBuilderContentCollector in one step — equivalent to calling New-PSScriptBuilderCollector and then its AddCollector() method by hand. Returns the same ContentCollector it was given, so multiple calls chain in a single pipeline expression.

Every collector's -CollectionKey must be unique within the ContentCollector — a duplicate throws an error. To initialize a ContentCollector with several pre-created collectors at once instead, use -Collector on New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -ContentCollector PSScriptBuilderContentCollector Required. The ContentCollector to add the collector to. Accepts pipeline input, enabling fluent chaining. -Type string Required. One of Using, Enum, Class, Function, File — see Collector Types. -CollectionKey string Unique identifier for the new collector, and the template placeholder name it corresponds to. Defaults to the type's own default key (see Default Keys and Tokens) if not specified. -IncludePath string[] Directories to scan. Relative to the project root or absolute. -IncludeFile string[] Specific files or glob patterns to include, bypassing -ExcludePath/-ExcludeFile. -ExcludePath string[] Directories excluded from scanning. Takes precedence over -IncludePath. -ExcludeFile string[] File name patterns excluded from scanning. -FileExtension string[] File extensions to scan. Default: @(".ps1"). -NoRecurse switch Scan only the top-level directory of each -IncludePath instead of recursing.

docs.title: Chain multiple collectors onto a new ContentCollector
docs.text:
$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class -CollectionKey "CLASSES" -IncludePath "src\Classes" |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -CollectionKey "FUNCTIONS" -IncludePath "src\Public"

docs.title: Add a single collector via the pipeline
docs.text:
$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector
$contentCollector | Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Using -IncludePath "src"

docs.title: Add multiple collectors of the same type with different keys
docs.text:
$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class -CollectionKey "DOMAIN" `
        -IncludePath "src\Classes\Domain" -ExcludeFile "*.Internal.ps1" |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class -CollectionKey "UTILS" `
        -IncludePath "src\Classes\Utils"

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Returns the same PSScriptBuilderContentCollector passed in via -ContentCollector, with the new collector registered.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Collectors Guide
  • Cmdlet Reference: New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector
  • Cmdlet Reference: New-PSScriptBuilderCollector
  • Cmdlet Reference: Remove-PSScriptBuilderCollector
  • Cmdlet Reference: Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector

docs.title: Compress-PSScriptBuilderScript
docs.text: Post-processes a built PowerShell script by removing comments, blank lines, or output statements.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Applies one or more independent, freely-combinable transformations to an already-built script file — typically to produce a leaner deployment artifact from a build output that's otherwise kept readable (comments, blank lines, and diagnostic logging intact) during development.

Whatever operations are selected, they always run in this fixed order regardless of the order the switches were passed in: -RemoveComments, then -RemoveOutputStatements, then -RemoveBlankLines — so removing comments or output statements never leaves behind blank lines that -RemoveBlankLines would otherwise have to clean up separately.

The original file is never modified unless -DestinationPath explicitly points back at it — typically it points at a separate deploy location instead.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -Path string Required. Path to the script file to process. Aliased as OutputPath, so a PSScriptBuilderBuildResult can be piped in directly from Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild. -RemoveComments switch Remove every comment — single-line, block, and #region/#endregion markers. #Requires statements are always preserved. -RemoveBlankLines switch Remove every line containing only whitespace. -RemoveOutputStatements string[] Remove isolated calls to the given cmdlets: Write-Verbose, Write-Debug, Write-Host, Write-Warning, Write-Information. A call counts as isolated only when it stands alone as its own statement — not piped, and not nested inside if/foreach/other control flow. Non-isolated calls are skipped silently; use -Verbose to see which ones and why. -DestinationPath string Path to write the processed script to. Omit to get the processed content back as a string instead. -Force switch Overwrite -DestinationPath if it already exists. Without it, an existing file causes an IOException.

docs.title: Remove comments and blank lines before deploying
docs.text:
Compress-PSScriptBuilderScript -Path '.\build\Output\MyScript.ps1' `
    -RemoveComments -RemoveBlankLines `
    -DestinationPath '.\deploy\MyScript.ps1' -Force

docs.title: Chain directly onto a build
docs.text:
Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild -ContentCollector $contentCollector -TemplatePath '.\template.ps1' -OutputPath '.\output\MyScript.ps1' |
    Compress-PSScriptBuilderScript -RemoveComments -RemoveBlankLines -DestinationPath '.\deploy\MyScript.ps1' -Force

docs.title: Strip diagnostic logging calls only
docs.text:
Compress-PSScriptBuilderScript -Path '.\output\MyScript.ps1' `
    -RemoveOutputStatements 'Write-Verbose', 'Write-Debug' `
    -DestinationPath '.\deploy\MyScript.ps1' -Force

docs.title: Get the result without writing a file
docs.text: $compressed = Compress-PSScriptBuilderScript -Path '.\output\MyScript.ps1' -RemoveComments

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Returns the processed script as a string when -DestinationPath is omitted; otherwise writes the file and returns nothing.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Build Pipeline Guide: Post-Processing
  • Cmdlet Reference: Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild

docs.title: ConvertTo-PSScriptBuilderComponentDependencyTree
docs.text: Converts component dependency entries to a hierarchical tree string.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Renders the array of PSScriptBuilderComponentDependencyEntry objects returned by Get-PSScriptBuilderComponentDependency as an indented Unicode tree diagram, showing the full path from the root to each dependency. Returns the diagram as a string — for display, writing to a file, or embedding in documentation.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -InputObject PSScriptBuilderComponentDependencyEntry Required. The dependency entries to render. Accepts pipeline input.

docs.title: Render a dependency chain as a tree
docs.text:
$analysis | Get-PSScriptBuilderComponentDependency -Name 'New-Employee' |
    ConvertTo-PSScriptBuilderComponentDependencyTree
Output
New-Employee
├── Address
├── Department
└── Employee
    ├── EmploymentStatus
    └── Person

docs.title: Capture the tree and write it to a file
docs.text:
$analysis | Get-PSScriptBuilderComponentDependency -Name 'BaseClass' -Direction Dependents |
    ConvertTo-PSScriptBuilderComponentDependencyTree |
    Set-Content -Path '.\dependents.txt'

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Returns the tree diagram as a string.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Dependency Analysis Guide: Querying the Dependency Graph
  • Cmdlet Reference: Get-PSScriptBuilderComponentDependency

docs.title: Export-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult
docs.text: Exports a build result to a JSON file.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Serializes a PSScriptBuilderBuildResult to a structured JSON file — useful as a CI artifact for auditing, debugging, or tracking changes between builds. Always includes the build summary (output path, file size, syntax validation status, execution time, and component counts) plus an automatically-added UTC generation timestamp.

Add -Detailed to also include every processed source file and, per component, its source file and dependencies.

The target directory is created automatically if it doesn't exist; relative paths are resolved against the project root (see Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -BuildResult PSScriptBuilderBuildResult Required. The result to export, typically piped directly from Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild. -Path string Required. Path to the JSON file to write. -Detailed switch Also include every processed source file and each component's source file and dependencies. -Force switch Overwrite the target file if it already exists. Without it, an existing file causes an IOException.

docs.title: Export a compact build summary
docs.text: $result | Export-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult -Path ".\build\reports\build.json"

docs.title: Export the full detail, overwriting an existing report
docs.text: $result | Export-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult -Path ".\build\reports\build.json" -Detailed -Force

docs.title: Build, display, and export in one pipeline
docs.text:
$result = Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild @buildParams
$result | Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult
$result | Export-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult -Path ".\build\reports\build.json" -Force

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Returns the resolved absolute path of the written JSON file, as a string.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Build Pipeline Guide
  • Cmdlet Reference: Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild
  • Cmdlet Reference: Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult

docs.title: Export-PSScriptBuilderDependencyGraph
docs.text: Exports the dependency graph to a visual diagram format.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Renders a PSScriptBuilderDependencyGraph as a diagram — every component as a node, every dependency as an edge — in one of two formats:

  • Mermaid (default): flowchart syntax that renders natively on GitHub, GitLab, and MkDocs, well suited to small and medium projects.
  • Dot: Graphviz DOT language, rendered with the dot command-line tool or an online viewer. Handles hundreds of nodes far better than Mermaid, for larger projects.

When writing Mermaid output to a file with a .md/.markdown extension, the diagram is automatically wrapped in a fenced mermaid code block, so the file renders immediately. Piped output (no -OutputPath) always returns the raw diagram string, unwrapped.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -DependencyGraph PSScriptBuilderDependencyGraph Required. The graph to export. Accepts pipeline input by property name, enabling direct piping from Get-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis (its DependencyGraph property). -Format string "Mermaid" (default) or "Dot". -OutputPath string Path to write the diagram to. Omit to get the diagram string back on the pipeline instead. -IncludeEdgeTypes switch Annotate each edge with its dependency type (Inheritance, TypeReference, FunctionCall, StaticInitializer). -Force switch Overwrite -OutputPath if it already exists. Without it, an existing file causes an IOException.

docs.title: Generate an architecture diagram for code review
docs.text:
$analysis | Export-PSScriptBuilderDependencyGraph -OutputPath '.\docs\architecture.md' -Force

The resulting file contains a fenced Mermaid code block that renders as an interactive diagram on GitHub, GitLab, and MkDocs.

docs.title: Export to Graphviz for a large project
docs.text:
$analysis | Export-PSScriptBuilderDependencyGraph -Format Dot -IncludeEdgeTypes -OutputPath '.\graph.dot'
Render with Graphviz
dot -Tsvg graph.dot -o graph.svg

docs.title: Regenerate the diagram automatically on every build (CI)
docs.text:
$analysis | Export-PSScriptBuilderDependencyGraph -OutputPath '.\docs\dependency-graph.md' -Force

Commit the generated file so pull request diffs show architecture changes alongside source changes.

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Returns the diagram as a string when -OutputPath is omitted; otherwise writes the file and returns nothing.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Dependency Analysis Guide: Architecture Overview for Code Review
  • Dependency Analysis Guide: Large Projects with Graphviz
  • Cmdlet Reference: Get-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis

docs.title: Find-PSScriptBuilderUnusedComponent
docs.text: Finds unused components in a PSScriptBuilder content collector configuration.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Analyzes the dependency graph to find Enum, Class, and Function components nothing else references — in two modes:

  • Without -EntryPoint: reports every component with no incoming dependency edge at all. Since public cmdlets are only ever called from outside the graph, they always appear "unused" in this mode — a false positive, not a real finding.
  • With -EntryPoint: performs a transitive reachability analysis from every component whose name matches one of the given glob patterns, and reports everything unreachable from any of them. Passing every public cmdlet as an entry point removes the false-positive noise from the first mode and answers the real question: is there anything even the public API can't reach?

If the dependency graph contains a cycle, a warning is emitted, and components inside that cycle may not be reported as unused — they reference each other, so each has an incoming edge.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -ContentCollector PSScriptBuilderContentCollector Required. The collector set to analyze. Accepts pipeline input, enabling fluent chaining from Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector. -EntryPoint string[] Glob patterns (*, ?, matched case-insensitively) identifying entry point components. Only components unreachable from a match are reported. Without this, every component with no incoming edge is reported.

docs.title: Find dead code relative to the public API
docs.text:
$unused = $contentCollector | Find-PSScriptBuilderUnusedComponent -EntryPoint '*-PSScriptBuilder*'
Write-Host "Unreachable from the public API: $($unused.Count)"
Output
Unreachable from the public API: 0

docs.title: Find components with no incoming dependencies at all
docs.text:
$results = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath "src\Classes"   |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath "src\Functions" |
    Find-PSScriptBuilderUnusedComponent

Useful for a class-only project without public cmdlets, where the entry-point false positive from the first mode doesn't apply.

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Returns an array of PSScriptBuilderUnusedComponentEntry, one per component found unused.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Dependency Analysis Guide: Dead Code Detection
  • Cmdlet Reference: Get-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis

docs.title: Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult
docs.text: Formats and displays the result of a build operation.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Renders a PSScriptBuilderBuildResult as a human-readable summary: output path, file size, execution time, backup/source map paths (when present), and a per-type component count with a total.

Add -Detailed to also list every processed source file and, per component, its source file and dependencies.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -BuildResult PSScriptBuilderBuildResult Required. The result to display, typically piped directly from Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild. -Detailed switch Also list every processed source file and each component's source file and dependencies.

docs.title: Display a compact build summary
docs.text:
$result = Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild -ContentCollector $contentCollector -TemplatePath "template.psm1" -OutputPath "output.psm1"
Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult -BuildResult $result
Output
Build Summary
  Output : ...\build\Output\MyProject.ps1
  Size   : 734 bytes
  Time   : 830.15 ms

Components
  Enums     : 1
  Classes   : 1
  Functions : 1
  Total     : 3

docs.title: Display the full detail via the pipeline
docs.text: $result | Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult -Detailed

docs.title: Output
docs.text: None — writes directly to the host with Write-Host.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Build Pipeline Guide
  • Cmdlet Reference: Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild
  • Cmdlet Reference: Export-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult

docs.title: Format-PSScriptBuilderBumpResult
docs.text: Formats and displays the result of a bump operation.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Renders a PSScriptBuilderBumpFilesResult's changes as a human-readable summary, one section per modified file, listing each change's token, old value, and new value. Displays a message instead if no files were modified.

The Pattern line is shown only when it differs from Old Value: Simple and Placeholder Mode always set them equal, so showing both would be redundant; Regex Mode's Pattern (the {REGEX_TOKEN} config template) legitimately differs from the actual matched value, so it's always shown there.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -BumpResult PSScriptBuilderBumpFilesResult Required. The result to display, typically piped directly from Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles.

docs.title: Display what a bump run changed
docs.text: Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles | Format-PSScriptBuilderBumpResult

docs.title: Output
docs.text: None — writes directly to the host with Write-Host.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Release Management Guide
  • Cmdlet Reference: Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles

docs.title: Format-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis
docs.text: Formats and displays the result of a dependency analysis operation.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Renders a PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysisResult as a human-readable summary: total nodes and edges, cycle status, cross-dependency status, and a per-type component count with a total.

If a cycle was detected, its path is always shown, regardless of -Detailed. Add -Detailed to also list the full topologically-sorted component sequence — or, if a cycle prevents sorting, a note explaining why the list isn't available.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -AnalysisResult PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysisResult Required. The result to display, typically piped directly from Get-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis. -Detailed switch Also list the full ordered component sequence (or a note if cycles prevent sorting).

docs.title: Display a compact summary
docs.text:
$analysis | Format-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis
Output
Analysis Summary
  Components : 8
  Nodes      : 8
  Edges      : 11
  Cycles     : None
  Cross-Deps : None

Components
  Enums     : 2
  Classes   : 3
  Functions : 3
  Total     : 8

docs.title: Display the full ordered component sequence
docs.text:
$analysis | Format-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis -Detailed
Output
Ordered Components (8)
  Department
  EmploymentStatus
  Address
  Person
  Employee
  Get-EmployeesByDepartment
  New-Employee
  Set-EmployeeStatus

docs.title: Output
docs.text: None — writes directly to the host with Write-Host.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Dependency Analysis Guide
  • Cmdlet Reference: Get-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis

docs.title: Format-PSScriptBuilderReleaseDataResult
docs.text: Formats and displays the result of a release data update operation.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Renders a PSScriptBuilderReleaseDataResult's changes as a human-readable summary, grouped by category (Version, Build, Git) with each property's old and new value. Displays a message instead if no changes were made.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -ReleaseDataResult PSScriptBuilderReleaseDataResult Required. The result to display, typically piped directly from Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData.

docs.title: Display what a version bump changed
docs.text:
Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData -Patch | Format-PSScriptBuilderReleaseDataResult
Output
Category: Version

  Property  : patch
  Old Value : 0
  New Value : 1

  Property  : full
  Old Value : 0.1.0
  New Value : 0.1.1

docs.title: Output
docs.text: None — writes directly to the host with Write-Host.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Release Management Guide
  • Cmdlet Reference: Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData

docs.title: Format-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage
docs.text: Formats and displays per-source-file code coverage results.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Renders one or more PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverageResult objects — as returned by Get-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage — as an aligned table: one row per source file, with its coverage percentage and hit/total command count. SourceFile is shown relative to the project root, falling back to the original path for a file outside it (for example a collector IncludePath pointed at a network share).

Add -Detailed to also list, beneath each file's row, every distinct source line not covered by any test — consecutive lines collapsed into a range (e.g. uncovered: lines 12-14, 20), and a file at 0% coverage shown as uncovered: entire file instead of enumerating every line. Long lists wrap at a fixed width with a hanging indent.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -CoverageResult PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverageResult Required. The result to display. Accepts pipeline input — all piped objects are collected and rendered together as one aligned table. -Detailed switch Also list the uncovered source lines beneath each file's row.

docs.title: Display a compact coverage table
docs.text:
$result | Get-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage -CodeCoverage $pesterResult.CodeCoverage |
    Format-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage

docs.title: Display the table with uncovered lines per file
docs.text:
$coverage | Format-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage -Detailed
Output
SourceFile                                   Coverage  Hit/Total
-------------------------------------------  --------  ---------
src\Classes\Person.ps1                        100.0 %        2/2
src\Classes\Employee.ps1                      100.0 %        2/2
src\Functions\Get-EmployeeById.ps1             71.4 %        5/7
  uncovered: lines 12-13
src\Functions\New-Employee.ps1                100.0 %        1/1
src\Functions\Get-EmployeesByDepartment.ps1     0.0 %        0/4
  uncovered: entire file

docs.title: Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector
docs.text: Retrieves collectors from a ContentCollector.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Retrieves one or more collectors registered on a ContentCollector. Without -CollectionKey or -Type, returns every registered collector, sorted by CollectorType (Using, Enum, Class, Function, File) — the same order they execute in during a build (see Execution Order).

Returns the actual collector objects (not simplified copies), so the result can be inspected directly (.IncludePaths, .ExcludePaths, etc.), piped straight into Remove-PSScriptBuilderCollector, or passed to Get-PSScriptBuilderCollectorContent for data inspection.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Description -ContentCollector PSScriptBuilderContentCollector Required. The ContentCollector to query. Accepts pipeline input. -CollectionKey string Returns only the collector with this exact key (case-insensitive). If no collector has this key, writes a non-terminating error and returns $null. -Type PSScriptBuilderCollectorType Returns every collector of this type: UsingCollector, EnumCollector, ClassCollector, FunctionCollector, or FileCollector. Matches collectors of the same type registered under different keys (e.g. "CLASSES_DOMAIN", "CLASSES_UTILS").

-CollectionKey and -Type select collectors two different ways — one exact collector by its unique key, or every collector of a given type — and cannot be combined; passing both together is rejected by PowerShell's own parameter binding.

docs.title: Retrieve all collectors
docs.text: $contentCollector | Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector

docs.title: Retrieve one collector by key
docs.text: Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector -ContentCollector $contentCollector -CollectionKey "CLASSES"

docs.title: Retrieve every collector of a given type
docs.text: Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector -ContentCollector $contentCollector -Type ClassCollector

docs.title: Inspect a specific collector's configuration
docs.text:
$classCollector = Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector -ContentCollector $contentCollector -CollectionKey "CLASSES"
$classCollector.IncludePaths

docs.title: Find collectors missing an IncludePath
docs.text:
Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector -ContentCollector $contentCollector |
    Where-Object { -not $_.IncludePaths -or $_.IncludePaths.Count -eq 0 }

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
• Every registered collector as a PSScriptBuilderCollectorBase[], sorted by CollectorType, when neither -CollectionKey nor -Type is passed
  • A single PSScriptBuilderCollectorBase-derived object when -CollectionKey is passed
  • A PSScriptBuilderCollectorBase[] filtered by type when -Type is passed

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Collectors Guide
  • Cmdlet Reference: Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector
  • Cmdlet Reference: Remove-PSScriptBuilderCollector
  • Cmdlet Reference: Get-PSScriptBuilderCollectorContent

docs.title: Get-PSScriptBuilderCollectorContent
docs.text: Retrieves collected data from a collector.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Runs .Collect() on the given collector, then returns everything it collected — classes, functions, enums, using statements, or file contents, depending on the collector's type — as the matching Collected Data Type (PSScriptBuilderClassData, PSScriptBuilderFunctionData, and so on).

Without -ItemName, every collected item is returned. With -ItemName, only the item matching that name is returned (case-insensitive) — a class or function name, an enum name, a using statement's exact text, or a file name, depending on the collector's type.

Mainly useful for inspection and debugging while developing a project's collector configuration — a real build processes the collected data itself, without needing to call this cmdlet.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -Collector PSScriptBuilderCollectorBase Required. The collector to retrieve data from — typically obtained from Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector or created directly with New-PSScriptBuilderCollector. Accepts pipeline input. -ItemName string Returns only the item with this name (case-insensitive), instead of every collected item.

docs.title: Retrieve everything a collector found
docs.text:
$classCollector | Get-PSScriptBuilderCollectorContent |
    Where-Object { $_.BaseClass -eq "PSScriptBuilderBase" }

docs.title: Retrieve one item by name
docs.text:
$baseClass = Get-PSScriptBuilderCollectorContent -Collector $classCollector -ItemName "PSScriptBuilderBase"
Write-Host $baseClass.SourceCode

docs.title: Validate that all expected components were collected
docs.text:
$functions = Get-PSScriptBuilderCollectorContent -Collector $functionCollector
$expected = @("Get-Data", "Set-Data", "Remove-Data")
$missing = $expected | Where-Object { $_ -notin $functions.Name }

if ($missing) {
    throw "Missing functions: $($missing -join ', ')"
}

docs.title: Check whether a collector found anything at all
docs.text:
$collector = Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector -ContentCollector $contentCollector -CollectionKey "FUNCTIONS"
$content = Get-PSScriptBuilderCollectorContent -Collector $collector

if ($content.Count -eq 0) {
    Write-Warning "No functions collected. Check IncludePaths configuration."
}

docs.title: Inspect using statements and where they were found
docs.text:
$usingData = Get-PSScriptBuilderCollectorContent -Collector $usingCollector

foreach ($using in $usingData) {
    Write-Host "Statement: $($using.Statement)"
    Write-Host "  Found in $($using.SourceFiles.Count) file(s):"
    $using.SourceFiles | ForEach-Object { Write-Host "    - $_" }
}

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Always returns an array of the Collected Data Type matching the collector's CollectorType — for example PSScriptBuilderClassData[] for a Class collector — even when -ItemName narrows the result to a single item.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Collectors Guide
  • Cmdlet Reference: Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector
  • Cmdlet Reference: New-PSScriptBuilderCollector

docs.title: Get-PSScriptBuilderComponentDependency
docs.text: Retrieves all dependencies or dependents of a named component from the dependency graph.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Performs a breadth-first traversal of a dependency graph starting from -Name, returning every reachable component as a PSScriptBuilderComponentDependencyEntry — its name, depth from the starting component (1 = direct, 2+ = transitive), and the full path that reaches it.

-Direction controls which way the traversal runs: Dependencies (the default) shows what the named component needs; Dependents shows what needs it — the PowerShell equivalent of an IDE's "Find All References", useful for assessing a refactor's impact before touching a shared base class. -EdgeType restricts traversal to specific relationship kinds — for example Inheritance alone, to build a pure inheritance hierarchy.

The named component itself is never included in the results. Component name lookup is case-insensitive.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -DependencyGraph PSScriptBuilderDependencyGraph Required. The graph to traverse. Accepts pipeline input by property name, enabling direct piping from Get-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis (its DependencyGraph property). -Name string Required. The component to start the traversal from. Must exist in the graph. -Direction PSScriptBuilderTraversalDirection Dependencies (default) or Dependents. -EdgeType PSScriptBuilderDependencyEdgeType[] Restricts traversal to these edge types: Inheritance, TypeReference, FunctionCall, StaticInitializer. Combines multiple types as a union. All types are traversed when omitted.

docs.title: Find everything a component depends on
docs.text:
$analysis | Get-PSScriptBuilderComponentDependency -Name 'New-Employee'
Output
Name              Depth  DependencyPath
----              -----  --------------
Address               1  {New-Employee, Address}
Department            1  {New-Employee, Department}
Employee              1  {New-Employee, Employee}
EmploymentStatus      2  {New-Employee, Employee, EmploymentStatus}
Person                2  {New-Employee, Employee, Person}

docs.title: Assess the impact of changing a shared base class
docs.text:
$analysis | Get-PSScriptBuilderComponentDependency -Name 'Person' -Direction Dependents
Output
Name                       Depth  DependencyPath
----                       -----  --------------
Employee                       1  {Person, Employee}
Get-EmployeesByDepartment      2  {Person, Employee, Get-EmployeesByDepartment}
New-Employee                   2  {Person, Employee, New-Employee}
Set-EmployeeStatus             2  {Person, Employee, Set-EmployeeStatus}

docs.title: Build a pure inheritance hierarchy
docs.text:
$analysis | Get-PSScriptBuilderComponentDependency -Name 'ValidatorBase' -Direction Dependents -EdgeType Inheritance

Only subclasses are included — components that merely reference ValidatorBase as a type are excluded.

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Returns an array of PSScriptBuilderComponentDependencyEntry, one per reachable component.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Dependency Analysis Guide
  • Cmdlet Reference: Get-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis
  • Cmdlet Reference: ConvertTo-PSScriptBuilderComponentDependencyTree

docs.title: Get-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis
docs.text: Analyzes dependencies between components without performing a build.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Runs the same analysis pipeline a build performs internally — collecting components, building the dependency graph, detecting cycles, and topologically sorting — but produces no output file. Useful for validating a project's dependency structure, planning a refactor's impact, or checking for problems before committing to a full build.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -ContentCollector PSScriptBuilderContentCollector Required. The collector set to analyze. Accepts pipeline input, enabling fluent chaining from Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector.

docs.title: Run an analysis and check its summary properties
docs.text:
$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Enum     -IncludePath "src\Enums"     |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath "src\Classes"   |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath "src\Functions"

$analysis = Get-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis -ContentCollector $contentCollector

Write-Host "Total components: $($analysis.TotalComponents)"
Write-Host "Cross-dependencies: $($analysis.HasCrossDependencies)"

docs.title: Check for cycles before building
docs.text:
$analysis = Get-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis -ContentCollector $contentCollector

if ($analysis.HasCycles) {
    Write-Error "Circular dependency detected: $($analysis.CyclePath -join ' -> ')"
    return
}

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Returns a PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysisResult object. See the Dependency Analysis Guide for how to read every property, and the Pre-Build Validation Pattern for combining this with a build.

docs.text:

docs.title: Get-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData
docs.text: Retrieves the current release data configuration.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Loads psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json without modifying it — version, build metadata, and Git information. By default, returns a hierarchical object with Version, Build, and Git sections, ideal when only one section is needed. Use -Flat for a flat object instead, with every property prefixed by category (Version*, Build*, Git*) — more convenient for enumerating every property uniformly or passing all values to another function.

Both forms are OrderedDictionary objects that preserve categorical order; sort either with GetEnumerator() | Sort-Object -Property Key.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -Flat switch Return a flat, prefixed structure instead of the default hierarchical one.

docs.title: Read one section of the hierarchical object
docs.text:
$data = Get-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData
Write-Host "Number:    $($data.Build.Number)"
Write-Host "Timestamp: $($data.Build.Timestamp)"
Output
Number:    1
Timestamp: 2026-09-14T14:18:03Z

$flat = Get-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData -Flat
Write-Host "Version:     $($flat.VersionFull)"
Write-Host "CommitShort: $($flat.GitCommitShort)"
Output
Version:     0.1.1
CommitShort: 55d9437
