docs.title: Get-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage
docs.text: Translates Pester code coverage data back to the original source files.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Reads the .sourcemap.json sidecar written by Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild's -WriteSourceMap and translates a Pester CodeCoverage result — reported in terms of the built output script — back to per-source-file coverage aggregates.

This translation is necessary whenever tests load the built output as a single unit (for example via using module for a class-based project) rather than the original per-file sources — CodeCoverage.Path must then point at the build output, since that's the only file PowerShell has any execution record of, and its line numbers are otherwise meaningless against a multi-file source tree. See Translating Pester Code Coverage for the full setup, including why pointing CodeCoverage.Path at the source tree fails silently.

Accepts either the build result directly (-BuildResult, sidecar path derived from its SourceMapPath) or an explicit -OutputPath (sidecar path derived by appending .sourcemap.json) — mirroring Resolve-PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation.

A SHA-256 hash comparison against the output file detects a stale source map and emits a warning. Coverage entries referencing a file other than the build output, or falling outside any tracked component, are skipped and reported as one consolidated warning each.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Description -BuildResult PSScriptBuilderBuildResult The build result to translate coverage against. Accepts pipeline input. Requires a build run with -WriteSourceMap. -OutputPath string Path to the output script to translate coverage against, as an alternative to -BuildResult. -CodeCoverage object Required. The CodeCoverage property of a Pester result (e.g. $pesterResult.CodeCoverage), exposing CommandsExecuted and CommandsMissed.

Exactly one of -BuildResult or -OutputPath is required.

docs.title: Translate coverage from a Pester run against the build output
docs.text:
$result = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath 'src\Classes'   |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath 'src\Functions' |
    Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild -TemplatePath 'build\Templates\HRTools.ps1.template' `
                                -OutputPath   'build\Output\HRTools.ps1' `
                                -WriteSourceMap

$config = [PesterConfiguration]::Default
$config.Run.Path             = 'tests'
$config.Run.PassThru         = $true
$config.CodeCoverage.Enabled = $true
$config.CodeCoverage.Path    = $result.OutputPath

$pesterResult = Invoke-Pester -Configuration $config

$result | Get-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage -CodeCoverage $pesterResult.CodeCoverage |
    Format-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage
Output
SourceFile                                    Coverage  Hit/Total
--------------------------------------------  --------  ---------
src\Classes\Person.ps1                         100.0 %        2/2
src\Classes\Employee.ps1                       100.0 %        2/2
src\Functions\Get-EmployeeById.ps1              71.4 %        5/7
src\Functions\New-Employee.ps1                 100.0 %        1/1
src\Functions\Get-EmployeesByDepartment.ps1      0.0 %        0/4

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Returns an array of PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverageResult, one per distinct source file referenced by the resolved coverage entries.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Source Maps Guide
  • Cmdlet Reference: Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild
  • Cmdlet Reference: Format-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage
  • Cmdlet Reference: Resolve-PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation

docs.title: Get-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis
docs.text: Analyzes a PSScriptBuilder template file and returns comprehensive analysis information.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Validates a template against the current collector configuration and returns a detailed result: validation status and errors, the detected validation mode (Free, Hybrid, or Ordered), and a full placeholder comparison — found, expected, missing, and unknown. See Validation Modes for how the mode is determined, and Validate Your Template for the full workflow.

For a plain $true/$false result instead, use Test-PSScriptBuilderTemplate. This cmdlet focuses on template-specific information only — for topological order, component counts, or the dependency graph itself, use Get-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis separately.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -ContentCollector PSScriptBuilderContentCollector Required. The collector configuration to validate against. Accepts pipeline input, enabling fluent chaining from Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector. -TemplatePath string Required. Path to the template file to analyze. -OrderedComponentsKey string The combined-components placeholder key, for Ordered/Hybrid Mode templates. Default: "ORDERED_COMPONENTS".

docs.title: Analyze a template and branch on validity
docs.text:
$result = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class -IncludePath "src\Classes" |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath "src\Public" |
    Get-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis -TemplatePath "template.psm1"

if ($result.IsValid) {
    Write-Host "Template is valid - Mode: $($result.ValidationMode)"
}
else {
    Write-Warning "Template validation failed:"
    $result.ValidationErrors | ForEach-Object { Write-Warning "  $_" }
}

docs.title: Inspect placeholder mismatches
docs.text:
$result = Get-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis -ContentCollector $contentCollector -TemplatePath "template.psm1"

if ($result.MissingPlaceholders.Count -gt 0) {
    Write-Host "Missing placeholders: $($result.MissingPlaceholders -join ', ')"
}

if ($result.UnknownPlaceholders.Count -gt 0) {
    Write-Host "Unknown placeholders: $($result.UnknownPlaceholders -join ', ')"
}

docs.title: Pipe into Format-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis for a full report
docs.text:
Get-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis -ContentCollector $contentCollector -TemplatePath "template.psm1" |
    Format-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Returns a PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysisResult object.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Templates Guide
  • Cmdlet Reference: Format-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis
  • Cmdlet Reference: Test-PSScriptBuilderTemplate
  • Cmdlet Reference: Get-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis

docs.title: Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild
docs.text: Executes the complete PowerShell build process.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Runs the entire build workflow: loads the template, collects components from every registered collector, analyzes dependencies (failing with a detailed error on a circular dependency), topologically sorts them, processes the template, optionally backs up an existing output file, writes the final output file, and validates its syntax.

All relative paths (-TemplatePath, -OutputPath, -BackupPath) are resolved against the project root (see Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -ContentCollector PSScriptBuilderContentCollector Required. The fully configured collector set to build from. Accepts pipeline input, enabling fluent chaining from Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector. -TemplatePath string Required. Path to the template file. -OutputPath string Required. Path to write the final output file to. -BackupPath string Directory for backup files, used only when -EnableBackup is specified. Defaults to the output file's own directory. -OrderedComponentsKey string The combined-components placeholder key, for Ordered/Hybrid Mode templates. Default: "ORDERED_COMPONENTS". -EnableBackup switch Back up an existing output file (timestamped, e.g. MyScript.ps1.260309_153045.bak) before overwriting it. Off by default — see Backup for why. -SkipSyntaxValidation switch Skip the post-write syntax check. Only needed if the output contains syntax the PowerShell parser can't handle at all — TypeNotFound errors from externally-loaded assemblies are already filtered automatically and never fail validation. -WriteSourceMap switch Write a .sourcemap.json sidecar alongside the output, enabling Resolve-PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation to map output lines back to source files.

docs.title: Fluent pipeline build
docs.text:
$result = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class -IncludePath "src\Classes" |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath "src\Public" |
    Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild -TemplatePath "template.psm1" -OutputPath "output.psm1"

docs.title: Build using paths from a configuration file
docs.text:
$config = Get-PSScriptBuilderConfiguration
$result = Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild -ContentCollector $contentCollector `
    -TemplatePath $config.Build.TemplatePath `
    -OutputPath $config.Build.OutputPath `
    -BackupPath $config.Build.BackupPath `
    -EnableBackup:$config.Build.BackupEnabled

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Returns a PSScriptBuilderBuildResult object. See Interpreting the Build Result for how to read it.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Build Pipeline Guide
  • Cmdlet Reference: Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult
  • Cmdlet Reference: Export-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult
  • Cmdlet Reference: Watch-PSScriptBuilderProject

docs.title: New-PSScriptBuilderCollector
docs.text: Creates a new collector for PowerShell script components.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Creates a standalone collector instance for extracting one specific kind of PowerShell component — using statements, enums, classes, functions, or entire file contents — from source files. Use it on its own to explore or inspect a codebase, or pass it to New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector or Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector to include it in a build.

A non-existent -IncludePath produces a warning, not an error, at creation time — the collector is still created, to support paths that are generated later. See File Resolution Rules for the full behavior, including what happens if the path is still missing once the collector actually runs.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -Type string Required. One of Using, Enum, Class, Function, File — see Collector Types. -CollectionKey string Unique identifier for this collector, and the template placeholder name it corresponds to. Defaults to the type's own default key (see Default Keys and Tokens) if not specified. -IncludePath string[] Directories to scan. Relative to the project root or absolute. -IncludeFile string[] Specific files or glob patterns to include, bypassing -ExcludePath/-ExcludeFile. -ExcludePath string[] Directories excluded from scanning. Takes precedence over -IncludePath. -ExcludeFile string[] File name patterns excluded from scanning. -FileExtension string[] File extensions to scan. Default: @(".ps1"). -NoRecurse switch Scan only the top-level directory of each -IncludePath instead of recursing.

docs.title: Create a collector with the default key
docs.text: New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class -IncludePath "src\Classes"

docs.title: Create a collector with a custom key
docs.text: New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class -CollectionKey "CLASSES" -IncludePath "src\Classes"

docs.title: Include a file that would otherwise be excluded
docs.text:
New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class -IncludePath "src\Classes" `
    -ExcludeFile "*.Internal.ps1" -IncludeFile "src\Classes\Legacy.Internal.ps1"

docs.title: Exclude a subdirectory
docs.text:
New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class -CollectionKey "DOMAIN" `
    -IncludePath "src\Classes" -ExcludePath "src\Classes\Legacy"

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Returns a PSScriptBuilderCollectorBase-derived object (the concrete type matches -Type). Calling .Collect() on it populates a type-specific data property — .FunctionData for a Function collector, .ClassData for a Class collector, and so on — with entries of the corresponding Collected Data Type.

docs.title: New-PSScriptBuilderConfiguration
docs.text: Creates a new PSScriptBuilder configuration file with default values.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Writes a new psscriptbuilder.config.json with default values into -Path, or — if omitted — the currently set project root (Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot), falling back to the current working directory. The target directory is created automatically if it doesn't exist yet.

Fails with an error if the file already exists, unless -Force is specified.

This cmdlet also supports -WhatIf and -Confirm (PowerShell's ShouldProcess pattern).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -Path string Directory to create the configuration file in. Defaults to the current project root, or the current working directory if none is set. -Force switch Overwrite the configuration file if it already exists.

docs.title: Create a configuration file in the current project
docs.text: New-PSScriptBuilderConfiguration

docs.title: Create a configuration file in a specific directory
docs.text: New-PSScriptBuilderConfiguration -Path "C:\Projects\MyProject"

docs.title: Reset an existing configuration file to its defaults
docs.text: New-PSScriptBuilderConfiguration -Force

docs.title: Output
docs.text: None.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Configuration Guide
  • Cmdlet Reference: Get-PSScriptBuilderConfiguration
  • Cmdlet Reference: Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot

docs.title: New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector
docs.text: Creates a new content collector for managing multiple component collectors.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Creates an empty PSScriptBuilderContentCollector that manages a collection of component collectors (Using, Enum, Class, Function, File), orchestrates their execution, and provides centralized access to what they collect.

Populate it either by piping it into Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector one collector at a time, or by passing pre-created collectors up front via -Collector. Every collector's CollectionKey must be unique — a duplicate throws an error immediately, whichever way it was added.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -Collector PSScriptBuilderCollectorBase[] Pre-created collector instances (see New-PSScriptBuilderCollector) to initialize the ContentCollector with.

docs.title: Populate via the pipeline
docs.text:
$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class -CollectionKey "CLASSES" -IncludePath "src\Classes" |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -CollectionKey "FUNCTIONS" -IncludePath "src\Public"

docs.title: Pre-populate with collectors created up front
docs.text:
$collectors = @(
    New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Using -CollectionKey "USINGS" -IncludePath "src"
    New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class -CollectionKey "CLASSES" -IncludePath "src\Classes"
    New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -CollectionKey "FUNCTIONS" -IncludePath "src\Public"
)
$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector -Collector $collectors

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Returns a PSScriptBuilderContentCollector object.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: • Collectors execute in a fixed order regardless of registration order — Using, Enum, Class, Function, File — see Execution Order.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Collectors Guide
  • Cmdlet Reference: New-PSScriptBuilderCollector
  • Cmdlet Reference: Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector
  • Cmdlet Reference: Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector
  • Cmdlet Reference: Remove-PSScriptBuilderCollector

docs.title: New-PSScriptBuilderProject
docs.text: Scaffolds a new PSScriptBuilder project structure.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Creates a complete project directory structure for a new PSScriptBuilder project: a configuration file, a template, a build script, and all required source directories.

If -IncludeReleaseManagement is specified, the cmdlet also creates release management files — psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json and psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json — and a release script with -Major, -Minor, and -Patch switches.

If the target directory already exists and is not empty, the cmdlet fails with an error unless -Force is specified. To add release management to an existing project, run the cmdlet again with -IncludeReleaseManagement -Force — this overwrites all existing project files, including the configuration file, the build script, and the template.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -Name string Required. The name of the project to scaffold. Used to derive file and directory names. -Path string The directory in which to create the project folder. Defaults to the current working directory. -IncludeReleaseManagement switch Also creates release management files (see Description). -NoSampleFiles switch Suppresses creation of the sample source files that by default demonstrate enum, class, and function definitions with dependency relationships. -Force switch Overwrites existing files in the target directory instead of failing with an error.

docs.title: Scaffold a new project
docs.text:
New-PSScriptBuilderProject -Name "MyProject"

Creates a new project named "MyProject" in the current working directory, including the configuration file, a template, a build script, and sample source files.

docs.title: Scaffold a project with release management
docs.text:
New-PSScriptBuilderProject -Name "MyModule" -Path "C:\Projects" -IncludeReleaseManagement

Creates a new project in C:\Projects\MyModule with full release management support: psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json, psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json, and a release script with -Major, -Minor, and -Patch switches.

docs.title: Recreate a project, overwriting existing files
docs.text:
New-PSScriptBuilderProject -Name "MyProject" -Force

Resets an existing project's scaffolding back to its default state.

docs.title: Scaffold a project without sample source files
docs.text:
New-PSScriptBuilderProject -Name "MyProject" -NoSampleFiles

Useful when starting from scratch, or in automated environments where the sample code would need to be removed anyway.

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Returns a PSScriptBuilderScaffoldingResult object describing what was created.

docs.text:

docs.title: New-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData
docs.text: Creates a new release data file with default values.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Creates psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json (path read from the loaded PSScriptBuilder configuration) with SemVer's starting defaults — 0.1.0, build number 0, and every timestamp/Git field left $null until explicitly refreshed. See Set Up the Release Data File for the full resulting file and what each field means.

Fails with an error if the file already exists, unless -Force is specified.

This cmdlet also supports -WhatIf and -Confirm (PowerShell's ShouldProcess pattern).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -Force switch Overwrite the release data file if it already exists.

docs.title: Create the release data file
docs.text: New-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData

docs.title: Preview without writing
docs.text: New-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData -WhatIf

docs.title: Reinitialize an existing project
docs.text: New-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData -Force

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Returns the same hierarchical structure Get-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData returns by default, describing the newly created release data.

docs.title: New-PSScriptBuilderTemplate
docs.text: Generates a PSScriptBuilder template file from a content collector configuration.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Analyzes the registered collectors and their dependencies to generate a ready-to-use template file with the correct placeholders, automatically choosing the appropriate mode:

  • Free — no cross-dependencies detected; an individual {{CollectionKey}} placeholder is generated for each registered collector
  • Ordered — cross-dependencies detected between component types; a combined {{ORDERED_COMPONENTS}} placeholder is generated instead, along with {{USING_STATEMENTS}} and {{FILE_CONTENTS}} if those collectors are registered
  • Hybrid — no cross-dependencies detected, but -OrderedMode was specified; same placeholders as Ordered mode

See the Templates Guide for the full mode-selection rules.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Description -ContentCollector PSScriptBuilderContentCollector Required. The collector configuration to generate the template from. Accepts pipeline input — typically chained directly from New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector/Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector. -OutputPath string Required. Path to the template file to generate. Supports both absolute paths and paths relative to the project root (see Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot). -OrderedComponentsKey string The placeholder key used for the combined components block in Ordered/Hybrid mode. Default: "ORDERED_COMPONENTS". Must match the key passed to Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild and Get-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis. -OrderedMode switch Forces Hybrid mode even when no cross-dependencies are detected — use this to keep a template valid ahead of cross-dependencies you expect to introduce later. -Force switch Overwrites the template file if it already exists.

This cmdlet also supports -WhatIf and -Confirm (PowerShell's ShouldProcess pattern).

docs.title: Generate a template with automatic mode detection
docs.text:
$result = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class -IncludePath "src\Classes" |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath "src\Public" |
    New-PSScriptBuilderTemplate -OutputPath "build\Templates\MyProject.ps1.template"

Write-Host "Generated template: $($result.OutputPath)"
Write-Host "Mode: $($result.Mode)"
Write-Host "Placeholders: $($result.Placeholders -join ', ')"

docs.title: Force Ordered/Hybrid mode ahead of expected cross-dependencies
docs.text:
New-PSScriptBuilderTemplate -ContentCollector $contentCollector `
    -OutputPath "build\Templates\MyScript.ps1.template" `
    -OrderedMode

docs.title: Overwrite an existing template
docs.text:
New-PSScriptBuilderTemplate -ContentCollector $contentCollector `
    -OutputPath "build\Templates\MyScript.ps1.template" `
    -Force

docs.title: Preview template generation without writing any files
docs.text:
New-PSScriptBuilderTemplate -ContentCollector $contentCollector `
    -OutputPath "build\Templates\MyScript.ps1.template" `
    -WhatIf

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Returns a PSScriptBuilderTemplateGenerationResult object describing what was generated.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Templates are written using UTF-8 with a byte order mark (BOM).
  • The generated file is a minimal starting point — add any surrounding PowerShell code (module header, footer, etc.) before using it in a build.

docs.title: Remove-PSScriptBuilderCollector
docs.text: Removes a collector from a ContentCollector.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Removes the collector matching -CollectionKey from a ContentCollector, and returns the same ContentCollector for further pipeline chaining.

If no collector with that key exists, the cmdlet writes a warning rather than an error — safe to call from a cleanup or idempotent script even if the collector was already removed. This is a RAM-only change: nothing on disk is affected, and the collector can always be re-registered later with Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -ContentCollector PSScriptBuilderContentCollector Required. The ContentCollector to remove the collector from. Accepts pipeline input, enabling fluent chaining. -CollectionKey string Required. The exact key (case-insensitive) of the collector to remove.

docs.title: Remove a collector via the pipeline
docs.text: $contentCollector | Remove-PSScriptBuilderCollector -CollectionKey "TEMP_FUNCTIONS"

docs.title: Replace a collector in a single pipeline
docs.text:
$contentCollector = $contentCollector |
    Remove-PSScriptBuilderCollector -CollectionKey "TEMP" |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class -IncludePath "src\New"

docs.title: Remove every collector matching a key pattern
docs.text:
$collectorsToRemove = Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector -ContentCollector $contentCollector |
    Where-Object { $_.CollectionKey -like "TEMP_*" }

foreach ($collector in $collectorsToRemove) {
    $contentCollector = Remove-PSScriptBuilderCollector -ContentCollector $contentCollector -CollectionKey $collector.CollectionKey
}

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Returns the same PSScriptBuilderContentCollector passed in via -ContentCollector — always, even when the key wasn't found.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Collectors Guide
  • Cmdlet Reference: Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector
  • Cmdlet Reference: Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector

docs.title: Resolve-PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation
docs.text: Resolves an output script line number or ErrorRecord back to its source file location.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Reads the .sourcemap.json sidecar written by Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild's -WriteSourceMap (or Watch-PSScriptBuilderProject's Build mode with the same switch) and resolves a specific output line, or the line from a caught ErrorRecord, back to the original source file and line. Omit both -LineNumber and -ErrorRecord to retrieve every entry in the source map at once.

Accepts either the build result directly (-BuildResult, sidecar path derived from its SourceMapPath) or an explicit -OutputPath (sidecar path derived by appending .sourcemap.json).

A SHA-256 hash comparison against the output file detects a stale source map — one written before the output was rebuilt without -WriteSourceMap again — and emits a warning, but resolution still proceeds using the (possibly outdated) data.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Description -BuildResult PSScriptBuilderBuildResult The build result to resolve against. Accepts pipeline input. Requires a build run with -WriteSourceMap. -OutputPath string Path to the output script to resolve against, as an alternative to -BuildResult. -LineNumber int The 1-based output line to resolve. Cannot be combined with -ErrorRecord. -ErrorRecord ErrorRecord An error whose InvocationInfo.ScriptLineNumber is resolved. Cannot be combined with -LineNumber.

Exactly one of -BuildResult or -OutputPath is required. -LineNumber and -ErrorRecord are optional and mutually exclusive; passing both throws an ArgumentException.

docs.title: Resolve a caught error back to its source
docs.text:
$result = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath 'src\Classes' |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath 'src\Public'  |
    Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild -TemplatePath 'template.psm1' -OutputPath 'output.psm1' -WriteSourceMap

try {
    . $result.OutputPath
}
catch {
    $result | Resolve-PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation -ErrorRecord $_
}

docs.title: Resolve a specific output line number
docs.text: Resolve-PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation -OutputPath 'build\Output\MyProject.ps1' -LineNumber 1000

docs.title: Inspect the full source map
docs.text: $result | Resolve-PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation | Format-Table

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
• A single PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation (or $null if no component covers that line) when -LineNumber or -ErrorRecord is passed
  • Every entry in the source map, as PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation[], when neither is passed

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Source Maps Guide
  • Cmdlet Reference: Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild
  • Cmdlet Reference: Get-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage

docs.title: Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot
docs.text: Sets the PSScriptBuilder project root directory.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Explicitly sets the project root and caches it in $Global:PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot for every subsequent PSScriptBuilder operation in the session.

Calling this cmdlet is optional — without it, the project root is auto-discovered by walking up from the current working directory until a directory containing psscriptbuilder.config.json is found. Call this instead when auto-discovery would fail or pick the wrong directory: in CI, or when a script's working directory differs from the project root. See Project Root Discovery for the full auto-discovery behavior.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -Path string Required. The directory to set as the project root. Must already exist. Accepts pipeline input.

docs.title: Set the project root explicitly at the top of a build script
docs.text:
Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot -Path $PSScriptRoot

$PSScriptRoot resolves to the currently running script's own directory — call this before any other PSScriptBuilder cmdlets.

docs.title: Output
docs.text: None.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Configuration Guide
  • Cmdlet Reference: New-PSScriptBuilderConfiguration

docs.title: Test-PSScriptBuilderBumpConfiguration
docs.text: Tests the bump configuration file for validity.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Validates psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json on disk against the expected structure and checks that every referenced file exists. Useful before any automated bump operation, or after an external tool has modified the file, to verify its integrity first.

Validation errors are reported via Write-Error; add -Verbose for additional validation detail.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: This cmdlet takes no parameters beyond the common ones.

docs.title: Validate before updating bump files
docs.text:
if (Test-PSScriptBuilderBumpConfiguration) {
    Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles
}
else {
    Write-Warning "Bump configuration has errors, fix them first"
}

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Returns $true if the bump configuration file is valid, $false otherwise.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:

docs.title: Test-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData
docs.text: Tests the release data file for validity.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Validates psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json on disk against the expected structure — for example, that all required fields exist and the version components are valid integers. Useful before any automated release operation, or after an external tool has modified the file, to verify its integrity first.

Validation errors are reported via Write-Error; add -Verbose for additional validation detail.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: This cmdlet takes no parameters beyond the common ones.

docs.title: Validate before bumping the version
docs.text:
if (Test-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData) {
    Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData -Patch
}
else {
    Write-Warning "Release data has errors, fix them first"
}

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Returns $true if the release data file is valid, $false otherwise.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Release Management Guide
  • Cmdlet Reference: Test-PSScriptBuilderBumpConfiguration
  • Cmdlet Reference: Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData

docs.title: Test-PSScriptBuilderTemplate
docs.text: Validates a PSScriptBuilder template file without performing a build.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Runs the same collection and dependency analysis a real build would — so it sees the same cross-dependencies — then reports whether the template is valid, without writing any output. Returns a plain $true/$false; for the specific errors when it's $false, or a full report of which placeholders are missing or unknown, use Get-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis instead — or add -Verbose here to see the same validation detail logged as it runs.

See Placeholder Rules and Validation Modes for what's actually checked, and Validation Error Reference for what each failure means and how to fix it.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Description -ContentCollector PSScriptBuilderContentCollector Required. The collector configuration to validate against. Accepts pipeline input, enabling fluent chaining from Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector. -TemplatePath string Required. Path to the template file to validate. -OrderedComponentsKey string The combined-components placeholder key, for Ordered/Hybrid Mode templates. Default: "ORDERED_COMPONENTS".

docs.title: Validate before building
docs.text:
$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath "src\Classes" |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath "src\Public"

if (Test-PSScriptBuilderTemplate -ContentCollector $contentCollector -TemplatePath "build\Templates\MyProject.ps1.template") {
    Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild -ContentCollector $contentCollector `
        -TemplatePath "build\Templates\MyProject.ps1.template" `
        -OutputPath   "build\Output\MyProject.ps1"
}

docs.title: Validate with a custom combined-components key
docs.text:
Test-PSScriptBuilderTemplate -ContentCollector $contentCollector `
    -TemplatePath "template.psm1" `
    -OrderedComponentsKey "ALL_COMPONENTS"

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Returns $true if the template is valid, $false otherwise. Only unexpected errors (e.g. a missing template file) are terminating — a failed validation is a normal $false result, not an error.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Templates Guide
  • Cmdlet Reference: Get-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis
  • Cmdlet Reference: Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild

docs.title: Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles
docs.text: Updates configured project files with current version information.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Applies the current release data's tokens to every file configured in psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json — Simple Token Mode, Regex Pattern Mode, or a mix of both. See Apply Tokens to Project Files for the full workflow, and Configure Bump Files for how a file's tokens/patterns are set up in the first place.

Before writing any change to disk, a backup of each target file is created; if an error occurs during processing, the originals are restored from their backups, leaving every project file in a consistent state.

A warning is emitted for any configured file whose entries all failed to match its current content — most commonly a Placeholder-mode entry with no Regex-mode fallback, already consumed by an earlier run. Add a Regex-mode entry (Mixed Mode) to keep matching on subsequent runs.

This cmdlet also supports -WhatIf and -Confirm (PowerShell's ShouldProcess pattern).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: This cmdlet takes no parameters beyond the common ones and -WhatIf/-Confirm.

docs.title: Preview which files would change
docs.text: Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles -WhatIf

docs.title: Apply tokens and display what changed
docs.text:
Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles | Format-PSScriptBuilderBumpResult
Output
File : C:\Projects\MyProject\src\MyProject.ps1

  Token     : VERSION
  Old Value : {{VERSION}}
  New Value : 0.1.1

  Token     : BUILD_TIMESTAMP
  Old Value : {{BUILD_TIMESTAMP}}
  New Value : 2026-09-14T12:55:50Z

File : C:\Projects\MyProject\build\Output\MyModule.psd1

  Pattern   : ModuleVersion\s*=\s*'({REGEX_VERSION})'
  Token     : VERSION
  Old Value : ModuleVersion = '0.1.0'
  New Value : ModuleVersion = '0.1.1'

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Returns a PSScriptBuilderBumpFilesResult object.

  • Cmdlet Reference: Test-PSScriptBuilderBumpConfiguration
  • Cmdlet Reference: Get-PSScriptBuilderBumpConfiguration

docs.title: Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData
docs.text: Updates release data including version and metadata.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Performs atomic release data management operations with transactional semantics and automatic rollback capability. Supports:

  • Semantic version bumping (Major/Minor/Patch)
  • Explicit version setting via -Version (e.g., "1.0.0", "2.1.0-beta")
  • Build metadata updates (automatic or manual)
  • Git metadata updates (automatic from repository)
  • Prerelease and build metadata management

Operations are transactional with automatic rollback on failure.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Name Type Description -Major switch Increments the major version (X.0.0), resetting minor and patch to 0. -Minor switch Increments the minor version (0.X.0), resetting patch to 0. -Patch switch Increments the patch version (0.0.X). -Version string Sets an explicit version string (e.g., "1.0.0", "2.1.0-beta", "v1.0.0"), supporting full SemVer including prerelease and build metadata. -Prerelease string Sets the prerelease identifier (e.g., "alpha.1", "beta", "rc.1"). Must match ^[0-9a-zA-Z-.]+$. -ClearPrerelease switch Removes the prerelease identifier. -BuildMetadata string Sets build metadata (not auto-updated). Must match ^[0-9a-zA-Z-.]+$. -ClearBuildMetadata switch Removes build metadata. -UpdateBuildDetails switch Re-stamps the build date, time, timestamp, and number. -UpdateGitDetails switch Captures the current Git commit, short commit, branch, and latest tag. Requires git to be available in PATH.

-Major, -Minor, -Patch, and -Version are mutually exclusive — at most one may be used per call. Every other parameter in this table can be combined freely with a version switch, or used entirely on its own. -Prerelease and -ClearPrerelease are likewise mutually exclusive with each other, as are -BuildMetadata and -ClearBuildMetadata. This cmdlet also supports -WhatIf and -Confirm (PowerShell's ShouldProcess pattern).

docs.title: Bump the major version and refresh build metadata
docs.text: Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData -Major -UpdateBuildDetails

docs.title: Preview a minor bump with a prerelease identifier, without writing it
docs.text: Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData -Minor -Prerelease "beta.1" -WhatIf

docs.title: Set an explicit version and refresh build metadata
docs.text: Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData -Version "1.0.0" -UpdateBuildDetails

docs.title: Refresh only the Git metadata, without changing the version
docs.text: Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData -UpdateGitDetails

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Returns a PSScriptBuilderReleaseDataResult object describing what changed.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Requires a loaded PSScriptBuilder configuration and an existing release data file.
  • Automatic rollback on failure restores all modified files — the release data is never left in a partially updated state.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Release Management Guide
  • Cmdlet Reference: New-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData
  • Cmdlet Reference: Get-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData
  • Cmdlet Reference: Format-PSScriptBuilderReleaseDataResult

docs.title: Watch-PSScriptBuilderProject
docs.text: Watches project source files and triggers a build or custom script block on every change.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Monitors every registered collector's -IncludePath directories, and optionally the template file's directory, for changes. On a change, either reruns a full build (Build mode) or invokes a custom script block (Script mode) — never both.

Multiple changes within the debounce window are collapsed into a single execution; a change that arrives while a build or script is still running triggers exactly one more execution afterward, without waiting through another debounce period.

The watcher runs until stopped with Ctrl+C. It does not build once on startup — only on the first detected change. Build failures and script errors are reported but never stop the watcher.

docs.title: Common to Both Modes
docs.text: Name Type Description -ContentCollector PSScriptBuilderContentCollector Required. Determines which directories are watched, via its collectors' -IncludePath values. -TemplatePath string Path to the template file. Required in Build mode; optional in Script mode (only needed if a template change should also trigger the script block). When provided, its directory is watched too, and a change there always triggers a run regardless of -IncludeExtension. -Debounce int Milliseconds to wait after a change before triggering a run. Default: 500. -IncludeExtension string[] File extensions that trigger a run. Replaces the default list rather than adding to it — include ".ps1" again if still wanted. Default: @(".ps1"). Pass @() to react to a change in any file.

docs.title: Build Mode
docs.text: Name Type Description -OutputPath string Required. Path to the output file. Automatically excluded from the watch to prevent rebuild loops. -BackupPath string Backup directory, used only when -EnableBackup is specified. -OrderedComponentsKey string The combined-components placeholder key. Default: "ORDERED_COMPONENTS". -EnableBackup switch Back up an existing output file before each rebuild overwrites it. -SkipSyntaxValidation switch Skip the post-write syntax check. -WriteSourceMap switch Write a .sourcemap.json sidecar after each build. -OnSuccess scriptblock Runs after each successful build, receiving the PSScriptBuilderBuildResult as its first argument. -OnError scriptblock Runs after each failed build, receiving a PSScriptBuilderWatchBuildErrorResult as its first argument.

docs.title: Script Mode
docs.text: Name Type Description -ScriptBlock scriptblock Required. Runs instead of a build on every change, receiving the changed file paths as a string[].

docs.title: Rebuild on every source change (Build mode)
docs.text:
$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath 'src\Classes' |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath 'src\Public'

Watch-PSScriptBuilderProject -ContentCollector $contentCollector `
                             -TemplatePath     'build\MyProject.ps1.template' `
                             -OutputPath       'build\Output\MyProject.ps1'

docs.title: Run tests after every successful rebuild
docs.text:
Watch-PSScriptBuilderProject -ContentCollector $contentCollector `
                             -TemplatePath     'build\MyProject.ps1.template' `
                             -OutputPath       'build\Output\MyProject.ps1' `
                             -OnSuccess        { Invoke-Pester -Path 'tests' -Output Minimal }

docs.title: Run a custom script block instead of building (Script mode)
docs.text:
Watch-PSScriptBuilderProject -ContentCollector $contentCollector `
                             -ScriptBlock      {
                                 param([string[]] $changedFiles)
                                 Write-Host "Changed: $($changedFiles -join ', ')"
                                 & '.\my-build.ps1'
                             }

docs.title: Output
docs.text: None. Blocks the current thread until stopped with Ctrl+C; the ContentCollector cannot be modified while the watcher is running.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
Getting Started gets PSScriptBuilder installed and a first script built end to end, with just enough explanation at each step to keep things moving. Work through it in order: install the module first, then scaffold a project and run your first build. From a clean machine to a working, dependency-ordered script takes only a handful of commands and requires nothing beyond PowerShell 5.1 or later — no external dependencies, and the same steps work on Windows, Linux, and macOS.

This section favors speed over explanation. For the same journey with a full walkthrough of why each step works the way it does and what happens under the hood, see Building Your First Project in the Tutorials section instead.

  • Installation

    Install PSScriptBuilder from the PowerShell Gallery, confirm it installed correctly, and load it with using module — required for its classes and enums to be available.

    Installation

  • Quick Start

    Scaffold a project, run the build, and inspect the resulting dependency-ordered script, with an optional path to add release management.

    Quick Start

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
PSScriptBuilder is distributed through the PowerShell Gallery and has no dependencies beyond the PowerShell runtime itself — see the Requirements section for exact version support.

Getting it set up is a one-time process with three steps:

  • Install the module from the Gallery
  • Verify it landed correctly
  • Import it the one specific way its classes and enums require

All three are covered in full — including the two confirmation prompts you are likely to see the first time you install anything from the PowerShell Gallery on a given machine, and the correct way to import a module that exposes PowerShell classes. That last part is worth reading even if you have installed PowerShell modules many times before: most modules only export functions, so the usual Import-Module habit does not raise any warning signs — it simply produces confusing errors once you try to use a class.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Requirement Version PowerShell 5.1 or later (Windows PowerShell and PowerShell 7+) Operating System Windows, Linux, macOS

docs.title: Step 1 — Install the Module
docs.text:
The first time you install anything from the PowerShell Gallery on a machine, Install-Module commonly stops for one of two reasons before it gets to actually installing anything:

  • Untrusted repository — PSGallery is not trusted by default; you are asked to confirm
  • Publisher verification — only if a differently-signed copy of the module already exists locally

Neither is specific to PSScriptBuilder, and both are safe to resolve — at most, you may need to answer a prompt or add one flag to the install command itself. Both are explained here first, since you are reasonably likely to run into at least the first one.

Untrusted repository. The PowerShell Gallery is not marked as a trusted repository by default. Unless it has already been trusted on this machine — from installing some other module previously — Install-Module stops and asks for confirmation before proceeding:

Prompt shown on first install from an untrusted repository
You are installing the modules from an untrusted repository. If you trust this
repository, change its InstallationPolicy value by running the Set-PSRepository
cmdlet. Are you sure you want to install the modules from 'PSGallery'?
[Y] Yes  [A] Yes to All  [N] No  [L] No to All  [S] Suspend  [?] Help (default is "N"):

Answer Y (or A for "Yes to All" if you are installing several modules at once) to proceed for this command only. To skip this prompt permanently for PSGallery, mark it trusted once, before running Install-Module:

Set-PSRepository -Name PSGallery -InstallationPolicy Trusted

Publisher verification. PSScriptBuilder is not Authenticode-signed. This only becomes a problem if a differently-signed (or likewise unsigned) copy of a module with the same name is already present on this machine — for example, from an earlier manual install — in which case Install-Module fails outright with a publisher check error instead of merely prompting. If that happens, add -SkipPublisherCheck to the install command.

Install the module:

Install-Module -Name PSScriptBuilder -Scope CurrentUser

To install for all users on the machine instead (requires elevated permissions):

Install-Module -Name PSScriptBuilder -Scope AllUsers

docs.title: Step 2 — Verify the Installation
docs.text:
Get-Module -Name PSScriptBuilder -ListAvailable

This lists every installed version of PSScriptBuilder together with the folder it was installed into. A successful installation shows at least one entry:

Expected output
    Directory: C:\Users\<you>\Documents\PowerShell\Modules

ModuleType Version Name            ExportedCommands
---------- ------- ----            ----------------
Script     1.2.0   PSScriptBuilder {Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector, Compress-PSScriptBuilderScript, ...}

If the command returns nothing, that does not necessarily mean the installation failed.

On Windows, the most likely reason is that you are checking from a different PowerShell edition than the one you used to install. Windows is the only platform where PowerShell exists as two separate editions — Windows PowerShell (powershell.exe) and PowerShell 7+ (pwsh.exe) — each with its own default module folder, even for the same -Scope. A module installed under one edition is simply not visible from the other. On Linux and macOS, where only PowerShell 7+ exists, this particular cause does not apply.

Fix: run the verification command in the same PowerShell window you used for Install-Module. If you need PSScriptBuilder available in both editions, install it once from each — or see Troubleshooting: sharing a module path across PowerShell editions for a one-time fix that unifies the two.

docs.title: Step 3 — Import the Module
docs.text:
PSScriptBuilder exposes PowerShell classes and enums. PowerShell only makes class and enum definitions available when a module is imported with using module.

Import PSScriptBuilder this way, as the very first statement in your script, before any other code:

✅ Correct — classes and enums are available
using module PSScriptBuilder

Do not import it this way:

❌ Wrong — classes and enums will NOT be available
Import-Module PSScriptBuilder

Why this matters: using module and Import-Module do different things:

  • using module is a parser directive While parsing the script, PowerShell reads the module's class and enum definitions and registers them as resolvable type literals.
  • Import-Module is an ordinary cmdlet It loads the module's exported functions into the session like any other module, but it never performs that type-literal registration.

In practice, if you import PSScriptBuilder the wrong way and your script then references one of its enum values:

[PSScriptBuilderCollectorType]::ClassCollector

— it fails:

Result
Unable to find type [PSScriptBuilderCollectorType].

Because using module needs to be processed by the parser, PowerShell's grammar requires it to be the very first statement in the script. Comments and blank lines are fine before it — an actual statement is not:

Result of a real statement before using module
A 'using' statement must appear before any other statements in a script.

This applies to a script file, parsed as a whole. At an interactive PowerShell prompt, each line you enter is parsed and run on its own, so using module just needs to run before you reference one of PSScriptBuilder's types — not necessarily as the first command you've ever typed in that session.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: With the module installed, verified, and importable, setup is complete. Head to Quick Start to scaffold a new project and run your first build in under a minute.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
Keeping PSScriptBuilder up to date

Checks the PowerShell Gallery for a newer version and installs it: 

Update-Module -Name PSScriptBuilder
This goes through the Gallery the same way Install-Module does, so the same untrusted-repository prompt described for installing the module can reappear here too, if the repository has not been marked trusted. The new version is installed alongside any older ones already present — Update-Module does not remove them. To remove an old version once you no longer need it: 
Uninstall-Module -Name PSScriptBuilder -RequiredVersion <old version>

docs.title: See Also
docs.text: • Troubleshooting: environment diagnostics — sharing a module path across PowerShell editions, and other environment questions

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
You write your PowerShell classes, enums, and functions in separate, focused files — but a deployable script needs everything in a single file, in the correct dependency order. PSScriptBuilder resolves the dependencies and assembles that file automatically.

This guide gets you from zero to a working, dependency-ordered script in three steps:

  • Scaffold a new project
  • Run the build
  • Run the generated output

Prerequisites:

  • PSScriptBuilder installed — see Installation

docs.title: Step 1 — Scaffold a New Project
docs.text:
Open a PowerShell session, then import the module — none of the cmdlets work without it:

using module PSScriptBuilder

With the module imported, scaffold a new project:

New-PSScriptBuilderProject -Name "MyProject"

By default, the project folder is created in the current working directory. To create it somewhere else, pass -Path:

New-PSScriptBuilderProject -Name "MyProject" -Path "C:\Projects"

Either way, the command creates the complete directory structure, a configuration file, a template, and a build script in one step. It also creates three sample source files that are deliberately chosen to demonstrate dependency resolution:

  • WorkStatus.ps1 — an enum with three values
  • Employee.ps1 — a class that uses WorkStatus as a property type
  • Get-EmployeeInfo.ps1 — a function that accepts an Employee parameter

These files depend on each other. PSScriptBuilder analyses the dependencies and determines the correct output order automatically — regardless of how the files are arranged on disk. For a real project without sample files, pass -NoSampleFiles:

New-PSScriptBuilderProject -Name "MyProject" -NoSampleFiles

docs.title: Step 2 — Run the Build
docs.text:
Build-MyProject.ps1 was generated by the scaffold command. It configures the collectors, points them at the source directories, and runs the build:

cd MyProject
.\Build-MyProject.ps1
Expected output
WARNING: 2 cross-collector dependency(s) detected. Verify template placeholder order. Run with -Verbose for details.

Build Summary
  Output : ...\build\Output\MyProject.ps1
  Size   : 734 bytes
  Time   : 1.05 s

Components
  Enums     : 1
  Classes   : 1
  Functions : 1
  Total     : 3

The warning is expected — Employee references WorkStatus and Get-EmployeeInfo references Employee, spanning three different collectors. It's a feature, not a problem to fix: see Building Your First Project for the full explanation.

The build output is written to build\Output\MyProject.ps1.

docs.title: Step 3 — Run the Generated Script
docs.text:
Open build\Output\MyProject.ps1 and you will see WorkStatus, Employee, and Get-EmployeeInfo appear in exactly that sequence — resolved from the actual dependencies, not from the file names. At the bottom of the generated script you will find a sample invocation that was included in the template:

Sample invocation (inside MyProject.ps1)
$employee = [Employee]::new("Alice", [WorkStatus]::Active)
Get-EmployeeInfo -Employee $employee

Run the generated script to see it in action:

.\build\Output\MyProject.ps1
Output
Alice [Active]

With the project scaffolded, built, and run, all three steps are complete.

Want to understand what's happening under the hood?

See Building Your First Project for a step-by-step walkthrough that explains each part of the pipeline.

docs.title: What Gets Created
docs.text:
Now that it works, here is the complete project layout for reference:

MyProject/
├── psscriptbuilder.config.json       ← build and release settings
├── Build-MyProject.ps1               ← run this to build
├── src/
│   ├── Enums/
│   │   └── WorkStatus.ps1            ← sample: enum with Active, OnLeave, Terminated
│   ├── Classes/
│   │   └── Employee.ps1              ← sample: class referencing WorkStatus
│   └── Public/
│       └── Get-EmployeeInfo.ps1      ← sample: function referencing Employee
└── build/
    ├── Templates/
    │   └── MyProject.ps1.template    ← defines the output structure
    └── Output/                       ← generated files go here

Replace the sample files with your own source files and run Build-MyProject.ps1 again. PSScriptBuilder will resolve the dependency order of whatever you put there.

docs.title: With Release Management
docs.text:
If your project needs version tracking — bumping a version number before each build and recording when it was built — add -IncludeReleaseManagement to the scaffold command:

New-PSScriptBuilderProject -Name "MyProject" -IncludeReleaseManagement

This creates everything Scaffold a New Project does, plus a build\Release\ directory with two configuration files and a dedicated release script in the project root, and two extra lines in the generated template:

  • build\Release\psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json — stores the full release state: version, build metadata, and Git details. You edit this file (or let PSScriptBuilder update it) when preparing a release.
  • build\Release\psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json — defines which files receive version updates and how. Pre-configured for the generated template.
  • Release-MyProject.ps1 — a dedicated release script that runs the full release workflow in a single command. It accepts -Major, -Minor, or -Patch to bump the version, updates the release data file, updates the version and timestamp already written into the template, and then runs the build.
  • # Version: and # Timestamp: — two lines near the top of the generated template, holding placeholder values until the first release.

The full project layout, with release management included:

MyProject/
├── psscriptbuilder.config.json
├── Build-MyProject.ps1
├── Release-MyProject.ps1                     ← run this to release
├── src/
│   ├── Enums/
│   │   └── WorkStatus.ps1
│   ├── Classes/
│   │   └── Employee.ps1
│   └── Public/
│       └── Get-EmployeeInfo.ps1
└── build/
    ├── Templates/
    │   └── MyProject.ps1.template            ← now includes # Version: and # Timestamp: lines
    ├── Output/
    └── Release/
        ├── psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json  ← version, build metadata, Git details
        └── psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json   ← which files get version updates, and how

Run Release-MyProject.ps1 to see the release workflow in action. Any of -Major, -Minor, or -Patch works for a demo like this — -Patch is used here simply as the smallest bump:

.\Release-MyProject.ps1 -Patch
Expected output
Category : Version

  Property  : patch
  Old Value : 0
  New Value : 1

  Property  : full
  Old Value : 0.1.0
  New Value : 0.1.1

...

The release script also builds the project — producing the same warning and Build Summary shown in Run the Build.

The generated psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json is pre-configured for repeatable releases: it finds the # Version: and # Timestamp: lines already written into the template and updates them with the real values, on every run. See Release Management for how this mechanism works in full.

The build script Build-MyProject.ps1 remains unchanged — it always produces an output from whatever state the template is currently in. The separation keeps the build concern and the release concern distinct: you build as often as you like, and you release when you are ready.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
You now have a working PSScriptBuilder project — from scaffold to a deployable, dependency-ordered script — without writing any ordering logic yourself.

In short: PSScriptBuilder resolves the order of your components for you, regardless of how the source files are arranged on disk.

docs.title: Guides
docs.text: These guides explain each PSScriptBuilder feature in depth. They assume you already have a working PSScriptBuilder project — if you are new, start with the Quick Start. The guides are grouped into four areas that follow the natural workflow: the core concepts every build relies on, assembling and running a build, analyzing its structure, and publishing a release.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Every build depends on three things, covered here in the order you'll set them up.

  • Configuration centralizes settings in a single file — creating and reading it, the full field reference, and how paths resolve relative to the project root.
  • Collectors scan source files and extract components — the five collector types, combining and filtering them, and the properties each one exposes.
  • Templates define how those collected components are assembled into the output script — the three placeholder modes (Free, Ordered, Hybrid) and how validation catches mistakes before a build.

Every other guide in this section — and the Analysis guides that inspect a project without building it — builds directly on these three.

  • Configuration

    Centralizes build and release settings in a single JSON file.

    Configuration

  • Collectors

    Scan source files and extract classes, functions, enums, using statements, and raw file content.

    Collectors

  • Templates

    Define the output script structure with placeholder tokens and validation modes.

    Templates

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
Once configuration, collectors, and templates are in place, these guides cover turning them into a build.

  • Build Pipeline runs the build, interprets the result, exports a report, and covers logging, backups, and post-processing.
  • Tool Integrations combines a build with Invoke-Build, PSScriptAnalyzer, Pester, and ModuleBuilder for a complete development workflow.
  • File Watching automates the build itself, rebuilding — or running a custom script — every time a source file changes.

  • Build Pipeline

    Run the full pipeline, interpret the result, configure backups, and post-process the output.

    Build Pipeline

  • Tool Integrations

    Combine PSScriptBuilder with Invoke-Build, PSScriptAnalyzer, Pester, and ModuleBuilder.

    Tool Integrations

  • File Watching

    Automatically rebuild, or run a custom script block, whenever source files change.

    File Watching

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
These guides inspect a project's structure and behavior without necessarily running a build.

  • Dependency Analysis builds and queries the dependency graph that determines component load order, including circular and cross-collector dependencies.
  • Code Analysis inspects collector content, dependency data, and template validation mode — all without running a build.
  • Source Maps is the exception: it traces a completed build's output, and Pester coverage measured against it, back to the original source.

  • Dependency Analysis

    Build a dependency graph, detect cycles, and determine the correct component load order.

    Dependency Analysis

  • Code Analysis

    Inspect your project's structure and collector content without running a build.

    Code Analysis

  • Source Maps

    Trace runtime errors back to source and translate Pester code coverage back to per-source-file results.

    Source Maps

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text:
These guides cover tracking a project's version across releases and wiring the whole workflow into an automated pipeline.

  • Release Management tracks and propagates version numbers, build metadata, and Git context across a project's files, using bump files configured in Simple Token Mode or Regex Pattern Mode.
  • CI/CD Integration takes the whole workflow — build, analyze, release — and runs it in an automated pipeline, illustrated with a GitHub Actions example.

  • Release Management

    Track and propagate version numbers, build metadata, and Git context across all registered project files.

    Release Management

  • CI/CD Integration

    Integrate PSScriptBuilder into any CI/CD system with a GitHub Actions example.

    CI/CD Integration

docs.title: Build Pipeline
docs.text:
The build pipeline collects your source files through your configured collectors and combines them with a template to produce a single, deployable PowerShell file.

This guide assumes both are already configured — see Collectors and Templates if you haven't set them up yet — and focuses on everything that happens once you actually run a build, from invoking it through interpreting and troubleshooting the result.

docs.title: How a Build Works
docs.text:
A build turns your project's independently written source files into one correctly ordered, deployable output. Rather than concatenating files in whatever order they happen to sit on disk, PSScriptBuilder analyzes how your classes and functions actually depend on each other and assembles them in the order that dependency requires — a class that inherits from another, for example, always ends up after its base class in the output, regardless of which file was written first.

PSScriptBuilder runs this analysis, and everything else a build needs, through a single call to Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild, which walks through the following phases in order:

  1. Loads the template file
  2. Runs all registered collectors
  3. Builds and analyzes the dependency graph
  4. Detects circular dependencies
  5. Performs topological sorting
  6. Replaces template placeholders with collected and dependency-resolved components
  7. Optionally backs up the existing output file
  8. Writes the final output file
  9. Optionally writes a source map sidecar alongside the output file

The same phases, grouped:

%%{init: {'flowchart': {'subGraphTitleMargin': {'top': 10, 'bottom': 10}}}}%%
flowchart TD
    A[Load Template] --> B[Collect Sources]
    B --> C

    subgraph C[Analyze Dependencies]
        direction LR
        C1[Build Dependency Graph] --> C2[Detect Circular Dependencies]
        C2 --> C3[Topological Sort]
    end

    C --> D[Assemble Output]
    D --> E[Write Result]

    classDef failStyle stroke:#e53935,stroke-width:2px,stroke-dasharray: 3 3
    C -.->|error| X[Build fails immediately]:::failStyle

This is a fail-fast pipeline: any step failing stops the build immediately, rather than producing partial output. See Error Handling for what each failure looks like and how to resolve it.

docs.title: Build Styles
docs.text:
Each style's example uses the same MyProject project from the Quick Start — if you haven't read it yet, start there. All paths are relative to the project root ($Global:PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot), see Configuration for setup.

PSScriptBuilder supports multiple styles for setting up a build — choose based on how much control and readability you need:

  • Explicit — each collector and parameter is a named variable; easy to follow, easy to extend
  • Pipeline — collectors are chained inline; build parameters are passed as a variable
  • Fluent — the entire build is a single pipeline expression; most concise, best for stable scripts

docs.title: Explicit
docs.text:
Each collector and build parameter is a named variable. This makes it easy to follow what happens at each step and to add conditional logic if needed:

Build-MyProject.ps1
$enumCollector     = New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Enum     -IncludePath 'src\Enums'
$classCollector    = New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath 'src\Classes'
$functionCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath 'src\Public'

$collectors = $enumCollector, $classCollector, $functionCollector
$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector -Collector $collectors

$result = Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild `
    -ContentCollector $contentCollector `
    -TemplatePath     'build\Templates\MyProject.ps1.template' `
    -OutputPath       'build\Output\MyProject.ps1'

The explicit style also makes it straightforward to register multiple collectors of the same type — for example, Domain and Utils classes that should be ordered separately, each with a unique -CollectionKey. See Example 10 for a complete walkthrough.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
Instead of creating collectors separately and passing them via -Collector, you can create and register a collector in one step, chained directly onto New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector in a pipeline. Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector is the cmdlet that does this. Use this form when each collector has a straightforward configuration and you don't need to reference them individually afterward:

Build-MyProject.ps1
$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Enum     -IncludePath 'src\Enums'   |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath 'src\Classes' |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath 'src\Public'

$result = Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild `
    -ContentCollector $contentCollector `
    -TemplatePath     'build\Templates\MyProject.ps1.template' `
    -OutputPath       'build\Output\MyProject.ps1'

docs.title: Fluent
docs.text:
The most concise form — all steps in a single pipeline expression. Best suited for simple, stable build scripts where no intermediate variables are needed and parameters don't change:

Build-MyProject.ps1
$result = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Enum     -IncludePath 'src\Enums'   |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath 'src\Classes' |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath 'src\Public'  |
    Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild `
        -TemplatePath 'build\Templates\MyProject.ps1.template' `
        -OutputPath   'build\Output\MyProject.ps1'

docs.title: Using a Configuration File
docs.text:
Any of the three build styles — Explicit, Pipeline, or Fluent — can be combined with values read from a configuration file, instead of hardcoded paths. The previous examples hardcode paths like 'build\Templates\MyProject.ps1.template' directly in the build script.

That works for simple projects, but as soon as you use the same build script in multiple environments — or want to change paths without touching the script — it becomes a maintenance problem.

Paths, backup settings, and output locations can instead be defined once in a configuration file, rather than duplicated across build scripts.

Get-PSScriptBuilderConfiguration reads psscriptbuilder.config.json from the project root and returns these settings as a typed $config object, with each value available as $config.Build.*. Splatting keeps the Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild call clean — no long backtick-continuation lines:

Build-MyProject.ps1
$config = Get-PSScriptBuilderConfiguration

$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Enum     -IncludePath 'src\Enums'   |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath 'src\Classes' |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath 'src\Public'

$buildParams = @{
    ContentCollector = $contentCollector
    TemplatePath     = Join-Path $config.Build.TemplatePath 'MyProject.ps1.template'
    OutputPath       = Join-Path $config.Build.OutputPath   'MyProject.ps1'
    BackupPath       = $config.Build.BackupPath
    EnableBackup     = $config.Build.BackupEnabled
}

$result = Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild @buildParams

If you'd rather not write a build script by hand at all, New-PSScriptBuilderProject can generate a ready-to-run build script for you — see Quick Start.

docs.title: Interpreting the Build Result
docs.text:
Every build returns a PSScriptBuilderBuildResult object ($result in the examples throughout this guide) summarizing what was collected, how long the build took, and where the output was written.

Use Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult for a quick human-readable summary, or access the properties directly when integrating into scripts or CI pipelines:

$result | Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult
Output
Build Summary
  Output : ...\build\Output\MyProject.ps1
  Size   : 734 bytes
  Time   : 830.15 ms

Components
  Enums     : 1
  Classes   : 1
  Functions : 1
  Total     : 3

Add -Detailed to include all processed source files and component dependencies:

$result | Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult -Detailed

Output — the same Build Summary and Components, now with this appended:

Processed Files (3)
  ...\src\Enums\WorkStatus.ps1
  ...\src\Classes\Employee.ps1
  ...\src\Public\Get-EmployeeInfo.ps1

Component Details
  Enum:
    WorkStatus
      File : ...\src\Enums\WorkStatus.ps1

  Class:
    Employee
      File : ...\src\Classes\Employee.ps1
      Deps : WorkStatus

  Function:
    Get-EmployeeInfo
      File : ...\src\Public\Get-EmployeeInfo.ps1
      Deps : Employee

For direct property access — for example in CI scripts or custom reporting — the result object exposes all details as typed properties:

$classCount    = $result.ComponentCounts.ClassDefinitions
$functionCount = $result.ComponentCounts.FunctionDefinitions
$durationMs    = $result.ExecutionTime.TotalMilliseconds

Write-Host "Built $($result.TotalComponents) components ($classCount classes, $functionCount functions) in $durationMs ms"
Write-Host "Output: $($result.OutputPath) ($($result.OutputFileSize) bytes)"
Write-Host "Syntax valid: $($result.SyntaxValid)"

if ($result.SourceMapPath) {
    Write-Host "Source map: $($result.SourceMapPath)"
}

For a complete property reference see Type Reference: Build Results.

docs.title: Exporting the Build Report
docs.text:
A build's result ($result, returned by Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild) can also be exported and persisted, rather than just displayed — useful for auditing, attaching to CI artifacts, or tracking changes between builds.

Pass $result to Export-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult to write it as a structured JSON file, which can be used directly in CI artifact upload steps:

$exportedPath = $result | Export-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult -Path 'build\reports\build.json' -Force

$exportedPath now holds the file's path as a string. The file itself (build\reports\build.json) contains:

{
    "generatedAt":  "2026-09-09T07:35:33Z",
    "outputPath":  "...\\build\\Output\\MyProject.ps1",
    "outputFileSizeBytes":  734,
    "backupPath":  "",
    "sourceMapPath":  "",
    "syntaxValid":  true,
    "executionTimeMs":  830,
    "totalComponents":  3,
    "componentCounts":  {
                            "usingStatements":  0,
                            "enumDefinitions":  1,
                            "classDefinitions":  1,
                            "functionDefinitions":  1,
                            "fileContents":  0
                        }
}

The compact output includes the build summary, component counts, and a UTC generation timestamp added automatically. Add -Detailed to also include the full list of processed source files and per-component details — type, name, source file, and dependencies:

$result | Export-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult -Path 'build\reports\build.json' -Detailed -Force

-Detailed adds two more top-level fields. processedFiles lists every source file path collected:

"processedFiles":  [
                       "...\\src\\Enums\\WorkStatus.ps1",
                       "...\\src\\Classes\\Employee.ps1",
                       "...\\src\\Public\\Get-EmployeeInfo.ps1"
                   ]

components has one entry per collected component, each with its type, name, source file, and dependencies. Here is one entry from that array, for Employee, as an example:

"components":  [
                   {
                       "type":  "Class",
                       "name":  "Employee",
                       "sourceFile":  "...\\src\\Classes\\Employee.ps1",
                       "dependencies":  [
                                            "WorkStatus"
                                        ]
                   }
               ]

Use the compact export for lightweight tracking, and -Detailed when you need to audit exactly which files and components went into a specific build.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
A build can produce a lot of diagnostic detail beyond its final result — which streams that detail goes to depends on what you need: watching progress interactively, keeping a permanent record, or feeding a CI system's own log capture.

PSScriptBuilder writes to three PowerShell output streams during a build:

Stream Content Success The PSScriptBuilderBuildResult object returned by Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild Verbose Step-by-step trace — collection, dependency analysis, template processing, output writing Warning Non-fatal notices, for example a stale source map detected during resolve

docs.title: Interactive Use
docs.text:
By default, a build runs quietly — only warnings and the final result appear. When developing or troubleshooting interactively, seeing the step-by-step trace as it happens is often more useful than waiting for the result alone.

Add -Verbose to see the full trace on the console:

Build-MyProject.ps1
$result = Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild `
    -ContentCollector $contentCollector `
    -TemplatePath     'build\Templates\MyProject.ps1.template' `
    -OutputPath       'build\Output\MyProject.ps1' `
    -Verbose

$result | Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult
