docs.title: Capturing to a Log File
docs.text:
By default, -Verbose output only appears on the console — nothing is written to disk. Redirecting it to a file lets you keep a permanent record, review it later, or attach it as a CI artifact alongside the build.

Redirect all streams with *>&1 and pipe to Out-File. *>&1 merges every output stream — success, verbose, warning, and error — into the success stream, since Out-File only writes what actually reaches the pipeline:

Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild ... -Verbose *>&1 | Out-File 'build.log'

The trade-off: nothing appears on the console anymore while the build runs, since everything is redirected to the file instead. If you want to see the output and keep a copy, use Start-Transcript instead — it records everything written to the console without redirecting it away:

Start-Transcript -Path 'build.log' -Append
$result = Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild ... -Verbose
$result | Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult
Stop-Transcript

-Append preserves earlier log content when the file already exists.

In a CI pipeline, this manual redirection usually isn't necessary — see CI / CD for how CI systems capture output automatically.

docs.title: CI / CD
docs.text:
CI systems such as GitLab CI and GitHub Actions capture all console output as the job log automatically — no additional configuration is required. Run the build with -Verbose and the full trace is visible in the CI run log, the same way it would be on your own console.

For a structured, machine-readable artifact instead of console output, see Exporting the Build Report.

docs.title: Backup
docs.text:
By default no backup is created before overwriting the output file — Git is the recommended version control mechanism.

A file-based backup can still be useful as a local safety net — for example, before a risky change you want to undo instantly without a checkout, or in environments where the workspace is not a Git repository.

Use -EnableBackup together with -BackupPath to enable it:

Build-MyProject.ps1
$result = Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild `
    -ContentCollector $contentCollector `
    -TemplatePath     'build\Templates\MyProject.ps1.template' `
    -OutputPath       'build\Output\MyProject.ps1' `
    -BackupPath       'build\Backup' `
    -EnableBackup

Backup files are named with a timestamp:

build\Backup\MyProject.ps1.260422_103045.bak

The backup path is included in the build result ($result.BackupPath) and shown by Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult whenever a backup was actually created.

$result.BackupPath is $null in two cases:

  • -EnableBackup wasn't specified at all
  • It was specified, but there was no existing output file to back up yet — for example, on the very first build

A backup only makes sense once there's something to protect.

-BackupPath and -EnableBackup can also be set from a configuration file — see Using a Configuration File, whose example already includes both.

docs.title: Source Maps
docs.text:
When something goes wrong in the built script, or when Pester measures code coverage, both point at the compiled output file — not at the source file the problem actually lives in. A source map closes that gap: it records, for every line of the output, which source file and line it came from. Pass -WriteSourceMap to Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild to write a sidecar .sourcemap.json next to the build's output after each successful build:

Build-MyProject.ps1
$result = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Enum     -IncludePath 'src\Enums'   |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath 'src\Classes' |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath 'src\Public'  |
    Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild `
        -TemplatePath 'build\Templates\MyProject.ps1.template' `
        -OutputPath   'build\Output\MyProject.ps1' `
        -WriteSourceMap

The sidecar path is stored in $result.SourceMapPath and shown by Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult when present. -WriteSourceMap is also available on Watch-PSScriptBuilderProject (Build mode), and can be enabled for every configuration-based build by setting writeSourceMap: true in psscriptbuilder.config.json.

See the Source Maps Guide for resolving output line numbers and ErrorRecords back to source, translating Pester code coverage, and the full property reference for PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation and PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverageResult.

docs.title: Post-Processing
docs.text:
A PSScriptBuilder build output is readable, well-structured PowerShell source — comments intact, blank lines preserved, verbose logging included. That is ideal during development, but when deploying to production you may want to reduce file size, strip diagnostic output, or produce a leaner file that loads faster.

This post-processing step is handled by Compress-PSScriptBuilderScript, which operates on an already-built output file and selectively removes comments, blank lines, and isolated output statements — independently or in any combination. The original build output is never modified unless you explicitly point -DestinationPath at the same file; typically you write to a separate deploy location:

Compress-PSScriptBuilderScript `
    -Path            'build\Output\MyProject.ps1' `
    -RemoveComments `
    -RemoveBlankLines `
    -DestinationPath 'deploy\MyProject.ps1' `
    -Force

Compress-PSScriptBuilderScript also accepts pipeline input from Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild via the OutputPath property, so build and compress can be chained in a single expression instead of running them as two separate steps:

Build-MyProject.ps1
New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Enum     -IncludePath 'src\Enums'   |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath 'src\Classes' |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath 'src\Public'  |
    Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild `
        -TemplatePath 'build\Templates\MyProject.ps1.template' `
        -OutputPath   'build\Output\MyProject.ps1' |
    Compress-PSScriptBuilderScript `
        -RemoveComments `
        -RemoveBlankLines `
        -DestinationPath 'deploy\MyProject.ps1' `
        -Force

Both examples use -RemoveComments and -RemoveBlankLines together, but each operation works independently and is worth understanding on its own. Three operations are available, used independently or in any combination. Regardless of the parameter order you specify, they are always applied in this order:

  1. -RemoveComments
  2. -RemoveOutputStatements
  3. -RemoveBlankLines

This ensures that removing comments or output statements does not leave behind unexpected blank lines.

docs.title: Removing Comments
docs.text: Removes every comment in the script — single-line comments, block comments, and #region/#endregion markers — using PowerShell's own tokenizer rather than a text search, so a # inside a string or here-string is never mistaken for a comment. #Requires statements are always preserved, since the PowerShell runtime requires them to remain at the top of the script.

docs.title: Removing Isolated Output Statements
docs.text:
Removes isolated calls to Write-Verbose, Write-Debug, Write-Host, Write-Warning, or Write-Information. A call counts as isolated only when it stands completely alone as its own statement — not chained into a pipeline, and not nested inside an if, foreach, or other control-flow block:

Isolated - removed
Write-Verbose "Starting..."
Inside control flow - kept
if ($Verbose) { Write-Verbose "..." }
Part of a pipeline - kept
Write-Verbose "..." | Out-Null

Non-isolated calls like these are skipped silently, not treated as an error; use -Verbose on Compress-PSScriptBuilderScript itself to see which calls were skipped and why.

docs.title: Removing Blank Lines
docs.text: Removes every line that contains nothing but whitespace — not just genuinely empty lines, so a line with only spaces or tabs is removed too.

docs.title: Getting the Result Without Writing a File
docs.text:
Omit -DestinationPath to get the processed content as a string instead of writing to a file — useful for inspecting the result, calculating size reductions, or piping into further transformations:

$compressed = Compress-PSScriptBuilderScript `
    -Path 'build\Output\MyProject.ps1' `
    -RemoveComments

$compressed | Measure-Object -Line

Post-processing is optional — skip it during development, and add it as a final step before deploying to production.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
A build that fails partway through is harder to diagnose than one that fails immediately — a half-written output file looks complete but silently omits components. PSScriptBuilder avoids this entirely: Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild throws on the first error encountered and never writes partial output.

All errors are thrown as typed exceptions with detailed messages that include the affected component names and file paths. The most common error conditions, what causes them, and how to resolve them:

docs.title: Missing Template File
docs.text:
When the specified template file does not exist:

FileNotFoundException: Template file not found: 'build\Templates\MyProject.ps1.template'

Verify the path is correct and relative to the project root.

docs.title: Path Not Found
docs.text:
A collector accepts any path at creation time — path validation only happens at runtime, when Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild triggers collection. If an -IncludePath directory does not exist, the build fails with:

IOException: Path not found: C:\MyProject\src\Classes (original: src\Classes)

The message shows both the resolved absolute path and the original value you passed, which makes it easy to spot a typo or a missing directory. Verify that the path exists relative to the project root and that Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot was called before the build.

docs.title: Component Name Conflict
docs.text:
A class and a function with the same name within the same project are explicitly forbidden. PSScriptBuilder uses component names as graph node keys — a collision would cause silent incorrect ordering in the build output:

InvalidOperationException: Component name conflict: 'Employee' is defined as both a Class
(in 'src\Classes\Employee.ps1') and a Function (in 'src\Public\Employee.ps1').
Classes and Functions must have unique names within a PSScriptBuilder project.

Rename one of the conflicting components to resolve the conflict.

docs.title: Circular Dependency
docs.text:
When a circular dependency is detected, the build fails immediately with a detailed error message that includes the full cycle path:

InvalidOperationException: Circular dependency detected: Employee -> Manager -> Employee

Resolve the cycle by removing or redirecting one of the dependencies. The Dependency Analysis Guide explains how to query the dependency graph to locate the cycle before running a build.

docs.title: Syntax Validation Failure
docs.text:
After writing the output file, PSScriptBuilder parses it to verify syntactic correctness. If the parse fails, the build throws:

InvalidOperationException: Output syntax validation failed: <parser error message>

TypeNotFound errors caused by external assemblies not loaded at build time are automatically filtered and do not fail validation. Use -SkipSyntaxValidation only when the output contains syntax that cannot be parsed at all by the PowerShell parser.

  • Source Maps Guide — resolving line numbers/ErrorRecords and translating Pester code coverage

docs.title: CI/CD Integration
docs.text:
PSScriptBuilder is a PowerShell module, so integrating it into a CI/CD pipeline follows the same pattern as any other PowerShell-based build tool — no special CI-specific version or plugin is needed, just a PowerShell-capable runner.

A CI environment differs from a developer's own machine in a few important ways: it starts from a fresh, ephemeral runner with nothing pre-installed, runs entirely non-interactively — so anything requiring a manual prompt or confirmation will hang or fail — and communicates success or failure back to the pipeline exclusively through the process exit code, since there's no person watching the console output.

This guide explains what PSScriptBuilder specifically needs to run under these conditions, and illustrates it with a GitHub Actions example. The same principles apply to GitLab CI, Azure DevOps, Jenkins, or any other system that can run PowerShell — only the surrounding configuration syntax changes.

docs.title: What PSScriptBuilder Needs in CI
docs.text: Integrating PSScriptBuilder into CI splits cleanly into two concerns: your CI configuration and your build script. Keeping these separate — rather than inlining every PowerShell command directly into the CI configuration file — is what makes the setup portable across CI systems and testable on a developer's own machine before ever touching CI at all.

docs.title: In Your CI Configuration
docs.text:
1. Install the module — PSScriptBuilder must be available in the PowerShell module path. A fresh CI runner has nothing pre-installed, so this step runs on every single job.
  2. Run the build script — invoke your Build-MyScript.ps1 (or equivalent). The CI configuration's only remaining job is to call this one script; everything else happens inside it.

docs.title: Inside the Build Script
docs.text:
1. Set the project root — call Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot at the start of your build script; PSScriptBuilder resolves all relative paths from this root. Calling it inside the build script, rather than passing paths explicitly from the CI configuration, keeps CI configuration minimal and the build locally reproducible.
  2. Run the build — collect your project's content and call Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild to produce the output file.
  3. Handle the result — the build throws a typed exception on failure, so a non-zero exit code alone is sufficient for most CI systems to detect a failed job. For more granular control, wrap the call in try/catch — see Handling the Build Result.

Avoid platform-specific escaping issues

Complex PowerShell logic inlined directly into YAML (or another CI config format) is prone to quoting and escaping bugs that only surface once the pipeline actually runs. Keeping build logic in its own .ps1 file avoids this entirely.

docs.title: Example: GitHub Actions
docs.text:
The following workflow illustrates the two CI configuration steps from In Your CI Configuration using GitHub Actions. The workflow runs on every push and pull request, installs PSScriptBuilder from the PowerShell Gallery, and delegates the actual build logic to Build-MyScript.ps1. Keeping the build logic in a script — rather than inline YAML — means the same script works locally and in CI without any changes.

Adapt the YAML syntax to your CI/CD system. The PowerShell commands inside the steps remain the same regardless of the platform:

.github/workflows/build.yml
name: Build

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: windows-latest

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Install PSScriptBuilder
        shell: pwsh
        run: Install-Module PSScriptBuilder -Force -SkipPublisherCheck

      - name: Build
        shell: pwsh
        run: .\Build-MyScript.ps1

docs.title: Handling the Build Result
docs.text:
A build that fails in CI should fail loudly and stop the pipeline immediately — Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild does exactly that, throwing a typed exception on any failure (circular dependencies, missing files, name conflicts, syntax errors), which results in a non-zero PowerShell exit code. Most CI systems treat this as a job failure automatically, so no additional error handling is strictly required.

That said, wrapping the build in a try/catch block has two advantages in a CI context: the error message is written explicitly to the error stream (making it easier to spot in CI logs), and you have a single place to add cleanup logic or notifications if needed. This is what Build-MyScript.ps1 — the script called from Example: GitHub Actions — typically contains, covering all three steps from Inside the Build Script:

Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot -Path $PSScriptRoot

try {
    $result = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
        Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath 'src\Classes' |
        Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath 'src\Public'  |
        Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild `
            -TemplatePath 'build\Templates\MyScript.ps1.template' `
            -OutputPath   'build\Output\MyScript.ps1'

    $result | Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult
}
catch {
    Write-Error "Build failed: $($_.Exception.Message)"
    exit 1
}

Piping to Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult doesn't need a live audience — its output becomes part of the CI job's own log, which is exactly where a developer looks first when investigating a failed or unexpectedly slow build afterward.

docs.title: Exporting the Build Report
docs.text:
Most CI systems can archive files as build artifacts — exporting the build summary this way keeps it available for later inspection without digging through CI logs. Extending the same script from Handling the Build Result, pipe the result to Export-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult right after formatting it:

Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot -Path $PSScriptRoot

try {
    $result = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
        Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath 'src\Classes' |
        Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath 'src\Public'  |
        Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild `
            -TemplatePath 'build\Templates\MyScript.ps1.template' `
            -OutputPath   'build\Output\MyScript.ps1'

    $result | Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult
    $result | Export-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult -Path 'build\reports\build.json' -Detailed -Force
}
catch {
    Write-Error "Build failed: $($_.Exception.Message)"
    exit 1
}

See Build Pipeline: Exporting the Build Report for the full JSON structure and the effect of -Detailed.

docs.title: Compressing Before Deploy
docs.text:
A CI pipeline is a natural place to strip comments, blank lines, and diagnostic output before publishing — the deployed script never needs them. Extending the same script from Exporting the Build Report, pass the build's output to Compress-PSScriptBuilderScript right after exporting the report:

Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot -Path $PSScriptRoot

try {
    $result = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
        Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath 'src\Classes' |
        Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath 'src\Public'  |
        Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild `
            -TemplatePath 'build\Templates\MyScript.ps1.template' `
            -OutputPath   'build\Output\MyScript.ps1'

    $result | Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult
    $result | Export-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult -Path 'build\reports\build.json' -Detailed -Force

    Compress-PSScriptBuilderScript `
        -Path            $result.OutputPath `
        -RemoveComments `
        -RemoveBlankLines `
        -DestinationPath 'deploy\MyScript.ps1' `
        -Force
}
catch {
    Write-Error "Build failed: $($_.Exception.Message)"
    exit 1
}

See Build Pipeline: Post-Processing for what each operation removes, how they combine, and how to get the result as a string instead of writing a file.

docs.title: Code Analysis
docs.text:
PSScriptBuilder's analysis cmdlets let you inspect your project's structure without running a build. No output script is written — the collectors run, the data is extracted, and you get back strongly-typed result objects to work with directly.

Three distinct capabilities fall under this umbrella: querying the raw component data a collector extracted from your source files, examining the full dependency graph and load order, and checking which template validation mode your project activates. This guide's main focus is the first of these — direct, low-level access to collector content — since that level of detail isn't covered anywhere else. Dependency analysis and template analysis are each substantial enough to warrant their own guide, so they're introduced here only briefly, with a pointer to the full treatment.

Collector content queries are especially useful for debugging dependency issues without running a full dependency graph, understanding exactly how PSScriptBuilder sees your code, and building tooling or reports on top of the collected data.

docs.title: Collector Content
docs.text:
To inspect exactly what PSScriptBuilder extracted from your source files — without building anything — retrieve a collector's raw content directly. Get-PSScriptBuilderCollectorContent returns one strongly-typed object per collected component; pass a collector instance directly using -Collector or via the pipeline, and it executes the collector for you automatically.

The returned objects are typed data classes — not PSCustomObject. The exact properties depend on the collector type:

Collector Type Returned Type Key Properties Using PSScriptBuilderUsingData Statement, SourceFiles Enum PSScriptBuilderEnumData Name, SourceCode Class PSScriptBuilderClassData Name, SourceCode, BaseClass, TypeReferences, StaticInitializerReferences, CalledFunctions Function PSScriptBuilderFunctionData Name, SourceCode, CalledFunctions, TypeReferences File PSScriptBuilderFileData FileName, FullPath, Content

For a full explanation of what each property contains and how it is populated, see Collected Data Properties in the Collectors Guide.

Setup — PSScriptBuilder

All examples in this section query PSScriptBuilder's own source tree. Run the following from the root of a PSScriptBuilder checkout to populate $classes and $functions, reused by the Class and Function query examples that follow. The Enum, Using, and File examples under Other Collector Types are each self-contained instead, creating their own variable inline since each is used only once. 

$classes = New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class -IncludePath "src\Classes" |
    Get-PSScriptBuilderCollectorContent

$functions = New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath "src\Public" |
    Get-PSScriptBuilderCollectorContent

docs.title: Find classes with a base class
docs.text:
Filtering by BaseClass gives you a complete picture of your class hierarchy. This is useful when you want to verify that all expected derived classes are present, or when you are debugging a dependency error caused by a missing base class:

$classes | Where-Object { $_.BaseClass } | Select-Object Name, BaseClass
Output
Name                             BaseClass
----                             ---------
PSScriptBuilderBuildOptions      PSScriptBuilderOptionsBase
PSScriptBuilderReleaseOptions    PSScriptBuilderOptionsBase
PSScriptBuilderClassCollector    PSScriptBuilderCollectorBase
PSScriptBuilderEnumCollector     PSScriptBuilderCollectorBase
PSScriptBuilderFileCollector     PSScriptBuilderCollectorBase
PSScriptBuilderFunctionCollector PSScriptBuilderCollectorBase
PSScriptBuilderUsingCollector    PSScriptBuilderCollectorBase

Seven classes in PSScriptBuilder's own source inherit from something: two configuration classes share PSScriptBuilderOptionsBase, and five collector implementations share PSScriptBuilderCollectorBase.

docs.title: Find all subclasses of a specific base class
docs.text:
The reverse of the previous query — instead of asking "which classes have a base class?", this asks "which classes inherit from a specific type?". Useful when you want to verify a concrete class hierarchy or understand the full extent of a base class:

$classes |
    Where-Object { $_.BaseClass -eq "PSScriptBuilderCollectorBase" } |
    Select-Object Name
Output
Name
----
PSScriptBuilderClassCollector
PSScriptBuilderEnumCollector
PSScriptBuilderFileCollector
PSScriptBuilderFunctionCollector
PSScriptBuilderUsingCollector

docs.title: Find classes that reference a specific type
docs.text:
When you are about to change a class, this query shows which other classes depend on it directly — a lightweight impact analysis without running a full dependency graph:

$classes |
    Where-Object { $_.TypeReferences -contains "PSScriptBuilderFileSystemHelper" } |
    Select-Object Name

Output (18 matches; first 6 shown):

Name
----
PSScriptBuilderFileSystemHelper
PSScriptBuilderConfigLoader
PSScriptBuilderConfiguration
PSScriptBuilderBuildOptions
PSScriptBuilderBumpConfigFileManager
PSScriptBuilderBumpFilesProcessor

PSScriptBuilderFileSystemHelper is one of PSScriptBuilder's most widely used helper classes — 18 other classes reference it directly.

docs.title: Validate that expected components are present
docs.text:
Use this pattern in a CI pipeline or pre-build script to assert that all required components were collected. If a file is missing, misconfigured, or excluded by a filter, the check will catch it before the build fails with a harder-to-diagnose error:

$expected = @(
    "PSScriptBuilderCollectorBase",
    "PSScriptBuilderOptionsBase",
    "PSScriptBuilderNonExistentHelper"
)
$missing  = $expected | Where-Object { $_ -notin $classes.Name }

if ($missing) {
    Write-Error "Missing classes: $($missing -join ', ')"
}
Output
Write-Error: Missing classes: PSScriptBuilderNonExistentHelper

docs.title: Find classes with static initializer references
docs.text:
Static initializer references are types used in static property initializer expressions — for example static [MyClass] $Default = [MyClass]::new(). These create the same hard ordering constraint as inheritance: the referenced type must already be defined when PowerShell loads the class. See the Dependency Analysis Guide for details.

Use this query to identify classes that carry this constraint. If the referenced type is not a project-internal type — for example a .NET framework type — PSScriptBuilder will skip it when building the dependency graph, which is expected and correct:

$classes |
    Where-Object { $_.StaticInitializerReferences.Count -gt 0 } |
    Select-Object Name, StaticInitializerReferences
Output
Name                         StaticInitializerReferences
----                         ---------------------------
PSScriptBuilderFileIOHelper  {UTF8Encoding}
PSScriptBuilderAstEngine     {HashSet, StringComparer}

Only two classes in PSScriptBuilder's own source carry this constraint — both reference .NET framework types (UTF8Encoding, HashSet, StringComparer), which PSScriptBuilder correctly excludes from the dependency graph rather than treating as a project-internal ordering requirement.

docs.title: Count type references per class
docs.text:
TypeReferences contains all non-built-in types referenced in a class — in property declarations, method parameters, return types, and method bodies. The count gives you a rough measure of how many other components a class depends on. Classes with a high count tend to be orchestrators or aggregators that depend on many other types:

$classes |
    Select-Object Name, @{ Name = 'Dependencies'; Expression = { $_.TypeReferences.Count } } |
    Sort-Object Dependencies -Descending |
    Select-Object -First 5
Output
Name                                         Dependencies
----                                         ------------
PSScriptBuilderAstEngine                               29
PSScriptBuilderBuildOrchestrator                       27
PSScriptBuilderReleaseManagementOrchestrator           21
PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalyzer                        17
PSScriptBuilderProjectWatcher                          16

PSScriptBuilderAstEngine — the class responsible for parsing PowerShell source with the AST — references more other types than anything else in the project, which fits its role as the foundation the rest of the collectors build on.

docs.title: Retrieve the source code of a specific component
docs.text:
When debugging a build or inspecting what PSScriptBuilder extracted, you can retrieve the exact source code that will end up in the generated output script. This is especially useful when the generated script contains unexpected content and you want to trace it back to the source:

$classCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class -IncludePath "src\Classes"
$data = Get-PSScriptBuilderCollectorContent `
    -Collector $classCollector `
    -ItemName "PSScriptBuilderSourceRange"
Write-Host $data.SourceCode
Output
class PSScriptBuilderSourceRange {
    [int] $StartLineNumber
    [int] $EndLineNumber

    PSScriptBuilderSourceRange([int] $startLineNumber, [int] $endLineNumber) {
        $this.StartLineNumber = $startLineNumber
        $this.EndLineNumber   = $endLineNumber
    }
}

(Comment-based help trimmed for brevity — the real source includes full documentation for every member.)

docs.title: Find functions that call other functions
docs.text:
The Function collector records which other functions each function calls. This information is used to determine function call edges in the dependency graph. You can query it directly to understand which functions are entry points and which are helpers called by others:

$functions |
    Where-Object { $_.CalledFunctions.Count -gt 0 } |
    Select-Object Name, CalledFunctions

Output (29 matches; first 5 shown):

Name                                   CalledFunctions
----                                   ---------------
Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector           {New-PSScriptBuilderCollector}
Compress-PSScriptBuilderScript         {Write-Warning, Write-Verbose}
Export-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult      {Write-Verbose}
Export-PSScriptBuilderDependencyGraph  {Write-Verbose}
Find-PSScriptBuilderUnusedComponent    {Write-Warning}

CalledFunctions records every command called within the function body, not just other PSScriptBuilder functions — which is why most of these entries only list Write-Warning/Write-Verbose calls. Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector is the one shown here that also calls another PSScriptBuilder function directly (New-PSScriptBuilderCollector), reflecting genuine composition between the two cmdlets.

docs.title: Find public entry points
docs.text:
Functions that are never called by other functions are likely public entry points — the top-level cmdlets or commands that users invoke directly. This query builds a set of all internally called function names and filters them out, leaving only the uncalled ones:

$calledFunctions = $functions.CalledFunctions |
    ForEach-Object { $_ } |
    Sort-Object -Unique

$functions |
    Where-Object { $_.Name -notin $calledFunctions } |
    Select-Object Name

Output (37 matches; first 5 shown):

Name
----
Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector
Compress-PSScriptBuilderScript
ConvertTo-PSScriptBuilderComponentDependencyTree
Export-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult
Export-PSScriptBuilderDependencyGraph

Every one of PSScriptBuilder's 38 public functions except one turns out to be a genuine entry point — expected, since public cmdlets are meant to be called from outside the project, not from within it. The one exception is New-PSScriptBuilderCollector, called internally by Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector — the same composition already seen in Find functions that call other functions. It's still a genuine, independently useful public cmdlet; it just also happens to be composed into another one.

docs.title: Other Collector Types
docs.text: Using and Enum collectors have fewer queryable properties than Class and Function, but the same Get-PSScriptBuilderCollectorContent pattern applies to all of them.

docs.title: Enum collector
docs.text:
$enums = New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Enum -IncludePath "src\Enums" |
    Get-PSScriptBuilderCollectorContent

$enums | Select-Object Name
Output
Name
----
PSScriptBuilderBumpPatternMode
PSScriptBuilderBumpType
PSScriptBuilderCollectorType
PSScriptBuilderDependencyEdgeType
PSScriptBuilderTemplateValidationMode
PSScriptBuilderTraversalDirection
PSScriptBuilderUnusedComponentType

docs.title: Using collector
docs.text:
SourceFiles tracks every file where a given using statement appears, so its count shows how widely a namespace or module is used across the project:

$usings = New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Using -IncludePath "src" |
    Get-PSScriptBuilderCollectorContent

$usings |
    Select-Object Statement, @{ Name = 'FileCount'; Expression = { $_.SourceFiles.Count } } |
    Sort-Object FileCount -Descending |
    Select-Object -First 5
Output
Statement                                      FileCount
---------                                      ---------
using namespace System                                62
using namespace System.Collections.Generic            51
using namespace System.IO                             32
using namespace System.Text                           13
using namespace System.Collections.Specialized         7

docs.title: File collector
docs.text:
File collectors don't parse content as PowerShell at all — they pass through the raw text of any file unchanged. Use this for content with no AST to analyze: license headers, configuration files, or documentation you want to embed verbatim in the generated output. -IncludeFile targets a single file directly, rather than scanning a directory for a component type:

$file = New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type File -IncludeFile "CHANGELOG.md" |
    Get-PSScriptBuilderCollectorContent

$file.FileName
Output
CHANGELOG.md

FullPath and Content give you the same file's absolute path and complete text, for inspecting or re-embedding it elsewhere.

docs.title: Analysing a Monolithic Script
docs.text:
When migrating from a monolithic .ps1 or .psm1 to a PSScriptBuilder project — such as the one used in Example 02 — Classes and Enums — the first step is identifying all components in the existing file. Instead of scanning the file manually, point all collector types at the single file using -IncludeFile and let PSScriptBuilder extract the inventory automatically.

$scriptPath = 'C:\Projects\HRModule\HRModule.psm1'

$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Enum     -IncludeFile $scriptPath |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludeFile $scriptPath |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludeFile $scriptPath

$contentCollector | Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector | ForEach-Object {
    $items = $_ | Get-PSScriptBuilderCollectorContent
    "$($_.CollectorType) : $($items.Name -join ', ')"
}

This outputs:

EnumCollector     : Department, EmploymentStatus
ClassCollector    : Person, Address, Employee
FunctionCollector : New-Employee, Get-EmployeesByDepartment, Set-EmployeeStatus

This is the exact list of files to create when splitting the monolith — one file per component.

docs.title: Extracting Components to Individual Files
docs.text:
Since each collected component already carries its own SourceCode, the same collectors can write every component straight to its own file — no manual copy-pasting required. Map each CollectorType to the folder convention PSScriptBuilder projects use, then write one file per component:

$folderByType = @{
    EnumCollector     = 'Enums'
    ClassCollector    = 'Classes'
    FunctionCollector = 'Public'
}

$collectors = $contentCollector | Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector

foreach ($collector in $collectors) {
    $folderName = $folderByType[$collector.CollectorType.ToString()]
    $folder     = Join-Path 'src' $folderName
    New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $folder -Force | Out-Null

    $components = $collector | Get-PSScriptBuilderCollectorContent
    foreach ($component in $components) {
        $filePath = Join-Path $folder "$($component.Name).ps1"
        Set-Content -Path $filePath -Value $component.SourceCode
        Write-Host "Created $filePath"
    }
}

For Example 02, this creates:

src\Enums\Department.ps1
src\Enums\EmploymentStatus.ps1
src\Classes\Person.ps1
src\Classes\Address.ps1
src\Classes\Employee.ps1
src\Public\New-Employee.ps1
src\Public\Get-EmployeesByDepartment.ps1
src\Public\Set-EmployeeStatus.ps1

Each generated file matches the original component's source exactly — this is genuine extraction, not a reformatted copy.

For the step-by-step migration workflow — planning the directory structure, setting up PSScriptBuilder, and verifying the first build — see Migrating to PSScriptBuilder.

docs.title: Dependency Analysis
docs.text:
To understand load order, detect cycles, or check for cross-dependencies without running a build, run a full dependency analysis. Get-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis executes all collectors, builds the dependency graph, runs cycle detection, and returns a single result object with everything — there's no need to run the collectors separately first. The following example uses PSScriptBuilder's own real build configuration — the same collectors it uses to build itself:

Run a full dependency analysis
$usingCollector    = New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Using    -IncludePath "src"
$enumCollector     = New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Enum     -IncludePath "src\Enums"
$classCollector    = New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath "src\Classes"
$functionCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath "src\Private", "src\Public"

$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector `
    -Collector @($usingCollector, $enumCollector, $classCollector, $functionCollector)

$analysis = $contentCollector | Get-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis
$analysis | Format-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis
Output
Analysis Summary
  Components : 144
  Nodes      : 133
  Edges      : 337
  Cycles     : None
  Cross-Deps : Detected

Components
  Using     :  11
  Enums     :   7
  Classes   :  87
  Functions :  39
  Total     : 144

PSScriptBuilder's own source genuinely has cross-dependencies (classes and functions interleaved in the load order) but no cycles — exactly the mix a real, mature project accumulates over time.

The underlying $analysis object also exposes every property directly — HasCrossDependencies, OrderedComponents, HasCycles, CyclePath, ComponentCounts, and the full DependencyGraph — for scripts that need to branch on a specific value rather than just display it. For querying individual components, rendering dependency trees, and exporting the graph, see Get-PSScriptBuilderComponentDependency, ConvertTo-PSScriptBuilderComponentDependencyTree, and Export-PSScriptBuilderDependencyGraph in the Dependency Analysis Guide, which also contains a complete walkthrough of all result properties and use cases.

To identify unused components — classes, enums, or functions that nothing else depends on — use Find-PSScriptBuilderUnusedComponent; see Dead Code Detection in the Dependency Analysis Guide for a complete worked example.

docs.title: Template Analysis
docs.text:
Before running a build — while designing or reviewing a template — you can verify exactly which placeholders it declares, which validation mode it will activate, and whether anything is missing or unexpected. Get-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis extends the dependency analysis with exactly this template-specific information. The following example reuses PSScriptBuilder's own real build configuration and checks its own real template:

Run a template analysis
$usingCollector    = New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Using    -IncludePath "src"
$enumCollector     = New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Enum     -IncludePath "src\Enums"
$classCollector    = New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath "src\Classes"
$functionCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath "src\Private", "src\Public"

$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector `
    -Collector @($usingCollector, $enumCollector, $classCollector, $functionCollector)

$templateAnalysis = $contentCollector |
    Get-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis -TemplatePath ".\build\Templates\PSScriptBuilder.psm1.template"
$templateAnalysis | Format-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis
Output
Template Analysis
  Template   : C:\Projects\PSScriptBuilder\build\Templates\PSScriptBuilder.psm1.template
  Size       : 1025 characters
  Mode       : Ordered
  Key        : ORDERED_COMPONENTS
  Cross-Deps : Detected
  Status     : Valid

Placeholders
  Expected : {{ORDERED_COMPONENTS}}, {{USING_STATEMENTS}}
  Found    : {{ORDERED_COMPONENTS}}, {{USING_STATEMENTS}}

Every expected placeholder is present and nothing unexpected was found — confirming the template is complete and correct. The underlying $templateAnalysis object also exposes ValidationMode, IsValid, MissingPlaceholders, and UnknownPlaceholders directly, for scripts that need to check a specific value rather than just display it.

See the Templates Guide for a full explanation of validation modes, placeholder rules, and all analysis result properties.
