docs.title: Release Management
docs.text:
PSScriptBuilder includes a built-in release management system for tracking and propagating version numbers, build metadata, and Git context across all files in your project. It is built around two configuration files and a small set of cmdlets that work together to cover the full release workflow — from bumping the version to updating manifests, templates, and changelogs in a single step.

The workflow follows the same three-phase sequence on every release: bump the version and refresh metadata, propagate the updated values to your project files, then build the output script from the updated sources.

The release workflow, visualized:

flowchart LR
    A[1. Bump Version +<br/>Refresh Metadata] --> B[2. Propagate to<br/>Project Files]
    B --> C[3. Build Output<br/>Script]

    Backup[Backup created first,<br/>restored automatically on error]
    B -.- Backup

    classDef safetyStyle stroke:#43a047,stroke-width:2px,stroke-dasharray: 2 2
    class Backup safetyStyle

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text:
The following steps are grouped into three stages, one for each phase of the release workflow: working with the release data file itself, propagating its values to your project files, then validating and running the release.

Both configuration files are located via paths declared once, in psscriptbuilder.config.json — every release cmdlet used in the following steps reads this configuration to find them, so none of them ever needs an explicit path parameter of its own:

psscriptbuilder.config.json
{
    "release": {
        "dataFile":       ".\\build\\Release\\psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json",
        "bumpConfigFile": ".\\build\\Release\\psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json"
    }
}

Adjust dataFile and bumpConfigFile to match your own project's build layout; the rest of this guide assumes the defaults shown here.

docs.title: Working with Release Data
docs.text: Every release starts from a single JSON file that records the project's current version, build metadata, and Git context. psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json is this authoritative source of truth — every other cmdlet in this guide reads or writes it, directly or indirectly. The following steps cover creating this file, bumping its version, and reading its values back out.

docs.title: 1. Set Up the Release Data File
docs.text:
Every other cmdlet in this guide depends on psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json already existing. If it doesn't yet, create it with its starting defaults:

New-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData

To find out where to write the file, New-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData reads the configured path from psscriptbuilder.config.json before writing default values to it.

Use -Force to overwrite an existing file — for example, to reinitialise a project. This, and every other cmdlet in this guide that writes to disk, also supports -WhatIf (see Tips).

The resulting psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json contains three sections:

psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json
{
    "version": {
        "major":         0,
        "minor":         1,
        "patch":         0,
        "prerelease":    null,
        "buildmetadata": null,
        "full":          "0.1.0"
    },
    "build": {
        "number":    0,
        "date":      null,
        "time":      null,
        "timestamp": null,
        "year":      null,
        "month":     null,
        "day":       null,
        "hour":      null,
        "minute":    null,
        "second":    null
    },
    "git": {
        "commit":      null,
        "commitShort": null,
        "branch":      null,
        "tag":         null
    }
}

The version section follows Semantic Versioning: major, minor, and patch are the three required components, prerelease and buildmetadata are the specification's optional extensions (both null until set), and full is a derived convenience field combining all four into the single version string SemVer itself defines — it stays in sync automatically whenever any of the other fields change, as shown by the full Old Value/New Value pair in Bump the Version's own output. New projects start at 0.1.0 rather than 1.0.0 — SemVer's major-version-zero convention for initial development, where anything may still change.

The build section starts almost entirely empty: only number is initialized, to 0. Nothing stamps the date, time, or timestamp fields — or their individual year/month/day/hour/ minute/second components — automatically when the file is created; all of them stay null until explicitly refreshed in Update Build and Git Metadata.

The git section starts the same way, entirely null. There is no cmdlet that reads Git state on its own — it is populated only as part of that same step.

docs.title: 2. Bump the Version
docs.text:
Every version and metadata update goes through one cmdlet: Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData. It reads the current psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json, applies the requested changes, and writes the updated values back.

Three switches increment the version following standard SemVer rules:

  • -Major increments major and resets minor and patch to 0
  • -Minor increments minor and resets patch to 0
  • -Patch increments patch only

To set an explicit version instead of incrementing the current one — for example, jumping straight to a specific release number — use -Version, which sets major, minor, and patch directly from the given value:

Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData -Version '2.1.0'

-Major, -Minor, -Patch, and -Version are mutually exclusive — only one may be used per call.

Pipe the result to Format-PSScriptBuilderReleaseDataResult for a readable summary of what changed:

Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData -Patch | Format-PSScriptBuilderReleaseDataResult
Output
Category: Version

  Property  : patch
  Old Value : 0
  New Value : 1

  Property  : full
  Old Value : 0.1.0
  New Value : 0.1.1

Automatic rollback on error

If an error occurs while writing psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json, Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData automatically restores the original file. The release data is never left in a partially updated state.

docs.title: 3. Update Build and Git Metadata
docs.text:
Before a release, it's often useful to record exactly when it was built and which Git commit and branch it came from.

These are exactly the build and git sections introduced in Set Up the Release Data File — both start out empty, and stay that way until explicitly refreshed. Nothing populates them automatically as part of a version bump.

Two switches on Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData populate them independently of any version change:

  • -UpdateBuildDetails populates the build section
  • -UpdateGitDetails populates the Git section

To refresh the build section, -UpdateBuildDetails re-stamps the build timestamp and increments the build number:

Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData -UpdateBuildDetails | Format-PSScriptBuilderReleaseDataResult
Output
Category : Build

  Property  : number
  Old Value : 0
  New Value : 1

  Property  : date
  Old Value : <none>
  New Value : 2026-09-14

  Property  : time
  Old Value : <none>
  New Value : 14:18:03

  Property  : timestamp
  Old Value : <none>
  New Value : 2026-09-14T14:18:03Z

  Property  : year
  Old Value : <none>
  New Value : 2026

  Property  : month
  Old Value : <none>
  New Value : 9

  Property  : day
  Old Value : <none>
  New Value : 14

  Property  : hour
  Old Value : <none>
  New Value : 14

  Property  : minute
  Old Value : <none>
  New Value : 18

  Property  : second
  Old Value : <none>
  New Value : 3

To refresh the Git section, -UpdateGitDetails captures the current Git state — branch, commit hash, and the latest tag:

Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData -UpdateGitDetails | Format-PSScriptBuilderReleaseDataResult
Output
Category : Git

  Property  : commit
  Old Value : <none>
  New Value : 55d9437fc36f519f0d5721193840fc4afcba8dcd

  Property  : commitshort
  Old Value : <none>
  New Value : 55d9437

  Property  : branch
  Old Value : <none>
  New Value : development

  Property  : tag
  Old Value : <none>
  New Value : v1.2.0

Both switches are independent of each other and of any version bump. Combine them with any switch from Bump the Version — here, -Patch — to refresh everything in one call:

Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData -Patch -UpdateBuildDetails -UpdateGitDetails

-UpdateGitDetails requires git to be available in PATH. If the project is not inside a Git repository or git is not found, the cmdlet throws an error.

docs.title: 4. Working with Prerelease and Build Metadata
docs.text:
Not every release is a final, stable version. A prerelease identifier marks a version as a release candidate or preview — SemVer treats 1.0.0-rc.1 as coming before 1.0.0 in precedence, so consumers can tell it apart from the finished release. Build metadata, by contrast, doesn't affect version precedence at all. SemVer represents it as 1.0.0+build.5 — useful for tagging which build produced a given artifact, without implying it's newer or older than another with the same version.

PSScriptBuilder exposes both as separate switches on Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData:

  • -Prerelease "rc.1" sets the prerelease identifier
  • -BuildMetadata "build.5" sets build metadata
Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData -Patch -Prerelease "rc.1" | Format-PSScriptBuilderReleaseDataResult
Output
Category : Version

  Property  : patch
  Old Value : 0
  New Value : 1

  Property  : prerelease
  Old Value : <none>
  New Value : rc.1

  Property  : full
  Old Value : 0.1.0
  New Value : 0.1.1-rc.1

Build metadata works the same way:

Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData -Patch -BuildMetadata "build.5"

Both can be removed again, independently of each other:

  • -ClearPrerelease removes the prerelease identifier
  • -ClearBuildMetadata removes build metadata
Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData -ClearPrerelease
Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData -ClearBuildMetadata

Prerelease and build metadata identifiers follow the SemVer specification. The version.full sub-property in psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json reflects all components: 1.0.0-rc.1+build.5.

docs.title: 5. Read Release Data
docs.text:
At any point, the current release data can be read back without modifying it, using Get-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData. The default mode returns a hierarchical object — ideal when you only need specific sections. For example, you can access $data.Build or work exclusively with $data.Git without touching the rest:

$data = Get-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData
Write-Host "Number:    $($data.Build.Number)"
Write-Host "Timestamp: $($data.Build.Timestamp)"
Output
Number:    1
Timestamp: 2026-09-14T14:18:03Z

Similarly, $data.Git isolates just the Git fields:

$data = Get-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData
Write-Host "Branch: $($data.Git.Branch)"
Write-Host "Commit: $($data.Git.Commit)"
Write-Host "Tag:    $($data.Git.Tag)"
Output
Branch: development
Commit: 55d9437fc36f519f0d5721193840fc4afcba8dcd
Tag:    v1.2.0

Use -Flat to get a flat object with prefixed property names instead — more convenient, for example, in scripts that pass all token values to another function, or when you want to enumerate all properties uniformly:

$flat = Get-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData -Flat
Write-Host "Version:     $($flat.VersionFull)"
Write-Host "CommitShort: $($flat.GitCommitShort)"
Output
Version:     0.1.1
CommitShort: 55d9437

docs.title: Propagating Values to Project Files
docs.text: Once the release data is in place, its values still need to reach the files that actually ship — a module manifest, a script header, a changelog entry. psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json defines which project files get updated and how, via token replacement or regex patterns. The following steps cover inspecting available tokens, configuring bump files in each mode, reading the configuration back, and applying it to your project files.

docs.title: 6. Inspect Available Tokens
docs.text:
Release tokens are the version, build, and Git fields from psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json — the same ones bumped and refreshed in the previous steps — reformatted as named placeholders ready to be injected into project files.

Use Get-PSScriptBuilderReleaseDataTokens to see all current token values in a single table:

Get-PSScriptBuilderReleaseDataTokens | Format-Table -AutoSize
Output
Name                  Value
----                  -----
BUILD_DATE            2026-09-14
BUILD_TIME            12:53:24
BUILD_DAY             14
BUILD_MONTH           09
BUILD_YEAR            2026
BUILD_HOUR            12
BUILD_MINUTE          53
BUILD_SECOND          24
BUILD_TIMESTAMP       2026-09-14T12:53:24Z
BUILD_NUMBER          1
GIT_COMMIT            55d9437fc36f519f0d5721193840fc4afcba8dcd
GIT_COMMIT_SHORT      55d9437
GIT_BRANCH            development
GIT_TAG               v1.2.0
VERSION               0.1.1
VERSION_MAJOR         0
VERSION_MINOR         1
VERSION_PATCH         1
VERSION_FULL          0.1.1
VERSION_PRERELEASE
VERSION_BUILDMETADATA

This is useful to verify that the release data is correct before running Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles.

docs.title: 7. Configure Bump Files — Simple Token Mode
docs.text:
A project file that needs a release value — for example, a version stamp in a script header — would otherwise have to be edited by hand on every release. The simplest way to avoid that is a {{TOKEN}} placeholder, placed directly in the target file:

MyProject.ps1
# Version: {{VERSION}}
# Built: {{BUILD_TIMESTAMP}}

PSScriptBuilder finds and replaces each placeholder using the current value from psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json — but only for tokens explicitly listed in the entry's tokens array:

psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json — simple token mode
{
    "bumpFiles": [
        {
            "description": "Output script — inject version and build timestamp",
            "path": "src\\MyProject.ps1",
            "tokens": ["VERSION", "BUILD_TIMESTAMP"]
        }
    ]
}

After running Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles, the placeholders are replaced with the actual values. As explained in the Templates Guide, this mode only works once — on subsequent bumps, the placeholders are gone and the regex mode is needed.

docs.title: 8. Configure Bump Files — Regex Pattern Mode
docs.text:
After the first bump, a target file no longer contains any {{TOKEN}} placeholder to replace — Simple Token Mode has nothing left to find. Regex Pattern Mode solves this by matching the value itself with a regular expression, so it keeps working on every subsequent bump, on any file format, without needing a placeholder at all.

Each item in items defines a pattern (regex) and a tokens array. Use {REGEX_TOKEN} as a named capture group inside the pattern — it matches the current value and is replaced with the new one:

psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json — regex pattern mode
{
    "bumpFiles": [
        {
            "description": "Module manifest — update version",
            "path": "build\\Output\\MyModule.psd1",
            "items": [
                {
                    "pattern": "ModuleVersion\\s*=\\s*'({REGEX_VERSION})'",
                    "tokens": ["VERSION"]
                }
            ]
        }
    ]
}

The regex matches the surrounding context (e.g. ModuleVersion = '...') but only the value inside the parentheses ({REGEX_VERSION}) is replaced. Everything outside the capture group is preserved as-is.

Multiple items can target the same file, and the same path can appear more than once in bumpFiles. In both cases, all entries are applied sequentially to the same in-memory content before writing — making multi-phase processing possible.

docs.title: 9. Configure Bump Files — Mixed Mode
docs.text:
Simple Token Mode only works on the first bump, before any placeholder is replaced. Regex Pattern Mode only works once a real value already exists to match against. A single bump target commonly needs both — one to handle the very first release, the other for every release after it.

The following example, drawn from PSScriptBuilder's own real bump configuration, shows the template file handled by two separate entries — one for each mode:

psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json (real-world example)
{
    "bumpFiles": [
        {
            "description": "PSScriptBuilder root module template - Auto token replacement",
            "path": "build\\Templates\\PSScriptBuilder.psm1.template",
            "tokens": ["VERSION", "VERSION_FULL", "BUILD_TIMESTAMP", "BUILD_NUMBER", "GIT_COMMIT_SHORT", "GIT_BRANCH", "BUILD_DATE", "BUILD_TIME"]
        },
        {
            "description": "PSScriptBuilder root module template - Multi-phase bumping",
            "path": "build\\Templates\\PSScriptBuilder.psm1.template",
            "items": [
                {
                    "pattern": "Version\\s*=\\s*'({REGEX_VERSION_FULL})'",
                    "tokens": ["VERSION_FULL"]
                },
                {
                    "pattern": "BuildTimestamp\\s*=\\s*'({REGEX_BUILD_TIMESTAMP})'",
                    "tokens": ["BUILD_TIMESTAMP"]
                },
                {
                    "pattern": "BuildNumber\\s*=\\s*'({REGEX_BUILD_NUMBER})'",
                    "tokens": ["BUILD_NUMBER"]
                },
                {
                    "pattern": "GitCommit\\s*=\\s*'({REGEX_GIT_COMMIT_SHORT})'",
                    "tokens": ["GIT_COMMIT_SHORT"]
                },
                {
                    "pattern": "GitBranch\\s*=\\s*'({REGEX_GIT_BRANCH})'",
                    "tokens": ["GIT_BRANCH"]
                }
            ]
        }
    ]
}

Entry 1 — The module template contains {{TOKEN}} placeholders that are replaced on the first release using simple token mode.

Entry 2 — The same template file appears a second time using regex mode. After the first bump, all {{TOKEN}} placeholders are gone. This entry targets the already-substituted values and updates them on every subsequent release.

The same idea also works within a single entry — one item for the placeholder, one item for the already-substituted value — verified against Example 11's real AppConfig.psd1 manifest, which genuinely starts with a placeholder on first scaffold:

psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json (Example 11)
{
    "description": "AppConfig module manifest - Mixed bump mode",
    "path": "build\\Output\\AppConfig.psd1",
    "items": [
        {
            "pattern": "{{VERSION}}",
            "tokens": ["VERSION"]
        },
        {
            "pattern": "ModuleVersion\\s*=\\s*'({REGEX_VERSION})'",
            "tokens": ["VERSION"]
        }
    ]
}

This combination of Simple and Regex items in a single entry is referred to as Mixed Mode — the first item matches on the very first bump, the second on every bump after that.

If a bump file's entries all fail to match on a given run, Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles emits a warning naming the file — a sign it may need a Regex fallback like the ones above. The warning is file-level: as long as at least one entry for a file still matches (in the first example, any of Entry 2's five patterns), the file overall won't be flagged, even if VERSION, BUILD_DATE, or BUILD_TIME — which have no regex fallback there — have gone stale since the very first bump.

docs.title: 10. Escaping Literal Text in Bump Patterns
docs.text:
Simple Token Mode, Regex Pattern Mode, and Mixed Mode all give special meaning to certain characters — {{...}} marks a token placeholder, and (...) marks a regex capture group. If a target file's real content happens to contain either of these literally — a copyright notice with parentheses, or documentation text that mentions {{...}} — that text needs to be distinguished from an actual token or capture group, or PSScriptBuilder will misinterpret it.

If a Placeholder Mode pattern needs to include a literal parenthesis — not a regex capture group — escape it with \( and \). This is the same convention Regex Mode patterns already use for literal parentheses surrounding a capture group.

Placeholder Mode also supports escaping literal {{...}} text (\{/\}) for the same reason — so it is not mistaken for a real token. The table compares the resulting combinations directly, since several of them look similar but behave differently:

Pattern Result "Copyright \(c\) {{YEAR}}" ✅ Replaces {{YEAR}}, keeps (c) literal. "Copyright \(c\) \(all rights reserved\) {{YEAR}}" ✅ Both literal parentheses kept, {{YEAR}} replaced - escaping applies to each occurrence independently. "{{ site.name }} says {{GIT_BRANCH}}" with tokens: ["GIT_BRANCH"] ✅ No escaping needed: {{ site.name }} is not a declared token, so it is left untouched; only {{GIT_BRANCH}} is replaced. "\{\{ site.name \}\} says {{GIT_BRANCH}}" with tokens: ["GIT_BRANCH"] ✅ No escaping needed here either — escaping foreign {{...}} text is optional, but correctly supported for symmetry. "Example: \{\{GIT_BRANCH\}\} literal. Real: {{GIT_BRANCH}}" with tokens: ["GIT_BRANCH"] ✅ Only the unescaped occurrence is replaced; the escaped one stays as literal {{GIT_BRANCH}} text - useful for documentation/example text inside the same file. "Copyright \(c\) (2026) {{YEAR}}" ❌ Throws a mixed-syntax error. One parenthesis is escaped, but (2026) is not - every literal parenthesis in the pattern must be escaped, not just some of them. "\{\{GIT_BRANCH\}\}" with tokens: ["GIT_BRANCH"] ❌ Throws Token 'GIT_BRANCH' has no corresponding placeholder '{{GIT_BRANCH}}' in pattern. A declared token needs a real, unescaped occurrence somewhere in the pattern; to mention a token name as literal text without ever replacing it, remove it from the item's tokens array instead of escaping its braces.

docs.title: 11. Read Bump Configuration
docs.text:
To verify which files and patterns are currently configured before applying them, use Get-PSScriptBuilderBumpConfiguration. It reads psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json and returns its parsed bumpFiles array — for example, applied to PSScriptBuilder's own real bump configuration:

(Get-PSScriptBuilderBumpConfiguration).bumpFiles | Select-Object path -Unique
Output
path
----
build\Templates\PSScriptBuilder.psm1.template
build\Output\PSScriptBuilder.psd1

This is useful for confirming that a newly added bump target actually made it into the configuration file, without needing to open and parse the JSON by hand.

docs.title: 12. Apply Tokens to Project Files
docs.text:
Once the release data has been updated and bumpconfig.json is configured, apply all tokens to the configured project files with Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles, and pipe the result to Format-PSScriptBuilderBumpResult for a detailed change report:

Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles | Format-PSScriptBuilderBumpResult
Output
File : C:\Projects\MyProject\src\MyProject.ps1

  Token     : VERSION
  Old Value : {{VERSION}}
  New Value : 0.1.1

  Token     : BUILD_TIMESTAMP
  Old Value : {{BUILD_TIMESTAMP}}
  New Value : 2026-09-14T12:55:50Z

File : C:\Projects\MyProject\build\Output\MyModule.psd1

  Pattern   : ModuleVersion\s*=\s*'({REGEX_VERSION})'
  Token     : VERSION
  Old Value : ModuleVersion = '0.1.0'
  New Value : ModuleVersion = '0.1.1'

Automatic backups before writing

Before writing any changes to disk, Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles creates a backup of each target file. If an error occurs during processing, the originals are restored from their backups, leaving all project files in a consistent state.

docs.title: Validating and Running a Release
docs.text: Before running updates — especially in automated scripts — both configuration files should be validated. The following steps cover that check, then combine every previous step into one complete release script.

docs.title: 13. Validate Configuration
docs.text:
Always validate both files before running updates — especially in automated scripts where a silent failure could leave the project in an inconsistent state:

if (-not (Test-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData)) {
    Write-Error "Release data is invalid — fix it before bumping"
    return
}

if (-not (Test-PSScriptBuilderBumpConfiguration)) {
    Write-Error "Bump configuration is invalid — fix it before running Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles"
    return
}

Each cmdlet checks one of the two files. Test-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData validates the structure and values of psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json — for example, that all required fields exist and the version components are valid integers. Test-PSScriptBuilderBumpConfiguration validates the structure of bumpconfig.json and checks that all referenced files exist.

Both cmdlets return $true on success and write detailed error messages on failure. Add -Verbose for additional validation detail.

docs.title: 14. Full Release Workflow
docs.text:
A complete release script that combines all steps, in four phases: validate, bump, propagate, then build.

release.ps1
if (-not (Test-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData))       { return }
if (-not (Test-PSScriptBuilderBumpConfiguration)) { return }

Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData -Patch -UpdateBuildDetails -UpdateGitDetails |
    Format-PSScriptBuilderReleaseDataResult

Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles | Format-PSScriptBuilderBumpResult

$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath '.\src\Classes' |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath '.\src\Public'

Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild -ContentCollector $contentCollector `
    -TemplatePath '.\build\Templates\MyProject.ps1.template' `
    -OutputPath   '.\build\Output\MyProject.ps1'

The order matters: bump first, then propagate, then build. If the build template is configured as a bump file (see the Templates Guide), the version tokens in the template must be updated before Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild runs.

docs.title: Version Bump Switches
docs.text:
All version-changing switches accepted by Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData:

Switch Effect -Major Increments major, resets minor and patch to 0 -Minor Increments minor, resets patch to 0 -Patch Increments patch -Version "1.0.0" Sets an explicit version; cannot be combined with -Major, -Minor, or -Patch -Prerelease "alpha.1" Sets the prerelease identifier -ClearPrerelease Removes the prerelease identifier -BuildMetadata "build.5" Sets build metadata (not auto-updated) -ClearBuildMetadata Removes build metadata

-Major, -Minor, -Patch, and -Version are mutually exclusive — only one may be used per call. At least one parameter must be specified overall. -UpdateBuildDetails and -UpdateGitDetails are the exception — they can be used standalone without a version change, or combined with any version parameter.

docs.title: Metadata Switches
docs.text:
The two switches that refresh build and Git metadata independently of any version change:

Switch What it updates -UpdateBuildDetails build.date, build.time, build.timestamp, all time components, build.number (+1) -UpdateGitDetails git.commit, git.commitShort, git.branch, git.tag — requires git in PATH

docs.title: Version Tokens
docs.text:
Tokens derived from the version section of psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json — the same tokens seen in Inspect Available Tokens:

Token Example value Description VERSION 1.2.0 major.minor.patch VERSION_FULL 1.2.0-rc.1+build.5 Full SemVer including prerelease and metadata VERSION_MAJOR 1 Major number only VERSION_MINOR 2 Minor number only VERSION_PATCH 0 Patch number only VERSION_PRERELEASE rc.1 Prerelease identifier, or empty VERSION_BUILDMETADATA build.5 Build metadata, or empty

docs.title: Build Tokens
docs.text:
Tokens derived from the build section:

Token Example value Description BUILD_NUMBER 42 Incrementing build counter BUILD_DATE 2026-03-24 Date in yyyy-MM-dd format BUILD_TIME 18:00:00 Time in HH:mm:ss format BUILD_TIMESTAMP 2026-03-24T18:00:00Z ISO 8601 combined timestamp BUILD_YEAR 2026 Year component BUILD_MONTH 03 Month component (zero-padded) BUILD_DAY 24 Day component (zero-padded) BUILD_HOUR 18 Hour component (zero-padded) BUILD_MINUTE 00 Minute component (zero-padded) BUILD_SECOND 00 Second component (zero-padded)

docs.title: Git Tokens
docs.text:
Tokens derived from the git section:

Token Example value Description GIT_COMMIT 2a98ae58cc96e12c78614ec28ed044996ee86d43 Full 40-character SHA1 hash GIT_COMMIT_SHORT 2a98ae5 Short hash (7–40 characters) GIT_BRANCH main Current branch name GIT_TAG v1.2.0 Latest tag, or empty if none

docs.title: Regex Token Placeholders
docs.text:
Use these inside pattern values in bumpconfig.json to match the current value of a token:

Regex placeholder Matches {REGEX_VERSION} major.minor.patch (e.g. 1.2.0) {REGEX_VERSION_FULL} Full SemVer including optional prerelease and metadata {REGEX_VERSION_MAJOR} Major version number (one or more digits) {REGEX_VERSION_MINOR} Minor version number (one or more digits) {REGEX_VERSION_PATCH} Patch version number (one or more digits) {REGEX_VERSION_PRERELEASE} Prerelease identifier (e.g. rc.1, alpha) {REGEX_VERSION_BUILDMETADATA} Build metadata (e.g. build.5) {REGEX_BUILD_NUMBER} One or more digits {REGEX_BUILD_DATE} yyyy-MM-dd {REGEX_BUILD_TIME} HH:mm:ss {REGEX_BUILD_TIMESTAMP} ISO 8601 timestamp {REGEX_BUILD_YEAR} Four-digit year (e.g. 2026) {REGEX_BUILD_MONTH} Zero-padded month (e.g. 03) {REGEX_BUILD_DAY} Zero-padded day (e.g. 24) {REGEX_BUILD_HOUR} Zero-padded hour (e.g. 18) {REGEX_BUILD_MINUTE} Zero-padded minute (e.g. 00) {REGEX_BUILD_SECOND} Zero-padded second (e.g. 00) {REGEX_GIT_COMMIT} 40-character hex string {REGEX_GIT_COMMIT_SHORT} 7–40 character hex string {REGEX_GIT_BRANCH} Branch name (alphanumeric, -, _, /) {REGEX_GIT_TAG} Tag name, or empty string

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
Preview any change first with -WhatIf

Every cmdlet in this guide that writes to disk — New-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData, Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData, and Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles — supports -WhatIf, to preview what would change without writing anything.

Use Get-PSScriptBuilderReleaseDataTokens to verify values

Before running Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles, call Get-PSScriptBuilderReleaseDataTokens | Format-Table -AutoSize to confirm that all token values match what you expect. This catches a stale bump or a missing Git update before it propagates to project files.

Bump before build when the template is a bump file

If your build template contains release token placeholders, Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles must run before Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild. Otherwise, the build validator will report unknown placeholders and fail.

Non-Git environments

In a project that isn't a Git repository, omit -UpdateGitDetails and manage the git section of psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json manually instead.

docs.title: Source Maps
docs.text:
A source map links every line of the compiled output script back to the source file and line it was generated from. This makes it possible to resolve runtime errors in the output script directly to the originating source file, and to translate Pester code coverage — measured against the built output — back to per-source-file results, without manually searching through the combined output.

The following examples use Example 16 — Source Maps and Example 17 — Code Coverage — two closely related HR projects, both built around an Employee class inheriting from Person, a New-Employee factory function, and a Get-EmployeeById lookup function that throws when an ID isn't found. Example 17 adds one more function, Get-EmployeesByDepartment, specifically to demonstrate a third coverage outcome.

docs.title: Generating a Source Map
docs.text:
To make a build's output resolvable back to source later, write a source map alongside it. Pass -WriteSourceMap to Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild and PSScriptBuilder writes a sidecar .sourcemap.json file next to the output script after each successful build:

$result = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath 'src\Classes'   |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath 'src\Functions' |
    Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild `
        -TemplatePath 'build\Templates\HRTools.ps1.template' `
        -OutputPath   'build\Output\HRTools.ps1' `
        -WriteSourceMap

The sidecar is written alongside the output file with .sourcemap.json appended to the file name:

build\Output\HRTools.ps1
build\Output\HRTools.ps1.sourcemap.json   ← generated automatically

The sidecar path is stored in $result.SourceMapPath and shown by Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult when present.

The sidecar stores a SHA-256 hash of the output file at build time. If the output script is modified or rebuilt without -WriteSourceMap afterward, Resolve-PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation emits a warning before resolving — line numbers may no longer be accurate.

-WriteSourceMap is also available on Watch-PSScriptBuilderProject (Build mode). The sidecar is updated after every successful automatic rebuild.

docs.title: Enabling via Configuration File
docs.text:
To generate a source map for every configuration-based build, set writeSourceMap to true in psscriptbuilder.config.json:

"build": {
    "writeSourceMap": true
}

This is equivalent to always passing -WriteSourceMap to Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild.

docs.title: Resolving Source Locations
docs.text: Once a source map exists, you can resolve output locations back to source in three ways — from a specific line number, from a caught error, or by listing every entry at once.

docs.title: Resolving a Line Number
docs.text:
To map a specific output line number back to its source, read the sidecar with Resolve-PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation:

Resolve-PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation `
    -OutputPath 'build\Output\HRTools.ps1' `
    -LineNumber 41
Output
ComponentName       : Get-EmployeeById
ComponentType       : Function
SourceFile          : C:\Projects\HRTools\src\Functions\Get-EmployeeById.ps1
SourceLineNumber    : 11
ComponentLineNumber : 1
OutputLineNumber    : 31
Offset              : 10

OutputLineNumber is where Get-EmployeeById itself begins in the output — not the queried line. Offset is the distance from that start to line 41; adding it to ComponentLineNumber gives SourceLineNumber, the corresponding line inside the original source file.

docs.title: Resolving an ErrorRecord
docs.text:
The most common use case is tracing an error thrown when the output script is dot-sourced or executed. Pass the $_ ErrorRecord directly — Resolve-PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation extracts the line number from InvocationInfo.ScriptLineNumber automatically:

. $result.OutputPath

$employees = @(
    New-Employee -Id 1 -FirstName 'Anna'  -LastName 'Schmidt' -Department 'Engineering'
    New-Employee -Id 2 -FirstName 'James' -LastName 'Okafor'  -Department 'Finance'
)

try {
    Get-EmployeeById -Employees $employees -Id 999
}
catch {
    Write-Host "Error at output line $($_.InvocationInfo.ScriptLineNumber): $($_.Exception.Message)"
    $result | Resolve-PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation -ErrorRecord $_
}
Output
Error at output line 43: Employee with Id 999 was not found.

ComponentName       : Get-EmployeeById
ComponentType       : Function
SourceFile          : C:\Projects\HRTools\src\Functions\Get-EmployeeById.ps1
SourceLineNumber    : 13
ComponentLineNumber : 1
OutputLineNumber    : 31
Offset              : 12

Get-EmployeeById throws when no employee matches the given Id — line 13 of the source file is exactly the throw statement. The cmdlet accepts a PSScriptBuilderBuildResult from the pipeline, so no separate -OutputPath is needed when the build result is in scope.

docs.title: Inspecting the Full Source Map
docs.text:
To verify the final component order in the output — or just see everything the source map recorded at once — omit -LineNumber and -ErrorRecord to retrieve every entry as a formatted table:

$result | Resolve-PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation | Format-Table
Output
ComponentName    ComponentType SourceFile
-------------    ------------- ----------
Person           Class         C:\Projects\HRTools\src\Classes\Person.ps1
Employee         Class         C:\Projects\HRTools\src\Classes\Employee.ps1
Get-EmployeeById Function      C:\Projects\HRTools\src\Functions\Get-EmployeeById.ps1
New-Employee     Function      C:\Projects\HRTools\src\Functions\New-Employee.ps1

The order matches the topological sort — both classes before either function, Person before Employee since it inherits from it — the same guarantee described in the Dependency Analysis Guide.

docs.title: Translating Pester Code Coverage
docs.text:
In a typical PowerShell project, Pester's CodeCoverage.Path points directly at the source files you want to measure — the files Pester instruments are the same files that actually ran.

That assumption breaks whenever tests load the built, merged output as a single unit instead of the original per-file sources — most commonly because classes require using module to load correctly across files, but the same is true for a plain .ps1 output dot-sourced directly in a BeforeAll block.

Either way, every executed ScriptBlock's origin is the file that was actually parsed — the built output, not the individual source files it was assembled from. Pester has no record of executing code from files it never loaded.

CodeCoverage.Path must therefore point at the built output script, not at the source tree. Point it at the wrong location and Pester still runs without error — it just reports nothing useful, since it never sees any of the source files execute.

The following three steps put this into practice: build with a source map, run Pester against the output, then translate the result back to source.

docs.title: 1. Build with a Source Map
docs.text:
A source map is required to translate the results back in Step 3:

$result = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath 'src\Classes'   |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath 'src\Functions' |
    Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild `
        -TemplatePath 'build\Templates\HRTools.ps1.template' `
        -OutputPath   'build\Output\HRTools.ps1' `
        -WriteSourceMap

docs.title: 2. Run Pester with CodeCoverage.Path Pointed at the Built Output
docs.text:
Point CodeCoverage.Path at the build's output script, not at the source tree:

Import-Module -Name Pester -MinimumVersion 5.0 -Force

$config = [PesterConfiguration]::Default
$config.Run.Path             = 'tests'
$config.Run.PassThru         = $true
$config.CodeCoverage.Enabled = $true
$config.CodeCoverage.Path    = $result.OutputPath

$pesterResult = Invoke-Pester -Configuration $config

[PesterConfiguration] is only available once Pester 5 or later is loaded — if an older Pester version is already loaded in the session, -MinimumVersion 5.0 -Force ensures the correct one is used instead.

Pointing CodeCoverage.Path at src\Classes (or anywhere other than the built output) produces no error from Pester itself — it just measures nothing useful, and the problem only surfaces in Step 3. See Code coverage reports 0% or "referenced a file other than the build output" in Troubleshooting if you run into this.

docs.title: 3. Translate and Display
docs.text:
To translate the raw, output-line-based coverage result from Step 2 back to per-source-file aggregates, read the sidecar written in Step 1 with Get-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage:

$result | Get-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage -CodeCoverage $pesterResult.CodeCoverage |
    Format-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage

SourceFile is shown relative to the project root — falling back to the original absolute path for a file outside it, e.g. a collector IncludePath pointed at a network share.

Output
SourceFile                                    Coverage  Hit/Total
--------------------------------------------  --------  ---------
src\Classes\Person.ps1                         100.0 %        2/2
src\Classes\Employee.ps1                       100.0 %        2/2
src\Functions\Get-EmployeeById.ps1              71.4 %        5/7
src\Functions\New-Employee.ps1                 100.0 %        1/1
src\Functions\Get-EmployeesByDepartment.ps1      0.0 %        0/4

Add -Detailed to additionally list every distinct source line not covered by any test beneath its file — useful when deciding where to add a test next, rather than only knowing which file needs attention.

A single line can hold several missed commands (e.g. a pipeline inside a subexpression), but each line is only listed once; consecutive lines are collapsed into a single range, and long lists wrap at a fixed width with a hanging indent so a badly-fragmented file doesn't produce one unreadably long line:

$result | Get-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage -CodeCoverage $pesterResult.CodeCoverage |
    Format-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage -Detailed

SourceFile                                   Coverage  Hit/Total
-------------------------------------------  --------  ---------
src\Classes\Person.ps1                        100.0 %        2/2
src\Classes\Employee.ps1                      100.0 %        2/2
src\Functions\Get-EmployeeById.ps1             71.4 %        5/7
  uncovered: lines 12-13
src\Functions\New-Employee.ps1                100.0 %        1/1
src\Functions\Get-EmployeesByDepartment.ps1     0.0 %        0/4
  uncovered: entire file

A file at 0% coverage shows uncovered: entire file instead of enumerating every line - enumerating would always resolve to "the whole file" at that point, which the Coverage column already says.

Get-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage accepts a PSScriptBuilderBuildResult from the pipeline, as used in Step 3, or an explicit -OutputPath, mirroring Resolve-PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation. It also emits a warning if the source map itself is stale — the output script changed since -WriteSourceMap last wrote it.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
A template is a plain text file that defines the structure of the generated output script. PSScriptBuilder replaces placeholders with the collected and dependency-ordered source code from configured collectors. Static text before, between, and after placeholders is preserved as-is.

The template is what separates PSScriptBuilder from a simple file concatenation tool. It gives you full control over the structure of the output script — module header comments, #Requires statements, fixed boilerplate, and the order of component blocks are all defined in the template, not in the build script.

There isn't one fixed template structure that works for every project — whether your template needs a placeholder for each collector individually or one combined placeholder for all of them, and what order they must appear in, is determined by how your project's components depend on each other.

PSScriptBuilder analyzes your code as part of every build. The dependencies that analysis finds reveal which of three modes — Free Mode, Hybrid Mode, or Ordered Mode — is possible, or in some cases required. Your existing template is then either suitable for that mode, or it isn't.

Free Mode, possible whenever no dependency forces otherwise, is used throughout the Walkthrough below; see Ordered Mode and Hybrid Mode for when the other two apply.

Which mode applies, visualized:

flowchart TD
    A[Analyze code dependencies] --> B{Class depends on function?}
    B -->|yes| Ordered[Ordered Mode<br/>required]
    B -->|no| C{Combined placeholder already used?}
    C -->|yes| Hybrid[Hybrid Mode]
    C -->|no| Free[Free Mode]

    classDef orderedStyle stroke:#e53935,stroke-width:2px
    classDef hybridStyle stroke:#fb8c00,stroke-width:2px
    classDef freeStyle stroke:#43a047,stroke-width:2px
    class Ordered orderedStyle
    class Hybrid hybridStyle
    class Free freeStyle

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text:
A collector connects to the template through its CollectionKey — this is the value that appears in the corresponding placeholder. Write a placeholder as double curly braces around that key: {{Key}}. Matching is case-insensitive, so {{CLASS_DEFINITIONS}} and {{class_definitions}} are equivalent.

Which key to use, and whether you need one placeholder per collector or a single combined one, depends on the mode that applies:

  • Free Mode — one placeholder per registered collector, using that collector's CollectionKey (see Collection Keys in the Collectors Guide) — except Using collectors, which always share a single combined placeholder, in every mode (see Collectors Guide)
  • Ordered Mode and Hybrid Mode — a single combined placeholder for all Enum, Class, and Function collectors together, using an ordered-components key

The template's filename is entirely up to you — PSScriptBuilder reads it as plain text regardless of extension. This guide's examples use .ps1.template, but that final .template extension means most editors won't offer PowerShell syntax highlighting or IntelliSense for it. Naming it .template.ps1 instead keeps "template" visible in the name while still ending in .ps1, giving you that editor support too.

Each step below is a self-contained example illustrating one aspect of template syntax, the same way the Collectors Guide's Walkthrough does — neither builds on a single running $contentCollector carried across steps.

docs.title: 1. Create a Template
docs.text:
The simplest template maps each collector type to a separate placeholder, in the order Free Mode requires (see Validation Modes for the exact rules). Instead of writing one by hand, use New-PSScriptBuilderTemplate to generate it automatically from your collector configuration:

$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Enum     -IncludePath "src\Enums" |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath "src\Classes" |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath "src\Public"

New-PSScriptBuilderTemplate `
    -ContentCollector $contentCollector `
    -OutputPath       "build\Templates\MyScript.ps1.template"

By default, New-PSScriptBuilderTemplate won't overwrite an existing template file — pass -Force if you want to regenerate one, which replaces its entire content, including any manual changes you made after it was first generated.

The generated file looks like this:

MyScript.ps1.template
{{ENUM_DEFINITIONS}}

{{CLASS_DEFINITIONS}}

{{FUNCTION_DEFINITIONS}}

The token names match the default CollectionKey for each collector type — see the Collectors Guide for the full list.

docs.title: 2. Custom Collection Keys
docs.text:
To place two collectors of the same type in different sections of a template — for example, keeping domain classes separate from shared library classes — register each one with its own -CollectionKey, then use that key as the corresponding placeholder:

$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector `
        -Type          Class `
        -CollectionKey "CORE_CLASSES" `
        -IncludePath   "src\Core" |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector `
        -Type          Class `
        -CollectionKey "DOMAIN_CLASSES" `
        -IncludePath   "src\Domain"
MyScript.ps1.template
{{CORE_CLASSES}}

{{DOMAIN_CLASSES}}

docs.title: 3. Ordered Mode and Hybrid Mode
docs.text: Free Mode — what you've built so far — works whenever no dependency forces otherwise. The other two modes exist for when it doesn't:

docs.title: Ordered Mode
docs.text:
Activated automatically whenever a class depends on a function — even a single one-directional dependency, such as a constructor or method calling a project-defined function.

PSScriptBuilder always requires Ordered Mode for this case rather than trying to determine whether a simpler placeholder reordering would work: more complex projects can end up with functions and classes depending on each other in ways a fixed two-block order can't satisfy, so combining them into one dependency-ordered sequence handles every case correctly, simple or not.

docs.title: Hybrid Mode
docs.text:
Activated manually, by placing the combined components placeholder in a template whose code has no cross-dependencies yet.

Use it when you want a template that remains valid regardless of whether cross-dependencies are introduced later — for example, when your project is still growing and you want to avoid restructuring the template at the moment cross-dependencies first appear.

docs.title: The Combined Placeholder
docs.text:
Both modes combine Enum, Class, and Function components into a single combined placeholder. Using and File placeholders stay separate from it, and both remain optional. File keeps one placeholder per registered File collector; Using always shares a single combined placeholder across all registered Using collectors, in every mode (see Collectors Guide):

MyScript.ps1.template
{{USING_STATEMENTS}}
{{FILE_CONTENTS}}
{{ORDERED_COMPONENTS}}

The combined placeholder's default name is ORDERED_COMPONENTS — see Using a Custom Combined Placeholder Key to customize it.

Together, these three placeholders are governed by the following rules:

  • All Enum, Class, and Function components are combined into a single topologically ordered block at {{ORDERED_COMPONENTS}}
  • Per-type placeholders for Enum, Class, and Function are forbidden in both modes
  • Using and File placeholders remain valid and optional
  • Using must appear before every other placeholder — {{ORDERED_COMPONENTS}} and File included

The last rule is the same one Free Mode enforces (PowerShell requires using statements to open the script) — checked purely by template position, regardless of what a File placeholder's actual content is.

docs.title: Converting a Free Mode Template to Hybrid Mode
docs.text:
A Free Mode template fails validation the moment a class starts depending on a function — for example, when a class method calls a newly added, project-defined function.

Most other Free Mode validation failures are simple template mistakes — a missing placeholder, the wrong order, a typo — fixable within Free Mode itself. The one mentioned is different: no template fix restores Free Mode once the dependency exists; switching to Hybrid or Ordered Mode is the only way forward.

Converting to Hybrid Mode before that happens avoids the surprise, and the conversion itself is simple: only the template's placeholders change, with no restructuring of your build script or collectors.

The same template before and after converting to Hybrid Mode:

MyScript.ps1.template (Free Mode)
{{USING_STATEMENTS}}

{{FILE_CONTENTS}}

{{ENUM_DEFINITIONS}}

{{CLASS_DEFINITIONS}}

{{FUNCTION_DEFINITIONS}}
MyScript.ps1.template (Hybrid Mode)
{{USING_STATEMENTS}}

{{FILE_CONTENTS}}

{{ORDERED_COMPONENTS}}

The three collector-specific placeholders — {{ENUM_DEFINITIONS}}, {{CLASS_DEFINITIONS}}, {{FUNCTION_DEFINITIONS}} — combine into the single combined {{ORDERED_COMPONENTS}} placeholder; {{USING_STATEMENTS}} and {{FILE_CONTENTS}} stay exactly as they were.

docs.title: Using a Custom Combined Placeholder Key
docs.text:
Change the combined placeholder's default name only if your template already uses ORDERED_COMPONENTS for something else — otherwise, the default works fine. Override it with -OrderedComponentsKey on Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild and Test-PSScriptBuilderTemplate. To keep the template and the build call in sync, store a custom key in psscriptbuilder.config.json:

psscriptbuilder.config.json
{
    "build": {
        "orderedComponentsKey": "MY_COMPONENTS"
    }
}

Then use it in your build script like this:

$config = Get-PSScriptBuilderConfiguration
Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild -ContentCollector $contentCollector `
    -TemplatePath "build\Templates\MyProject.ps1.template" `
    -OutputPath   "build\Output\MyProject.ps1" `
    -OrderedComponentsKey $config.Build.OrderedComponentsKey

docs.title: 4. Combining with Release Management Tokens
docs.text:
A build template can also contain release metadata tokens — version numbers, build timestamps, Git commit hashes — using the same {{Token}} syntax as collector placeholders:

MyScript.ps1.template
# Version: {{VERSION}}
# Built: {{BUILD_TIMESTAMP}}

{{ENUM_DEFINITIONS}}

{{CLASS_DEFINITIONS}}

{{FUNCTION_DEFINITIONS}}

To replace these tokens with real values before the build runs, call Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles. By the time Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild validates the template, the release tokens are already gone, and the build validator only ever sees the collector placeholders it manages itself. If a release token is still present when the build runs — for example, because the bump step was skipped — the validator has no way to tell it apart from a genuine mistake, and reports it as an unknown placeholder.

See the Release Management Guide for how to configure which files and tokens get updated, the required call order, and the full token list.

docs.title: 5. Escaping Literal Placeholder Text
docs.text:
Sometimes a template needs to mention a {{Key}}-shaped placeholder in plain prose, without that mention being treated as a real, functioning placeholder.

Writing four braces instead of two around the key escapes it: {{{{Key}}}} renders as the literal, two-brace text {{Key}} in the output, and is never replaced or validated against a registered collector.

The text between the braces can be anything — it doesn't need to match a registered collector's key, or even look like a valid identifier. For example, {{{{this could be any text at all}}}} renders as the literal text {{this could be any text at all}}, with no relation to any registered collector.

In practice, this often looks like a comment that mentions a real collector key, such as the following:

MyScript.ps1.template
# Example: you could switch to Hybrid mode by using {{{{ORDERED_COMPONENTS}}}} instead
{{ENUM_DEFINITIONS}}

{{CLASS_DEFINITIONS}}

{{FUNCTION_DEFINITIONS}}

Without the extra braces, this comment's mention of {{ORDERED_COMPONENTS}} would itself be treated as the real placeholder, forcing Hybrid Mode and failing validation for a template that never intended to use it.

This also works with several escaped mentions together, for example when a template uses custom collection keys that a header comment should document:

MyScript.ps1.template
# This template accepts either individual placeholders ({{{{CORE_CLASSES}}}},
# {{{{DOMAIN_CLASSES}}}}) or the combined {{{{ORDERED_COMPONENTS}}}} placeholder,
# depending on your project's dependencies.

{{CORE_CLASSES}}

{{DOMAIN_CLASSES}}

Each {{{{...}}}} mention is escaped independently — the comment can name as many placeholders as needed, while the real, unescaped placeholders below it are still replaced normally.

If a placeholder-shaped mention is left unescaped by mistake, the resulting validation error includes a hint pointing at this syntax, to make the fix easy to find.

docs.title: 6. Validate Your Template
docs.text:
A mismatch between the collectors you registered and the placeholders in the template — a missing token, a typo in a key, or a wrong ordering — will cause the build to fail with a validation error. Whether your template is suitable for the mode your project's code requires isn't something you have to run a full build to find out. Test-PSScriptBuilderTemplate runs the same collection and dependency analysis a real build would — so it sees the same cross-dependencies — then reports whether the template is valid, without writing any output.

Validate your template whenever you add or rename a collector, change a -CollectionKey, or edit the template file:

$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath "src\Classes" |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath "src\Public"

if (Test-PSScriptBuilderTemplate `
        -ContentCollector $contentCollector `
        -TemplatePath     "build\Templates\MyProject.ps1.template") {
    Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild `
        -ContentCollector $contentCollector `
        -TemplatePath     "build\Templates\MyProject.ps1.template" `
        -OutputPath       "build\Output\MyProject.ps1"
}

Since Test-PSScriptBuilderTemplate returns only $true or $false, a failing result on its own doesn't say why — add -Verbose to see the specific validation error.

For a detailed result instead of a plain boolean — exactly which mode was detected, or which placeholders are missing or unknown — use Get-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis piped to Format-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis for the full analysis result:

Get-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis `
    -ContentCollector $contentCollector `
    -TemplatePath     "build\Templates\MyProject.ps1.template" |
    Format-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis

docs.title: Placeholder Rules
docs.text:
Placeholder matching is case-insensitive. Beyond that, PSScriptBuilder checks these rules for every template, in both Free and Ordered/Hybrid Mode, before any content is written to the output:

  • No whitespace inside the braces — {{ Key }} is invalid and causes a validation error
  • Each placeholder may appear only once in the template
  • Only keys matching a registered collector (or {{ORDERED_COMPONENTS}}) are valid
  • An escaped placeholder ({{{{Key}}}}) is never treated as a real placeholder — see Escaping Literal Placeholder Text

docs.title: Validation Modes
docs.text:
Which mode applies is determined by your code's actual dependencies, not by choice — see the Walkthrough above for how. This table is the complete summary:

Mode When activated Required Forbidden Free No cross-dependencies and no combined components placeholder in template One placeholder per collector (Using: exactly one shared placeholder, regardless of how many Using collectors are registered) — Hybrid No cross-dependencies, but combined components placeholder present in template Combined components placeholder Per-type placeholders for Enum, Class, Function Ordered A class depends on a function, even a single one-directional case (automatic) Combined components placeholder Per-type placeholders for Enum, Class, Function

In Free Mode, two ordering rules are enforced:

  • Using placeholders must appear before all others
  • Enum placeholders must appear before all Class and Function placeholders

The position of File placeholders is unrestricted relative to Enum, Class, and Function.

In Ordered and Hybrid mode, Using placeholders must appear before every other placeholder, including File placeholders and the combined components placeholder — the same rule Free Mode enforces.

docs.title: Validation Error Reference
docs.text:
Match the exact error text from a failed Test-PSScriptBuilderTemplate, Get-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis, or Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild call against this table:

Error Cause Fix Whitespace in placeholder {{ Key }} instead of {{Key}} Remove whitespace inside braces Missing combined components placeholder Ordered or Hybrid mode but placeholder absent Add the combined components placeholder to the template Forbidden placeholder in Ordered/Hybrid mode {{CLASS_DEFINITIONS}} etc. present when the combined components placeholder is used Remove per-type placeholders; use only the combined components placeholder Collector placeholder missing A registered collector (other than Using) has no matching placeholder Add {{CollectionKey}} for each collector Using placeholder missing One or more Using collectors are registered, but no Using placeholder is present Add a placeholder for one of the registered Using collectors Wrong placeholder order (Using) A non-Using placeholder appears before {{USING_STATEMENTS}} Move Using placeholders before all others Multiple Using placeholders More than one Using collector placeholder present when multiple Using collectors are registered Use only the placeholder for the first-registered Using collector; remove the others Wrong placeholder order (Enum) A Class or Function placeholder appears before {{ENUM_DEFINITIONS}} Move Enum placeholders before all Class and Function placeholders Duplicate placeholder Same {{Key}} appears more than once Remove the duplicate Unknown placeholder {{UNKNOWN}} has no corresponding collector Remove it or register a matching collector

docs.title: Tool Integrations
docs.text:
PSScriptBuilder focuses on one job: assembling your project's source files in dependency order. Task running, linting, and testing are already solved problems in the PowerShell ecosystem — PSScriptBuilder doesn't try to replace them. Since its output is a plain PowerShell file, the same established tools you'd use on any other PowerShell project work on it directly, with no special adapter needed.

This guide shows how to combine PSScriptBuilder with the most common ones:

  • Invoke-Build orchestrates the build as one task among others — testing, linting, or publishing.
  • PSScriptAnalyzer lints the assembled output script for style and correctness issues.
  • Pester tests the assembled output script to confirm it loads and behaves correctly.

A brief comparison with ModuleBuilder explains when each tool is the better fit.

docs.title: Invoke-Build
docs.text:
A build is rarely the only step — testing, linting, and publishing usually follow it, often with dependencies between them (testing should only run after a successful build, for example).

Invoke-Build is a task runner for PowerShell that handles exactly this: define named tasks with dependencies and run them selectively — similar to make or rake, but in pure PowerShell.

PSScriptBuilder works as an assembly step inside an Invoke-Build pipeline: one task assembles the output script, other tasks handle testing, linting, or publishing. Each task remains independently runnable.

.build.ps1
#Requires -Modules PSScriptBuilder, InvokeBuild

task SetRoot {
    Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot -Path $BuildRoot
}

task Build SetRoot, {
    $script:result = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
        Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class -IncludePath 'src\Classes' |
        Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath 'src\Functions' |
        Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild -TemplatePath 'build\MyProject.ps1.template' `
                                    -OutputPath   'build\Output\MyProject.ps1'
}

task Analyze Build, {
    $issues = Invoke-ScriptAnalyzer -Path 'build\Output\MyProject.ps1'
    if ($issues) { throw "PSScriptAnalyzer found $($issues.Count) issue(s)." }
}

task Test Build, {
    Invoke-Pester -Path 'tests' -CI
}

task . Build, Analyze, Test

Run the default task (Build → Analyze → Test):

Invoke-Build

Run only the build step:

Invoke-Build Build

Any task can be run in isolation during development, or the full chain in CI — the same .build.ps1 file serves both.

docs.title: PSScriptAnalyzer
docs.text:
Static analysis catches issues before they reach production — but only if you point it at what actually ships.

PSScriptAnalyzer is PowerShell's standard tool for this, checking for common coding issues, style violations, and potential bugs using a set of built-in and customizable rules.

Running PSScriptAnalyzer against the assembled output script — rather than the individual source files — verifies the final artifact, including any generated or injected content from the template.

$outputPath = 'build\Output\MyProject.ps1'

# Run with default rules
$issues = Invoke-ScriptAnalyzer -Path $outputPath

# Show results
$issues | Format-Table RuleName, Severity, Line, Message -AutoSize

# Fail if any errors or warnings found
$blocking = $issues | Where-Object { $_.Severity -in 'Error', 'Warning' }
if ($blocking) {
    throw "PSScriptAnalyzer: $($blocking.Count) blocking issue(s) found."
}

Some default rules don't fit assembled output the way they would hand-written source — a template might intentionally inject a Write-Host banner, which PSAvoidUsingWriteHost would otherwise flag. To suppress specific rules for the entire output file, use a PSScriptAnalyzer settings file:

PSScriptAnalyzerSettings.psd1
@{
    ExcludeRules = @(
        'PSAvoidUsingWriteHost',
        'PSAvoidTrailingWhitespace'
    )
}

Pass it to the analysis run:

$issues = Invoke-ScriptAnalyzer -Path $outputPath -Settings .\PSScriptAnalyzerSettings.psd1

Analyze source files during development

For fast feedback during development, run PSScriptAnalyzer against the individual source files in src\. Reserve the output-file analysis for CI — it catches issues introduced by the assembly process itself (e.g. template injection, ordering artifacts).

Add it as its own step in your workflow — an Invoke-Build task, for example — so linting failures are caught before a broken script reaches CI or production.

docs.title: Pester
docs.text:
Testing the assembled output — not just the individual source files — confirms that dependency ordering, template rendering, and everything else the build does actually produced a working script.

Pester, the standard testing framework for PowerShell, can target it directly: dot-sourcing the output in a BeforeAll block, then testing normally, confirms that all components load without errors and behave as expected.

tests\MyProject.Tests.ps1
BeforeAll {
    . $PSScriptRoot\..\build\Output\MyProject.ps1
}

Describe 'MyProject' {
    Context 'Class loading' {
        It 'loads without errors' {
            { [MyClass]::new() } | Should -Not -Throw
        }
    }

    Context 'Functions' {
        It 'Get-MyData returns a result' {
            Get-MyData | Should -Not -BeNullOrEmpty
        }
    }
}

Run the tests:

Invoke-Pester -Path 'tests' -Output Detailed

Run tests in a fresh PowerShell session

PowerShell class type definitions loaded via dot-sourcing cannot be unloaded from the session. If you rebuild and retest in the same session, stale types may cause unexpected failures. Use pwsh -NoProfile -Command "Invoke-Pester -Path tests" in CI or open a new terminal for each test run locally.

Combined with a file watcher, tests can rerun automatically after every rebuild — see Reacting to Build Results in the File Watching Guide.

Running Pester with CodeCoverage.Enabled against the assembled output reports coverage in output-script line numbers, not source file lines — see Translating Pester Code Coverage in the Source Maps Guide for mapping the results back to your original multi-file source.

docs.title: ModuleBuilder
docs.text:
Not every project has classes or enums with dependencies to resolve — sometimes a naming convention like 01-ClassName.ps1, 02-AnotherClass.ps1 is all the ordering a project needs.

ModuleBuilder is a well-established tool built around exactly that: assembling PowerShell modules from multiple files, handling dot-sourcing, manifest management, and file ordering via naming convention.

When ModuleBuilder is the better fit:

  • Your project uses only functions — no classes or enums
  • You prefer convention-based ordering (file prefixes) over automatic dependency analysis
  • You need tight integration with the PowerShell module manifest (.psd1) during the build

When PSScriptBuilder is the better fit:

  • Your project has components (classes, enums, functions) with dependencies that require a specific load order
  • You want automatic dependency resolution without manual file naming conventions
  • You need template-based output, release management, or post-build analysis as part of the same tool

The two tools are not mutually exclusive — ModuleBuilder can handle module structure and manifest management while PSScriptBuilder handles dependency-ordered assembly of the script body.
