docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
This section holds lookup material — content you consult for one specific fact (a parameter name, a default value, a property, a return type) rather than read from start to end. It complements the Guides, which explain how and why to use a feature with worked examples; here you look up exactly what a cmdlet accepts, or what an object you already have in hand actually contains.

This reference is split into two parts: the cmdlets themselves, and the PowerShell types they return.

  • Cmdlets

    Syntax, parameters, defaults, and usage examples for every public cmdlet — generated from the same comment-based help Get-Help -Full shows you directly in the console, organized here by category for browsing.

    Cmdlets

  • Types

    Property and method tables for the PowerShell classes PSScriptBuilder's cmdlets return — build results, source locations, coverage data, dependency graphs, and more. Useful when you already have an object in a variable and want to know exactly what it contains, without switching back to a guide for the full explanation.

    Types

docs.title: Type Reference
docs.text: Property and method tables for the PowerShell classes PSScriptBuilder's cmdlets return. This page is for looking up a specific type by name; for how-to explanations and worked examples of what produces these objects, see each section's own linked guide.

docs.title: Scaffolding
docs.text: New-PSScriptBuilderProject returns a PSScriptBuilderScaffoldingResult describing exactly what was created — the project name and path, the generated build script, and every file and directory written. See the Quick Start Guide for the full scaffolding workflow.

docs.title: PSScriptBuilderScaffoldingResult
docs.text:
Returned by New-PSScriptBuilderProject.

Property Type Description ProjectName string The name used when scaffolding the project ProjectPath string Absolute path to the project root directory BuildScriptPath string Absolute path to the generated Build-<Name>.ps1 script CreatedFiles string[] Absolute paths of all files created, in creation order CreatedDirectories string[] Absolute paths of all directories created, in creation order

docs.title: Build Results
docs.text: A single call to Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild returns one PSScriptBuilderBuildResult describing what happened: where the output went, how long it took, and whether a backup or source map was written. Two of its properties are themselves structured objects rather than plain values — ComponentCounts gives per-type totals (how many classes, functions, enums, and so on), and ComponentDetails (populated only when -Detailed is used) lists every individual component along with what it depends on. See the Build Pipeline Guide for the full build workflow and how to read this result.

docs.title: PSScriptBuilderBuildResult
docs.text:
Returned directly by Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild.

Property Type Description OutputPath string Absolute path of the generated output file OutputFileSize long Output file size in bytes ExecutionTime TimeSpan Total build duration BackupPath string Path of the backup file; $null if no backup was created SourceMapPath string Path of the source map sidecar; $null if -WriteSourceMap was not specified TotalComponents int Sum of all collected components across all collector types ComponentCounts PSScriptBuilderBuildComponentCounts Per-type component counts ProcessedFiles string[] Absolute paths of all source files processed during collection ComponentDetails PSScriptBuilderBuildComponentDetail[] Detailed info per component; shown by -Detailed SyntaxValid bool $true if the output file passed the syntax parse check

docs.title: PSScriptBuilderBuildComponentCounts
docs.text:
The value of PSScriptBuilderBuildResult.ComponentCounts; also reused as PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysisResult.ComponentCounts in Dependency Analysis.

Property Type Description UsingStatements int Number of using statements collected EnumDefinitions int Number of enum definitions collected ClassDefinitions int Number of class definitions collected FunctionDefinitions int Number of function definitions collected FileContents int Number of raw file contents collected

docs.title: PSScriptBuilderBuildComponentDetail
docs.text:
The value of each entry in PSScriptBuilderBuildResult.ComponentDetails, shown when -Detailed is passed to Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult.

Property Type Description Type PSScriptBuilderCollectorType Collector type (Enum, Class, Function, etc.) Name string Component name as defined in source code SourceFile string Absolute path to the file containing the component Dependencies string[] Names of components this component depends on

docs.title: Source Maps & Code Coverage
docs.text: Building merges many source files into one output script, so a line number reported by an error or by Pester refers to a position in that merged file, not to anything in your src\ tree. A source map (written via -WriteSourceMap) is what makes translating back possible. PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation is the basic unit of that translation — one resolved point, returned by Resolve-PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation for a single output line or ErrorRecord. PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverageResult builds on the same mechanism at a larger scale: Get-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage resolves every line in a Pester CodeCoverage result this way and aggregates the outcome per source file, so PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverageResult.MissedLocations is simply a collection of PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation entries. See the Source Maps Guide for the full workflow, including translating Pester code coverage.

docs.title: PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation
docs.text:
Returned by Resolve-PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation for each resolved entry, and reused as each element of PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverageResult.MissedLocations.

Property Type Description ComponentName string Name of the class, function, enum, or file component ComponentType string Collector type that produced this component SourceFile string Absolute path to the source file SourceLineNumber int 1-based line in SourceFile that corresponds to OutputLineNumber ComponentLineNumber int 1-based line within the component's source block OutputLineNumber int 1-based line in the compiled output script Offset int Lines between OutputLineNumber and the component's first output line

docs.title: PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverageResult
docs.text:
Returned by Get-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage, one instance per source file.

Property Type Description SourceFile string Absolute path to the source file (Format-PSScriptBuilderSourceCoverage displays it relative to the project root; the object itself always holds the absolute path) TotalCommands int Coverage-analyzed commands attributed to this source file HitCommands int Commands executed at least once MissedCommands int Commands never executed CoveragePercent double HitCommands / TotalCommands * 100 MissedLocations PSScriptBuilderSourceLocation[] Resolved location of every missed command

docs.title: File Watching
docs.text: Watch-PSScriptBuilderProject rebuilds automatically whenever a watched file changes, with no interactive session to display a normal error in. PSScriptBuilderWatchBuildErrorResult exists to carry a failed build's information out of that automated loop and into your own -OnError script block, so you can log it, alert on it, or otherwise react programmatically instead of losing the error entirely. See the File Watching Guide for the full callback setup, including how to combine -OnError with -OnSuccess.

docs.title: PSScriptBuilderWatchBuildErrorResult
docs.text:
Passed to the -OnError script block of Watch-PSScriptBuilderProject.

Property Type Description Exception Exception The exception that was thrown during the build operation ChangedFiles string[] Paths of the files whose changes triggered the failed build Timestamp datetime Date and time the build failure occurred

docs.title: Dependency Analysis
docs.text: Get-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis runs collectors, builds the full dependency graph, and returns one PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysisResult summarizing the whole project: whether a cycle exists, whether classes and functions need to be interleaved, and the resulting build order. That result's DependencyGraph property holds the underlying graph object itself, with its own set of query methods for anything the summary properties don't already answer directly — such as asking what a single named component depends on, or what would be affected if it changed. Get-PSScriptBuilderComponentDependency wraps exactly that kind of query, returning one PSScriptBuilderComponentDependencyEntry per dependency found. A related but distinct question — not "what does X depend on" but "is anything still using X at all" — is answered by Find-PSScriptBuilderUnusedComponent, which walks the same graph from a set of entry points and returns one PSScriptBuilderUnusedComponentEntry per component nothing reaches. See the Dependency Analysis Guide for the full workflow, diagram export, and drill-down traversal.

docs.title: PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysisResult
docs.text:
Returned by Get-PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysis.

Property Type Description HasCycles bool Whether a circular dependency was detected CyclePath string[] Components forming the cycle, e.g. A → B → C → A. Empty if no cycle. HasCrossDependencies bool Whether classes and functions are interleaved in the sorted order. Always false if HasCycles is true. OrderedComponents string[] Topologically sorted component names, enums first. Empty if HasCycles is true. ComponentCounts PSScriptBuilderBuildComponentCounts Per-type counts: UsingStatements, EnumDefinitions, ClassDefinitions, FunctionDefinitions, FileContents TotalComponents int Sum of all ComponentCounts fields TotalNodes int Number of nodes in the dependency graph TotalEdges int Number of edges (dependency relationships) in the graph DependencyGraph PSScriptBuilderDependencyGraph The full graph object for advanced queries

docs.title: PSScriptBuilderComponentDependencyEntry
docs.text:
Returned by Get-PSScriptBuilderComponentDependency, one instance per dependency.

Property Type Description Name string The name of the dependency Depth int Steps from the starting component: 1 = direct dependency, 2+ = transitive DependencyPath string[] Ordered path from the starting component to this dependency, e.g. {New-Employee, Employee, Person}

docs.title: PSScriptBuilderUnusedComponentEntry
docs.text:
Returned by Find-PSScriptBuilderUnusedComponent, one instance per unused component found.

Property Type Description Name string The component's name (enum, class, or function name) ComponentType PSScriptBuilderUnusedComponentType Which kind of component this is: Enum, Class, or Function CollectionKey string The collection key of the collector that provided this component SourceFile string Path to the file the component is defined in

docs.title: PSScriptBuilderDependencyGraph Methods
docs.text:
Methods available on PSScriptBuilderDependencyAnalysisResult.DependencyGraph, for queries beyond what the result object's own properties expose.

Method Returns Description GetDependencies(name) HashSet[string] All components name depends on (all edge types) GetDependencies(name, edgeType) HashSet[string] Dependencies filtered to a specific edge type GetDependents(name) HashSet[string] All components that depend on name GetDependents(name, edgeType) HashSet[string] Dependents filtered to a specific edge type GetAllNodes() HashSet[string] All component names in the graph HasNode(name) bool Whether a component is present in the graph GetNodeCount() int Total number of nodes GetEdgeCount() int Total number of dependency edges GetEdgeMap() Dictionary[string, List[PSScriptBuilderDependencyEdge]] Read-only access to every node's outgoing edges, for renderers and other consumers that need to iterate the full graph

The PSScriptBuilderDependencyEdgeType enum values used with the filtered overloads:

Value Meaning Fatal cycle? Inheritance class A : B — class inherits from another class Yes StaticInitializer Static property initializer references another type at load time Yes TypeReference Type used in a method body or property type annotation No FunctionCall Call to a standalone function defined elsewhere in the project No

All methods return a HashSet[string]. In PowerShell this behaves like any other collection — iterable with ForEach-Object, testable with .Count, joinable with -join. If no dependencies exist, the result is an empty collection, not an error.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text: New-PSScriptBuilderTemplate generates a template file automatically from your collector configuration — one placeholder per collector in Free Mode, or a single {{ORDERED_COMPONENTS}} block when cross-dependencies require it — and returns a PSScriptBuilderTemplateGenerationResult describing what it wrote. Later, whether a template was generated this way or written by hand, a build fails if its {{Placeholder}} tokens and the registered collectors don't match — a missing token, a typo, or the wrong ordering. PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysisResult, returned by Get-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis, surfaces exactly that comparison ahead of time: which placeholders were found in the template, which were expected given the collectors and validation mode, and where the two disagree. See the Templates Guide for validation modes, placeholder rules, and the validation error reference.

docs.title: PSScriptBuilderTemplateGenerationResult
docs.text:
Returned by New-PSScriptBuilderTemplate.

Property Type Description OutputPath string Absolute path to the generated template file Mode PSScriptBuilderTemplateValidationMode Validation mode applied during generation: Free, Ordered, or Hybrid Placeholders string[] All placeholder tokens written into the template, in the order they appear OrderedMode bool $true if -OrderedMode forced Hybrid mode; $false if Ordered mode was instead triggered automatically by cross-dependency detection

docs.title: PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysisResult
docs.text:
Returned by Get-PSScriptBuilderTemplateAnalysis.

Property Type Description IsValid bool Whether the template passed all validation rules ValidationErrors string[] Array of error messages (empty when valid) ValidationMode PSScriptBuilderTemplateValidationMode Free, Hybrid, or Ordered OrderedComponentsKey string The placeholder key used for the ordered components block (default: ORDERED_COMPONENTS) HasCrossDependencies bool Whether cross-dependencies were detected PlaceholdersFound string[] All {{...}} tokens found in the template (sorted, unique) PlaceholdersExpected string[] Tokens expected based on collectors and mode MissingPlaceholders string[] Expected but not found in template UnknownPlaceholders string[] Found in template but not matching any collector TemplatePath string Resolved absolute path to the template file TemplateSize int Template character count

docs.title: Collectors
docs.text: New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector returns a PSScriptBuilderContentCollector — the object every other collector cmdlet operates on, either via its own methods or via the Add-/Get-/Remove-PSScriptBuilderCollector cmdlets that wrap them. Before a build assembles anything, each individual collector registered on it extracts one raw data object per component it finds — the same objects Get-PSScriptBuilderCollectorContent returns for direct inspection, independent of running a build at all. Which type you get back depends on the collector. See the Collectors Guide for the full walkthrough.

docs.title: PSScriptBuilderCollectorBase
docs.text:
Returned by New-PSScriptBuilderCollector and Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector; the base type of every collector (PSScriptBuilderClassCollector, PSScriptBuilderFunctionCollector, etc.).

Property Type Description CollectorType PSScriptBuilderCollectorType Which kind of component this collector extracts: Using, Enum, Class, Function, or File CollectionKey string The unique key identifying this collector — also the template placeholder name IncludePaths string[] Directories scanned for source files ExcludePaths string[] Directories excluded from scanning IncludeFiles string[] Specific files or patterns always included, bypassing path exclusion ExcludeFiles string[] File name patterns excluded from scanning FileExtensions string[] File extensions scanned. Default: @(".ps1") Recurse bool Whether subdirectories are scanned. Default: $true HasCollected bool $true once Collect() has run successfully

Calling Collect() runs the collection and populates a type-specific data property (FunctionData for a Function collector, ClassData for a Class collector, and so on), each holding entries of the corresponding Collected Data Types.

docs.title: PSScriptBuilderContentCollector Methods
docs.text:
Methods available directly on the PSScriptBuilderContentCollector object, in addition to the collector cmdlets that wrap most of them.

Method Returns Cmdlet equivalent Description AddCollector(collector) void Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector Adds a collector to the collection RemoveCollector(key) bool Remove-PSScriptBuilderCollector Removes a collector by key. Returns $true if removed, $false if not found GetCollector(key) PSScriptBuilderCollectorBase Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector Returns the collector with the given key GetCollectors() PSScriptBuilderCollectorBase[] Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector Returns all collectors, sorted by CollectorType GetCount() int — Number of registered collectors Clear() void — Removes all collectors at once Execute() void — Runs Collect() on every registered collector, in CollectorType order GetCollectionKeys() string[] — Returns every registered collector's CollectionKey GetProcessedFiles() string[] — Returns every source file path collected, deduplicated GetDefinedComponentNames() HashSet[string] — Returns the names of all collected enums, classes, and functions GetDefinedComponentTypes() Dictionary[string, PSScriptBuilderCollectorType] — Maps every collected component's name to its collector type GetComponentSourceCode(componentName) string — Returns the source code of the named enum, class, or function GetComponentType(componentName) PSScriptBuilderCollectorType — Returns which collector type owns the named component BuildComponentCollectorMap() hashtable — Maps each class/function/enum name to its owning collector's CollectionKey GetUsingCollectors() PSScriptBuilderUsingCollector[] Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Using Returns all registered Using collectors GetFileCollectors() PSScriptBuilderFileCollector[] Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type File Returns all registered File collectors GetEnumCollectors() PSScriptBuilderEnumCollector[] Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Enum Returns all registered Enum collectors GetClassCollectors() PSScriptBuilderClassCollector[] Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class Returns all registered Class collectors GetFunctionCollectors() PSScriptBuilderFunctionCollector[] Get-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function Returns all registered Function collectors

Most of these methods have no cmdlet equivalent — they support scenarios (dependency analysis, cross-collector lookups, manual execution) that operate on the whole ContentCollector rather than exposing a dedicated top-level cmdlet. GetCount() is useful for asserting that all expected collectors were registered before starting a build. Clear() resets the object for reuse — for example in a script that dynamically rebuilds the collector configuration.

docs.title: Collected Data Types
docs.text:
Type Collector Holds PSScriptBuilderClassData Class Name, source code, base class, and type/call/static-initializer references PSScriptBuilderFunctionData Function Name, source code, and type/call references PSScriptBuilderEnumData Enum Name and source code PSScriptBuilderUsingData Using The using statement text and the source files it came from PSScriptBuilderFileData File Raw file name, path, and content

The dependency-related properties (BaseClass, TypeReferences, StaticInitializerReferences, CalledFunctions) carry semantics tied to how PSScriptBuilder orders components — what each one means and why it matters is explained where those concepts are taught, in Collected Data Properties in the Collectors Guide, rather than repeated here.

docs.title: Release Management
docs.text: Release management tracks two things across a project: the current version, build, and Git state (psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json), and which project files receive that state (psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json). Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData returns a PSScriptBuilderReleaseDataResult describing exactly which values changed; Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles returns a PSScriptBuilderBumpFilesResult describing which project files were updated. See the Release Management Guide for the full workflow.

docs.title: PSScriptBuilderReleaseDataResult
docs.text:
Returned by Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData.

Property Type Description TotalOperationsPerformed int Count of update operations performed Changes OrderedDictionary Changes grouped by category (Version, Build, Git), each an array of Property/OldValue/NewValue entries

docs.title: PSScriptBuilderBumpFilesResult
docs.text:
Returned by Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles.

Property Type Description TotalFilesProcessed int Count of all files processed, whether modified or not TotalFilesModified int Count of files that had actual content changes BumpDetails PSCustomObject[] One entry per modified file: Path, and ChangedItems (Pattern, Token, OldValue, NewValue) — only present for files that changed

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
Tutorials walk you through complete, end-to-end scenarios, each starting from a defined situation and ending with a working result. They are independent of each other, not a course to work through in sequence — pick the one that matches where you are today.

Two of them are alternative starting points depending on whether a PSScriptBuilder project exists yet: start from Building Your First Project with nothing in place, or from Migrating to PSScriptBuilder if your code already exists as a single file or as separate files without a build system. Setting Up Release Management builds on top of either one — it assumes a working PSScriptBuilder project is already in place.

If you are looking for an explanation of one specific feature rather than a full scenario, see the Guides instead.

  • Building Your First Project

    Create a small HR project from scratch — enums, classes, and a function — and produce your first dependency-ordered build.

    Building Your First Project

  • Migrating to PSScriptBuilder

    Adopt PSScriptBuilder in an existing codebase, whether it's one monolithic file or already split across several.

    Migrating to PSScriptBuilder

  • Setting Up Release Management

    Add version tracking to an existing project: a release data file, bump configuration, and a dedicated release script alongside your build script.

    Setting Up Release Management

docs.title: Building Your First Project
docs.text:
This tutorial walks you through building a complete PSScriptBuilder project from scratch. You will create the source files, configure PSScriptBuilder, write a template and a build script, and run your first build. By the end, you have a single deployable .ps1 script generated from multiple source files — with all dependencies automatically resolved.

If you already have an existing project and want to adopt PSScriptBuilder, see Migrating to PSScriptBuilder instead.

Prerequisites: PSScriptBuilder installed — see Installation.

docs.title: What We're Building
docs.text:
A small HR project with two enums, three classes, and one function — enough to demonstrate dependency resolution and multi-collector builds. The final project structure looks like this:

HRTools/
├── psscriptbuilder.config.json
├── Build-HRTools.ps1
├── src/
│   ├── Enums/
│   │   ├── Department.ps1
│   │   └── EmploymentStatus.ps1
│   ├── Classes/
│   │   ├── Address.ps1
│   │   ├── Person.ps1
│   │   └── Employee.ps1
│   └── Public/
│       └── New-Employee.ps1
└── build/
    ├── Templates/
    │   └── HRTools.ps1.template
    └── Output/

docs.title: 1. Create the Directory Structure
docs.text:
PSScriptBuilder collects each component type from its own directory — one collector per type:

  • src\Enums — this project's enums
  • src\Classes — this project's classes
  • src\Public — this project's functions

Two more directories hold the build's own files, not source code:

  • build\Templates — the template you write
  • build\Output — the generated script it produces

Create all five in one call — -Path accepts multiple values, and creates any missing intermediate folders along the way:

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path "HRTools\src\Enums",
                                   "HRTools\src\Classes",
                                   "HRTools\src\Public",
                                   "HRTools\build\Templates",
                                   "HRTools\build\Output"
Set-Location HRTools

Set-Location HRTools at the end puts you there — every remaining command in this tutorial assumes you're working from the project root.

docs.title: 2. Write the Source Files
docs.text: Each source file contains exactly one component, saved into the matching folder you created in Create the Directory Structure — the path shown in each code block's title is exactly where it goes. PSScriptBuilder discovers the files automatically — file names do not need to match class or enum names, but it is good practice.

docs.title: Enums
docs.text:
Two independent enums, with no dependencies on anything else in the project:

src\Enums\Department.ps1
enum Department {
    Engineering
    HumanResources
    Finance
    Marketing
}
src\Enums\EmploymentStatus.ps1
enum EmploymentStatus {
    Active
    OnLeave
    Terminated
    Retired
}

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
Address and Person are likewise independent — plain data classes with no references to other components:

src\Classes\Address.ps1
class Address {
    [string] $Street
    [string] $City
    [string] $PostalCode
    [string] $Country

    Address([string] $street, [string] $city, [string] $postalCode, [string] $country) {
        $this.Street     = $street
        $this.City       = $city
        $this.PostalCode = $postalCode
        $this.Country    = $country
    }
}
src\Classes\Person.ps1
class Person {
    [string] $FirstName
    [string] $LastName

    Person([string] $firstName, [string] $lastName) {
        $this.FirstName = $firstName
        $this.LastName  = $lastName
    }
}

Employee inherits from Person and references Address, Department, and EmploymentStatus.

PSScriptBuilder detects these dependencies automatically and ensures that all prerequisites appear before Employee in the output — regardless of the order files are on disk.

src\Classes\Employee.ps1
class Employee : Person {
    [Address]          $Address
    [Department]       $Department
    [EmploymentStatus] $Status
    [DateTime]         $HireDate
    [decimal]          $Salary

    Employee(
        [string]           $firstName,
        [string]           $lastName,
        [Address]          $address,
        [Department]       $department,
        [DateTime]         $hireDate,
        [decimal]          $salary
    ) : base($firstName, $lastName) {
        $this.Address    = $address
        $this.Department = $department
        $this.Status     = [EmploymentStatus]::Active
        $this.HireDate   = $hireDate
        $this.Salary     = $salary
    }
}

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
New-Employee in turn depends on Employee — completing a dependency chain that spans all three collector types (Enum, Class, Function):

src\Public\New-Employee.ps1
Function New-Employee {
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType([Employee])]
    param(
        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [string] $FirstName,

        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [string] $LastName,

        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [Address] $Address,

        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [Department] $Department,

        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [DateTime] $HireDate,

        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [decimal] $Salary
    )

    return [Employee]::new($FirstName, $LastName, $Address, $Department, $HireDate, $Salary)
}

docs.title: 3. Add the Configuration File
docs.text:
Run the following cmdlet to generate psscriptbuilder.config.json:

New-PSScriptBuilderConfiguration

The generated file contains all required fields pre-filled with sensible defaults. The two fields you will use most are build.templatePath and build.outputPath — both already point to the build\Templates and build\Output directories you created in Create the Directory Structure.

For a full explanation of all fields, see the Configuration Guide.

docs.title: 4. Create the Template
docs.text:
The template defines the structure of the generated output file. Each {{Token}} placeholder is replaced with the collected and dependency-ordered source code of the corresponding collector.

Create build\Templates\HRTools.ps1.template:

build\Templates\HRTools.ps1.template
{{ENUM_DEFINITIONS}}

{{CLASS_DEFINITIONS}}

{{FUNCTION_DEFINITIONS}}

The placeholders map to the collectors you will configure in the next step:

Placeholder Collector type {{ENUM_DEFINITIONS}} Enum {{CLASS_DEFINITIONS}} Class {{FUNCTION_DEFINITIONS}} Function

For a full explanation of placeholder syntax and the three validation modes, see the Templates Guide.

docs.title: 5. Write the Build Script
docs.text:
Create Build-HRTools.ps1. The build script loads the module, sets the project root, reads the configuration, configures the collectors, and invokes the build:

Build-HRTools.ps1
using module PSScriptBuilder

Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot -Path $PSScriptRoot

$config = Get-PSScriptBuilderConfiguration

$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Enum     -IncludePath 'src\Enums'   |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath 'src\Classes' |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath 'src\Public'

$buildParams = @{
    ContentCollector = $contentCollector
    TemplatePath     = Join-Path $config.Build.TemplatePath 'HRTools.ps1.template'
    OutputPath       = Join-Path $config.Build.OutputPath   'HRTools.ps1'
}

Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild @buildParams | Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult

Here's what each part does, in detail:

docs.title: Loading the Module
docs.text: using module PSScriptBuilder is the correct way to load PSScriptBuilder for any script, and must be the very first statement in it — see Installation for why Import-Module doesn't work the same way, and what happens if something precedes it.

docs.title: Setting the Project Root
docs.text: PSScriptBuilder needs to know where relative paths (like the collector -IncludePath values) should resolve from — that's set with Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot. Passing $PSScriptRoot (the directory of the currently running script) is always the correct value when calling this from a build script, since it points to that same directory regardless of where you run the script from or where the project is later moved to.

docs.title: Reading the Configuration
docs.text:
Rather than hardcoding the template and output paths, the build script reads them from psscriptbuilder.config.json — generated in Add the Configuration File — via Get-PSScriptBuilderConfiguration, which returns a typed object.

Using $config.Build.TemplatePath and $config.Build.OutputPath means you only need to update the config file if the directories change — not the build script.

docs.title: Configuring the Collectors
docs.text:
Every component type (enums, classes, functions) needs its own collector to scan its source directory. Here is that part of the script again, to keep the explanation next to the code it describes:

$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Enum     -IncludePath 'src\Enums'   |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath 'src\Classes' |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath 'src\Public'

New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector creates the container that holds all the collectors together, and each Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector call registers one collector on it:

  • -Type determines which kind of component the collector looks for — Enum, Class, or Function — which in turn determines which template placeholder its output fills:
    • Enum → {{ENUM_DEFINITIONS}}
    • Class → {{CLASS_DEFINITIONS}}
    • Function → {{FUNCTION_DEFINITIONS}}
  • -IncludePath tells it which directory to scan for source files

Piping the three Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector calls together registers all three on the same container.

docs.title: Assembling and Invoking the Build
docs.text:
Two things remain: bundling all the parameters together, then invoking the build with them.

$buildParams = @{
    ContentCollector = $contentCollector
    TemplatePath     = Join-Path $config.Build.TemplatePath 'HRTools.ps1.template'
    OutputPath       = Join-Path $config.Build.OutputPath   'HRTools.ps1'
}

Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild @buildParams | Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult

$buildParams collects every parameter into a single hashtable — the collector container from above, plus the template and output file paths built from the same $config values already read — instead of passing each one to Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild individually. Join-Path combines each configured directory with the specific file name (HRTools.ps1.template, HRTools.ps1).

Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild @buildParams then runs the build. The @ triggers splatting — it passes each hashtable key as a matching named parameter, equivalent to writing -ContentCollector $contentCollector -TemplatePath ... -OutputPath ... directly.

Piping the result into Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult turns the raw result object into the readable Build Summary shown in Run the Build.

docs.title: 6. Run the Build
docs.text:
With the source files, configuration, template, and build script all in place, run the build:

.\Build-HRTools.ps1

Expected output:

WARNING: 5 cross-collector dependency(s) detected. Verify template placeholder order. Run with -Verbose for details.

Build Summary
  Output : ...\build\Output\HRTools.ps1
  Size   : 2.14 KB
  Time   : 312.45 ms

Components
  Enums     : 2
  Classes   : 3
  Functions : 1
  Total     : 6

The warning is a feature, not a problem to fix: PSScriptBuilder sorts components correctly within each collector's placeholder, but it cannot reorder placeholders across collectors in your template — so instead of silently risking the wrong output order, it flags cross-collector dependencies and asks you to confirm the template placeholder order yourself.

Here are the five cross-collector dependencies it found:

  • Employee (Class) references Department (Enum)
  • Employee (Class) references EmploymentStatus (Enum)
  • New-Employee (Function) references Address (Class)
  • New-Employee (Function) references Department (Enum)
  • New-Employee (Function) references Employee (Class)

The generated build\Output\HRTools.ps1 contains all components in the correct load order: enums first, then classes in dependency order (Address and Person before Employee), then functions.

That correctness comes from two different places. PSScriptBuilder resolved the within-collector class order automatically by analyzing the actual code — you never told it Address and Person come before Employee. The across-collector order — enums before classes before functions — came from the template's placeholder arrangement written in Create the Template, which already lists {{ENUM_DEFINITIONS}} before {{CLASS_DEFINITIONS}} before {{FUNCTION_DEFINITIONS}}.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
You now have a complete PSScriptBuilder project that builds a dependency-ordered script from six separate source files, with no manual ordering required. Along the way, you configured three collectors, wrote a template with placeholder tokens, and saw PSScriptBuilder resolve dependencies automatically — both within a single collector and across collector boundaries, the same mechanism that produced the cross-collector warning earlier.

In short: you never had to think about component order yourself — PSScriptBuilder handled it every time, whether the dependency stayed within one collector or crossed into another.

docs.title: Migrating to PSScriptBuilder
docs.text:
This tutorial covers two scenarios: starting from a single monolithic file that contains all your code, and starting from a project that already uses separate files but has no build system yet. Both end in the same place — a working PSScriptBuilder project that generates a single deployable output file.

Prerequisites: PSScriptBuilder installed — see Installation.

docs.title: Scenario A: Starting from a Single File
docs.text:
This is the most common starting point. A single .psm1 or .ps1 file contains everything — enums, classes, and functions in one place. It works, but as the file grows it becomes harder to navigate, test, and maintain. The recommended PSScriptBuilder project structure uses one file per component — easier to navigate and version-control — so the first step is splitting.

This example reuses the same HR domain model as Building Your First Project — the same Department, EmploymentStatus, Address, Person, Employee, and New-Employee components, shown here as a single monolithic file instead of already split into one file per component.

You do not need to have worked through Building Your First Project before this one — this tutorial stands on its own. It does, however, explain the setup mechanics used here from Set Up PSScriptBuilder onward — configuration, template, build script — in much more depth than this tutorial does; if you want that depth, look there rather than here.

If you've already worked through it, the components here will already look familiar, so you can focus entirely on the migration steps rather than the domain model.

Automated inventory available

PSScriptBuilder can identify all components in a monolithic script automatically — enums, classes, and functions by name. This saves the manual inventory step and ensures nothing is missed. See Analysing a Monolithic Script in the Code Analysis Guide.

docs.title: 1. Identify the Components
docs.text:
Open your file and identify every component: enums, classes, and functions. A monolithic HR file might look like this:

HRTools.ps1 — before migration
enum Department {
    Engineering
    HumanResources
    Finance
    Marketing
}

enum EmploymentStatus {
    Active
    OnLeave
    Terminated
    Retired
}

class Address {
    [string] $Street
    [string] $City
    [string] $PostalCode
    [string] $Country

    Address([string] $street, [string] $city, [string] $postalCode, [string] $country) {
        $this.Street     = $street
        $this.City       = $city
        $this.PostalCode = $postalCode
        $this.Country    = $country
    }
}

class Person {
    [string] $FirstName
    [string] $LastName

    Person([string] $firstName, [string] $lastName) {
        $this.FirstName = $firstName
        $this.LastName  = $lastName
    }
}

class Employee : Person {
    [Address]          $Address
    [Department]       $Department
    [EmploymentStatus] $Status
    [DateTime]         $HireDate
    [decimal]          $Salary

    Employee(
        [string]           $firstName,
        [string]           $lastName,
        [Address]          $address,
        [Department]       $department,
        [DateTime]         $hireDate,
        [decimal]          $salary
    ) : base($firstName, $lastName) {
        $this.Address    = $address
        $this.Department = $department
        $this.Status     = [EmploymentStatus]::Active
        $this.HireDate   = $hireDate
        $this.Salary     = $salary
    }
}

Function New-Employee {
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType([Employee])]
    param(
        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [string] $FirstName,

        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [string] $LastName,

        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [Address] $Address,

        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [Department] $Department,

        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [DateTime] $HireDate,

        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [decimal] $Salary
    )

    return [Employee]::new($FirstName, $LastName, $Address, $Department, $HireDate, $Salary)
}

Note which components depend on which — you will need this later to verify that the generated output is correct. Employee inherits from Person and references Address, Department, and EmploymentStatus. PSScriptBuilder will detect all of these automatically.

docs.title: 2. Plan the Directory Structure
docs.text:
PSScriptBuilder uses separate collectors per component type. The recommended directory layout maps directly to those types:

HRTools/
├── psscriptbuilder.config.json
├── Build-HRTools.ps1
├── src/
│   ├── Enums/      ← one file per enum
│   ├── Classes/    ← one file per class
│   └── Public/     ← one file per public function
└── build/
    ├── Templates/
    └── Output/

docs.title: 3. Split the File
docs.text:
Create the directories and move each component into its own file. The file name should match the component name — this is not enforced but makes the project easier to navigate:

src/
├── Enums/
│   ├── Department.ps1
│   └── EmploymentStatus.ps1
├── Classes/
│   ├── Address.ps1
│   ├── Person.ps1
│   └── Employee.ps1
└── Public/
    └── New-Employee.ps1

Each file contains exactly one component — the same code as in the original, just separated. PSScriptBuilder handles the load order automatically.

PSScriptBuilder parses each file in isolation. Unable to find type warnings that PowerShell would normally emit when a class references types from other files are suppressed internally — they are expected and not actionable.

docs.title: 4. Set Up PSScriptBuilder
docs.text:
From the project root, open a PowerShell session and import the module — none of the cmdlets work without it:

using module PSScriptBuilder

Then generate the configuration file:

New-PSScriptBuilderConfiguration

Create the template at build\Templates\HRTools.ps1.template:

build\Templates\HRTools.ps1.template
{{ENUM_DEFINITIONS}}

{{CLASS_DEFINITIONS}}

{{FUNCTION_DEFINITIONS}}

Create the build script. It loads the module, sets the project root, reads the configuration, configures the collectors, and invokes the build:

Build-HRTools.ps1
using module PSScriptBuilder

Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot -Path $PSScriptRoot

$config = Get-PSScriptBuilderConfiguration

$contentCollector = New-PSScriptBuilderContentCollector |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Enum     -IncludePath 'src\Enums'   |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath 'src\Classes' |
    Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath 'src\Public'

$buildParams = @{
    ContentCollector = $contentCollector
    TemplatePath     = Join-Path $config.Build.TemplatePath 'HRTools.ps1.template'
    OutputPath       = Join-Path $config.Build.OutputPath   'HRTools.ps1'
}

Invoke-PSScriptBuilderBuild @buildParams | Format-PSScriptBuilderBuildResult

docs.title: 5. Run the First Build and Verify
docs.text:
.\Build-HRTools.ps1

Open build\Output\HRTools.ps1 and compare it with your original file. The content should be equivalent — same components, same logic — but in a PSScriptBuilder-determined load order: enums first, then classes in dependency order, then functions.

Once it matches, the migration is complete — your project is fully managed by PSScriptBuilder.

docs.title: Scenario B: Starting from Separate Files
docs.text: If your project already has separate files per component, the migration is usually straightforward — mostly configuration and a build script, with directory changes only if your current layout doesn't already match PSScriptBuilder's per-type model (see Map Your Directories to Collector Types).

docs.title: 1. Map Your Directories to Collector Types
docs.text:
PSScriptBuilder collects components by type. Check whether your existing structure maps cleanly:

What you have Collector type Recommended path Enum definitions Enum src\Enums Class definitions Class src\Classes Exported functions Function src\Public Internal functions Function src\Private Raw files (headers, footers) File src\Files

If your files are already laid out this way, skip ahead to Set Up PSScriptBuilder. If they're in a flat structure with mixed types instead — for example a single src/ folder containing both classes and functions — reorganising isn't required: a single directory can serve more than one collector, since each one only picks out the component type it was configured for and ignores everything else it finds there. Point one collector per type — Enum, Class, and Function — at the same directory:

Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Enum     -IncludePath 'src'
Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Class    -IncludePath 'src'
Add-PSScriptBuilderCollector -Type Function -IncludePath 'src'

If you'd still prefer the cleaner, one-type-per-folder layout shown in the table — purely for readability, not because it's required — move the files there and point each collector's -IncludePath at its own dedicated folder (src\Enums, src\Classes, and so on) instead of the shared folder shown above — the same per-type pattern shown in Scenario A's build script.

docs.title: 2. Set Up PSScriptBuilder
docs.text:
Follow steps 4 and 5 from Scenario A — generate the configuration file, create the template, write the build script, and run the first build. The only difference is the collector setup itself: use whichever -IncludePath/-Type configuration you worked out in Map Your Directories to Collector Types, rather than Scenario A's example paths.

Once the first build succeeds, the migration is complete — your project is fully managed by PSScriptBuilder.

docs.title: Setting Up Release Management
docs.text:
This tutorial walks you through setting up PSScriptBuilder's release management system. You will create a release data file, configure which files receive automatic version updates, and create a dedicated release script alongside your existing build script.

Along the way, you'll start with the simplest method for updating a file automatically and discover it doesn't hold up on its own. The obvious next step — switching to a different method entirely — turns out to have its own gap, one that only shows up on a first release. The fix is using both together. Seeing each limitation firsthand makes the reasoning stick far better than reading about it upfront.

By the end, running a single command will bump the version, update all registered files, and produce a correctly versioned build output — on every release, not just the first.

Prerequisites:

  • A working PSScriptBuilder project — see Building Your First Project

docs.title: The Two Release Files
docs.text:
Release management is built around two files, which you'll create over the next two steps:

File Purpose psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json Stores the current version and release metadata psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json Defines which project files get updated, and how

docs.title: 1. Create the Release Data File
docs.text:
The release data file psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json is the central store for your project's current version and release metadata. All other release management steps read from and write to this file.

Create it by running New-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData. Like every PSScriptBuilder cmdlet, it only works once the module has been imported. Open a PowerShell session in your project directory and import it:

using module PSScriptBuilder

Then run the cmdlet:

New-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData

Running the cmdlet writes the file to the path configured in psscriptbuilder.config.json's release.dataFile field.

Unless you've changed it, that's build\Release\psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json. If that directory doesn't exist yet, PSScriptBuilder creates it automatically.

Everything in the file starts at its initial value, always the same fixed default regardless of your project's actual state.

The version deserves a second look before you continue: unlike the build number and timestamps, which simply catch up on the next release, the version follows semantic versioning — once a release is tagged or published, others rely on major/minor/patch changes to mean something specific. Starting it at the wrong number — 0.1.0 for a project that already has real releases out — is not something that quietly corrects itself later.

If your project already has an established version, edit psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json and set the "major", "minor", "patch", and "full" fields under "version" to match your current version before continuing.

docs.title: 2. Create the Bump Configuration
docs.text:
The bump configuration file psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json defines which project files get updated, and how.

Unlike the release data file, there is no cmdlet to create the bump configuration file — create it yourself at the path set in psscriptbuilder.config.json's release.bumpConfigFile field.

By default, that's build\Release\psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json:

psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json
{
    "bumpFiles": []
}

For each file that should receive version updates, add an entry to bumpFiles.

In this tutorial, that file is HRTools.ps1.template — the same template you wrote in Building Your First Project. Since every build regenerates the output from this template, embedding the version and build timestamp directly in it means every future build carries the current release information automatically, without touching anything else:

psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json
{
    "bumpFiles": [
        {
            "description": "Output template — inject version and build metadata",
            "path": "build\\Templates\\HRTools.ps1.template",
            "tokens": ["VERSION", "BUILD_TIMESTAMP"]
        }
    ]
}

Here's what each field does:

  • description — sets the text that identifies this entry in the bump result (optional, but recommended)
  • path — sets the file this entry modifies: build\Templates\HRTools.ps1.template
  • tokens — defines which values get written into that file: VERSION and BUILD_TIMESTAMP

An entry like this — with just a tokens array — is PSScriptBuilder's Simple Token Mode.

For PSScriptBuilder to know where in the file each value belongs, the file itself must contain a matching placeholder for every name listed in tokens — written as {{TOKEN_NAME}}. This entry lists VERSION and BUILD_TIMESTAMP, so add a line for each at the top of the template:

build\Templates\HRTools.ps1.template
# Version: {{VERSION}}
# Built: {{BUILD_TIMESTAMP}}

{{ENUM_DEFINITIONS}}

{{CLASS_DEFINITIONS}}

{{FUNCTION_DEFINITIONS}}

With the release data file and bump configuration in place, nothing updates automatically yet — something needs to trigger the bump and the build together. That's what you'll create next.

Available tokens

PSScriptBuilder provides tokens for version components, build metadata, and Git details. To see all available tokens, run Get-PSScriptBuilderReleaseDataTokens. For the full token list with descriptions, see the Release Management Guide.

docs.title: 3. Create a Release Script
docs.text:
A release bumps the version, updates every registered file, and produces the build — all in one command, rather than three separate ones.

Rather than adding this logic to Build-HRTools.ps1 itself, create a separate script for it. Build and release are different actions with different consequences: a build is safe to run at any time, but a release changes the version and rewrites files on disk. Keeping them as separate scripts means running a release is always a deliberate, explicit choice — you run Release-HRTools.ps1 instead of Build-HRTools.ps1 — rather than a flag you could pass by accident, and Build-HRTools.ps1 never needs to know release management exists at all.

Bumping the version also means deciding which part to bump — major, minor, or patch, per the semantic versioning already covered in Create the Release Data File — so -Major, -Minor, and -Patch are three switches for that choice.

Create Release-HRTools.ps1:

Release-HRTools.ps1
using module PSScriptBuilder

[CmdletBinding(DefaultParameterSetName = 'None')]
param(
    [Parameter(ParameterSetName = 'Major')]
    [switch] $Major,

    [Parameter(ParameterSetName = 'Minor')]
    [switch] $Minor,

    [Parameter(ParameterSetName = 'Patch')]
    [switch] $Patch
)

Set-PSScriptBuilderProjectRoot -Path $PSScriptRoot

$releaseParams = @{
    UpdateBuildDetails = $true
}

switch ($PSCmdlet.ParameterSetName) {
    'Major' { $releaseParams.Major = $true }
    'Minor' { $releaseParams.Minor = $true }
    'Patch' { $releaseParams.Patch = $true }
}

$releaseDataResult = Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData @releaseParams
$releaseDataResult | Format-PSScriptBuilderReleaseDataResult

$bumpResult = Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles
$bumpResult | Format-PSScriptBuilderBumpResult

. "$PSScriptRoot\Build-HRTools.ps1"

What each release step does:

  • Update-PSScriptBuilderReleaseData — bumps the version in psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json and records the current build timestamp (-UpdateBuildDetails)
  • Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles — reads the updated release data and applies all registered replacements across every file in psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json
  • . "$PSScriptRoot\Build-HRTools.ps1" — runs the existing build script, producing the output with the version and files now up to date

The order matters:

  1. Release data is updated first
  2. Bump files are processed next
  3. Build-HRTools.ps1 runs last

Why it matters: Swap 2 and 3, and release management tokens such as {{VERSION}} would still be present when the build runs. The build validates that all {{...}} patterns are expected — and since it only recognizes the placeholders it manages itself, any remaining release management placeholder would cause a validation error.

docs.title: 4. Run a Release Build
docs.text:
With the release script in place, running a release is now a single command. Try it with a patch release — the smallest kind of version bump:

.\Release-HRTools.ps1 -Patch

You will see three blocks of output:

1. Release data result — the new version and the metadata that was recorded:

Release data result
Category : Version

  Property  : patch
  Old Value : 0
  New Value : 1

  Property  : full
  Old Value : 0.1.0
  New Value : 0.1.1

...

2. Bump files result — every changed file, with each replacement listed:

Bump files result
File : build\Templates\HRTools.ps1.template

  Token     : VERSION
  Old Value : {{VERSION}}
  New Value : 0.1.1

  Token     : BUILD_TIMESTAMP
  Old Value : {{BUILD_TIMESTAMP}}
  New Value : 2026-08-27T10:52:53Z

3. Build result — the output path, file size, build time, and component counts:

Build result
WARNING: 5 cross-collector dependency(s) detected. Verify template placeholder order. Run with -Verbose for details.

Build Summary
  Output : build\Output\HRTools.ps1
  Size   : 1.95 KB
  Time   : 770.56 ms

Components
  Enums     : 2
  Classes   : 3
  Functions : 1
  Total     : 6

To see the effect in the actual file, open the template — the placeholders shown above are now real values:

build\Templates\HRTools.ps1.template
# Version: 0.1.1
# Built: 2026-08-27T10:52:53Z

docs.title: 5. Run a Second Release Build
docs.text:
Run another release on the same template — another patch release, exactly like the first:

.\Release-HRTools.ps1 -Patch

The version and build metadata update correctly again, but the bump files result now reads:

Expected output
WARNING: Bump file '...\build\Templates\HRTools.ps1.template' is configured for release data substitution, but none of its patterns matched the current content - nothing was updated. If this file was already bumped by a prior run, add a Regex-mode fallback entry (Mixed Bump Mode) so subsequent runs keep matching.

No changes were made.

And the template is exactly what it was after the first release:

build\Templates\HRTools.ps1.template
# Version: 0.1.1
# Built: 2026-08-27T10:52:53Z

Identical to before the release — that's the point. This is a real limitation of Simple Token Mode: {{VERSION}} and {{BUILD_TIMESTAMP}} only ever existed in the file until the first release replaced them with real values. From the second release onward, there is nothing left to find — the placeholders are gone — so Update-PSScriptBuilderBumpFiles has nothing to do for this file, which is exactly what "No changes were made" reports.

This is also exactly the situation the warning above is for: every entry configured for this file failed to match. The next section fixes this permanently.

psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json itself is unaffected by any of this: it doesn't rely on placeholders, so it keeps updating correctly on every release regardless.

docs.title: 6. Keep the Template Up to Date on Every Release
docs.text:
To fix this permanently, add a second entry for the same file to psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json — this time using a different approach that looks for a pattern instead of a literal placeholder marker, so it keeps working after that marker is gone:

psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json
{
    "bumpFiles": [
        {
            "description": "Output template — inject version and build metadata (first release)",
            "path": "build\\Templates\\HRTools.ps1.template",
            "tokens": ["VERSION", "BUILD_TIMESTAMP"]
        },
        {
            "description": "Output template — update version and build metadata (every later release)",
            "path": "build\\Templates\\HRTools.ps1.template",
            "items": [
                {
                    "pattern": "# Version: ({REGEX_VERSION})",
                    "tokens": ["VERSION"]
                },
                {
                    "pattern": "# Built: ({REGEX_BUILD_TIMESTAMP})",
                    "tokens": ["BUILD_TIMESTAMP"]
                }
            ]
        }
    ]
}

Here's what each field does:

  • description — same as the first entry: identifies this entry in the bump result
  • path — the same file the tokens entry updates
  • items — one entry per value to replace: a pattern (regex, with the replaced part in parentheses) and tokens (which value fills it in)

An entry like this — with an items array instead of tokens — is PSScriptBuilder's Regex Pattern Mode.

The difference is what each mode looks for. Simple Token Mode looks for a literal marker — {{VERSION}} — which is why it stops working once that marker is gone. Regex Pattern Mode instead looks for a pattern: a description of where the value always sits in the line, regardless of what that value currently is.

You do not need to write that pattern yourself: every release token has a matching REGEX_* counterpart that PSScriptBuilder expands into a ready-made regular expression. {REGEX_VERSION} and {REGEX_BUILD_TIMESTAMP} are the ones used here — one recognizes a version number like 0.1.3, the other a timestamp like 2026-08-27T10:53:25Z.

Your job is only to say where in the line that value sits, by wrapping the placeholder in parentheses: everything inside the parentheses is the part that gets replaced; everything outside is only there to help PSScriptBuilder find the right spot in the line — it has to match, but it is never changed itself.

Both entries point at the same file and both stay. Using both together like this is PSScriptBuilder's Mixed Mode.

The tokens entry from Create the Bump Configuration already did its one job — replacing the literal placeholders during Run a Release Build's first release — and has nothing left to do for this project from here on.

The items entry is what actually keeps the template updated on every release after that, as you just saw.

The template is still stuck at 0.1.1 from the first release — the second didn't touch it. Meanwhile, the release data file moved on regardless: the second release already bumped it to 0.1.2. Any build produced in between would have embedded that stale 0.1.1, silently out of sync with the official 0.1.2 release.

The lesson carries beyond this one file: for any file you register going forward, use Mixed Mode from the start, rather than beginning with Simple Token Mode alone and hitting this same gap again.

Run the release again to see the fix in action:

.\Release-HRTools.ps1 -Patch
Expected output
File : build\Templates\HRTools.ps1.template

  Pattern   : # Version: ({REGEX_VERSION})
  Token     : VERSION
  Old Value : # Version: 0.1.1
  New Value : # Version: 0.1.3

  Pattern   : # Built: ({REGEX_BUILD_TIMESTAMP})
  Token     : BUILD_TIMESTAMP
  Old Value : # Built: 2026-08-27T10:52:53Z
  New Value : # Built: 2026-08-27T10:53:25Z

The version advanced to 0.1.3, and the template caught up from 0.1.1 straight to the current value — skipping 0.1.2 entirely. That gap only exists because this tutorial deliberately introduced Mixed Mode two releases late; with both entries in place from the start, Simple Token Mode handles the first release and Regex Pattern Mode every one after, so no file ever falls behind like this.

Open the template to see the actual file:

build\Templates\HRTools.ps1.template — after
# Version: 0.1.3
# Built: 2026-08-27T10:53:25Z

From here on, every future release updates the template the same way, automatically — no further configuration needed.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
You now have a complete release management setup: psscriptbuilder.releasedata.json tracks the version and build metadata, psscriptbuilder.bumpconfig.json keeps HRTools.ps1.template in sync with that data, and Release-HRTools.ps1 ties both to a build — calling Build-HRTools.ps1 once both files are up to date.

A single command now bumps the version, updates every registered file, and produces a correctly versioned build output.

Along the way, you also saw why Simple Token Mode alone isn't enough — it only ever fires on a file's first release — and fixed that permanently with Mixed Mode, pairing it with Regex Pattern Mode for every release after.

In short: version bumping and file updates only stay correct together when both keep working on every release, not just the first — that's what Mixed Mode guarantees, and why it belongs on every file you register from here on.
